5.34 GENERAL RECOMMENDATIONS
5.34.1  Besides the specific recommendations made on the clauses of the Bill in the
preceding paragraphs, the Committees also makes some general observations and
recommendations in the following paragraphs.
5.35 Compensation to the Victim of acid attack
5.35.1  The Committee is of the view that in case the convict is not in a position to pay
fine to the victim, both the Government of India and State Governments should take steps
to rescue the victim. In this regard, the Committee is given to understand that the issue
is already under consideration of the Ministry and Women and Child Development. The
Central Government, through the Ministry of Women and Child Development may evolve
a scheme to ensure that the compensation amount is taken care of and given to the victim.
Moreover, the Committee feels that the treatment of victim cannot wait till the final
disposal of the case. The Government should take necessary steps to ensure medical
treatment of victim.
5.36 Better Policing System
5.36.1  The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Home Affairs should impress
upon the State Governments to set up women cells compulsorily in all the police stations
throughout the country so that victim woman could be able to have free and easy access
to lodge complaints against the perpetrators. Women cell in each police station would

48
further enhance the participation of women in the policing system. The Committee also
took note of the fact that women police in over all police strength in the country is only
about 6% which is very inadequate. The Committee is of the view that the strength of the
women police force should be at least be 33 per cent of total strength, and therefore
recommends that Union Ministry of Home Affairs may impress upon the State Governments
to take suitable measures in this regard.
5.36.2  The Committee feels that registration of FIRs should be made mandatory. The
Committee is of the strong view that strict action should be taken for dereliction of duty
against the officer, who refuses to receive complaints on Sexual violence. The Committee
also recommends that once the FIR is lodged, it must be passed on to the higher police
officer for information and necessary direction in the matter to ensure time bound
investigation. The Committee further recommends that investigation should be done within
a period of 60 days, and charge sheet should be filed in time so that justice is not denied.
5.36.3  The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry of Home Affairs may impress
upon the State/ UT Governments to make suitable arrangements for installation and
enforcement of Global Positioning System (GPS) along with tracking system in police
vehicles and Surveillance Cameras at all strategic locations. The GPS and tracking system
would not only enhance the functional and operational efficiency of the Police but would
also inject transparency in the system besides smooth and easy tracking of crimes in the
country.
5.37 Better portrayal of woman
5.37.1  The Committee is concerned about increasing commodification of women in the
society. Women are portrayed in poor light through obscene, vulgar pictures/scenes. It is in
this context that the Committee feels that the content of entertainment programmes should
be without obscenity, vulgarity and violence, which is also in the interest of a healthy, moral
and ethical well being of the Society.
5.37.2  The Committee would appreciate if air-time on different channels of electronic
media is allocated for programmes for sensitization of viewers about cultural and human
values, traditions and customs and also portraying woman in high esteem. Programmes on
family values, respect for women culture and traditions can go a long way in strengthening
the moral fabric of the society. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Home
Affairs may take up the matter with the Ministry of Information & Broadcasting to address
the issue with all concerned stakeholders and issue necessary guidelines in this regard.
5.38 Judicial Reforms
5.38.1  The Committee is of the view that our judiciary is woefully short of infrastructure
which results in huge pendency of cases. There are a number of instances where cases come
for first hearing in the courts after years of wait. Such long delays shake the faith of
citizens in the system and breeds cynicism and hopelessness. The age old saying that justice
delayed is justice denied is particularly true for women victims of sexual assault who have
to face day-to-day trauma of re-living the painful experience for years during the trial.
5.38.2 It is in this light that establishment of fast track courts for speedy trial of sexual
assault cases becomes extremely important. The Committee recommends that adequate
funds should be dedicated for the establishment of fast track courts so that trials can take
place on a day-to-day basis. Government may consider setting up of fast-track courts in
every district wherever the pendency is very high. The Committee would like to impress

49
upon the Department of Justice to take up the matter with the Chief Justice of India and
Chief Justices of High Courts on the need of speedy trial of cases. The Judiciary must take
steps to see that the trial is completed within two months of filing of the charge-sheet.
5.38.3  The Committee was informed that in the light of the recent incident of gang rape
of a young women in the national capital, the Minister of Law and Justice has written to
the Chief Ministers of all States and Chief Justices of all High Courts to set up Fast Track
Courts for concluding trial in rape cases. The Committee recommends that the decision of
the Government to create 10% additional position of judges for creation of permanent fast
track courts, as directed by the Supreme Court in its judgment given in the case of Brij
Mohan Lal and others versus  Union of India and others given on 19.04.2012 may be
implemented.
5.38.4  The Committee was also informed that Rs. 5000 crores have been given as grants
to the States for the years 2010 to 2015 in order to undertake various initiatives such as
increasing court working hours, enhancing support to lok Adalats and providing additional
funds to State Legal Service Authorities etc. The Committee feels that the amount of
Rs. 5000 crores for five years is not sufficient for the purpose in view of the huge pendency
of cases in courts. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the amount of Rs. 5000
crores may be enhanced to Rs.10,000 crores. The Committee is of the view that more such
initiatives are required for providing sufficient infrastructure for the existing and the new
courts and for appointment of judges and recruitment of administrative staff.
5.39 Moral Education
5.39.1  The Committee is of the opinion that school curriculum plays an important role in
early socialization of children. A healthy school curriculum can lay foundation for an all
round development of adult personality. Several psychological studies indicate that values
imparted by agencies of early socialization such as schools and parents have life long impact
on the individual.
5.39.2  The Committee, therefore, feels that school curriculum should include values which
encourage children to respect their fellow human being specially women, poor and the
needy. School curriculum should reflect the best elements of our age old cultural values,
customs, traditions along with universal human values. The Committee recommends that
the Government may take necessary steps for promoting Gender sensitization among
teachers, parents and children so that gender bias may be removed. The Government should
also ensure that enough emphasis is laid on removing gender bias, strengthening family
system and inculcating moral and family values while preparing text books and modules
teacher training.
5.40 Ragging
5.40.1 The practice of ragging in educational institutions in the country is on the rise. Every
year several cases are reported in the media wherein innocent young students are subjected
to immense physical and psychological trauma which leaves deep scars on the psyche of the
students for the rest of their lives.
5.40.2 Though the act of ragging often starts with bullying of freshers by the seniors, at
times, it acquires sexual overtones causing deep embarrassment to students of both the
sexes, even leading to the extreme step of committing suicide. The Committee is of the
opinion that limiting punishment for ragging to rustication and other disciplinary acts by
educational institutions will not be enough to obliterate this menace. Therefore, it should

50
be made a cognizable offence with punishment attracting provisions Criminal Law,
particularly for the instances where ragging takes the overtones of sexual harassment/
assault.
5.41 Responsibility of Higher Officers
5.41.1 In case the crime committed by the subordinate is in the knowledge of the higher
officer and he does not take timely action, such superior officer should be held responsible
and omission of such acts on the part of superior officer must be recorded in his official
dossiers/ACR.
5.42 Repeat Offenders
5.42.1 The Committee has been given to understand that in our country, there is no system
of keeping a watch on repeat sex offenders. The Committee has also been given to
understand that, according to a study conducted on the sex offenders, majority of the
offenders had committed a sex crime earlier and escaped notice of the police authorities and
were roaming freely. The Committee has also been given to understand that Western
European countries and the US have developed a mechanism for tracking such type of sex
offenders and are maintaining a data base in this regard. The Committee recommends that
a suitable mechanism may be evolved to keep a watch on habitual and repeat sex offenders.
The Committee also recommends that after the conviction on first offence, the names of
the convicted persons should be publicized for information of the public. The Central Crime
Records Bureau should include the data in their records. The State and UT Governments
also should set up crime records bureaus and the data, including the names of convicted
people must be maintained and updated, from time to time.

51
NOTE OF DISSENT ON THE 167 th REPORT OF THE DRPS COMMITTEE ON
HOME AFFAIRS ON THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT BILL, 2012, GIVEN
BY SHRI D. RAJA, MEMBER, RAJYA SABHA AND SHRI PRASANTA
CHATTERJEE, MEMBER, RAJYA SABHA
We express our dissatisfaction with the way it the Verma Committee recommendations have
been diluted and we express the opinion that the Committee should recommend to the Government
to include those recommendations before placing the Bill in Parliament.
As far as the present Bill is concerned
1. Clause 5 adopts a gender neutral definition of sexual assault as has been done in Section
8 of the Ordinance. This is totally unacceptable, unjust and trivializes the large increase in the
number of rapes by men. This clause is against the recommendation of the Verma Committee
which had suggested that the perpetrator of the Crime should be defined as a man. The clause is
also against the earlier proposed Government Bill in 2010 which rightly made the law gender
specific as far as adults were concerned and the accused persons could only be men while the
complainants/victims were women.
2. The definition of rape in the Verma Committee report should be the definition used in the
Bill. The present Clause 5.24 dealing with Sec 375 of the IPC accepts the flawed definition. We
disagree with this.
3. Both the Ordinance and the Standing Committee exempt marital rape from being considered
a crime under Section 375 of the Indian Penal Code. This is contrary to the provisions of the
Indian Constitution which considers all women as equal human beings who have a right to live with
dignity and free from violence within and outside marriage. This is also contrary to the Verma
Committee report which had pointed out that the “exemption for marital rape stems from a long
outdated notion of marriage which regarded wives as no more than the property of their
husbands”……. “whereas marriage is in modern times regarded as a partnership of equals”.
4. Clause 5 raises the age of consent from 16 to 18 years in cases of sexual assault under
Section 375 IPC. However, the social reality is that there are many instances of consensual sexual
activity between adolescents between the ages of 16 and 18 and it would lead to injustice if in
these cases there was prosecution for rape. The Law Commission in its 205
th report has made a
recommendation which may form the basis of this amendment we suggest. By way of a proviso
to clause ‘sixthly’ to Section 375 IPC to exempt such consensual activity from the purview of
statutory rape provided the accused person is not more than 5 years older.
5. While the proposed Government Bill of 2010 had added that if rape is committed by a
person in a position of social, economic and political dominance this would be considered an
aggravated form of the offence, the Ordinance (3 of 2013) removes the word ‘political’ from this
definition. The Standing Committee has also agreed with this change in definition. We totally
disagree with the word “political” being deleted. The word ‘political’ should be added to Section
376 Clause (j) as this was meant to address rape which is often committed with impunity on the
most vulnerable sections of women in our society. Several instances of these forms of rape by
those in positions of political power have been highlighted in the past few years.
6. The Standing Committee echoes the Ordinance in making sexual assault on a legally
separated wife under Section 376B IPC punishable with a minimum imprisonment of two years and
51

52
a maximum of seven years. We completely disagree with this and see no reason why sexual assault
on any separated wife should be punishable with less imprisonment and should not be considered
as ordinary sexual assault.
7. In Clause 4A, the Standing Committee does not suggest any amendment of Section 354 of
the IPC that deals with non-penetrative sexual assault but only suggests enhancement of the
punishment. The wording of Section 354 which states that assault or use of criminal force to any
woman “intending to ……outrage her modesty” is archaic and inappropriate and should be changed
according to the suggestion of the Verma Committee.
8. The Verma Committee had suggested that the definition of sexual assault in Section 354 of
the Indian Penal Code should be replaced by the following words:
“(a) Intentional touching of another person when such act of touching is of a sexual nature and
is without the recipient’s consent.
 (b) Using words, acts or gestures towards or in the presence of another person which create an
unwelcome threat of a sexual nature or result in an unwelcome advance.
Explanation: For the purposes of this section, ‘acts’ shall include the display and dissemination of
pornographic material…..”
It had prescribed a punishment of imprisonment upto 5 years for the offence under the
suggested sub-clause (a) and upto 1 year for the offence under sub-clause (b). Since this clause
also replaced Section 509 of the IPC the Verma Committee had suggested repeal of Section 509
of the IPC. However, though Clause 4A in Section 354A defines Sexual Harassment it still retains
Section 509 IPC which again uses archaic language which is insulting to women. We object to this.
9. In Clause 2, the Standing Committee had suggested that in Section 166 A if a public servant
‘knowingly’ disobeys any direction of law he should be punished with rigorous imprisonment for
a term which may extend to one year. The term of rigorous imprisonment should extend to two
years and a minimum should be fixed. The word ‘knowingly’ should be deleted as lack of
knowledge of law cannot be allowed to be a defence and will always be used as a convenient
defence in these cases.
10. At present under Section 160 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, no woman or person
above 65 years of age or a male person below 15 years of age is required to attend at a Police
station and should be questioned in their residence. Though it had been suggested that the age of
the male person should be increased to 18 years the standing Committee in Clause 8 has not
accepted this. Anyone upto 18 years should ordinarily be questioned at his residence.
11. In point 5.47 on responsibility of higher official, the Committee report only recommends a
recording in his official Dossier – ACR. We disagree with this. The Higher officer must be held
responsible and also punished for this.
12. Death Penalty: Since there are many issues which have been raised about Death Penalty, it
is not necessary to include this in the present Bill.
13. Section 376 (2)
• Being a man, commits rape on a person in the course of communal or sectarian violence;
• Being a man, who is not a member of a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe, commits
rape on a person belonging to a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, knowing that the
person is a member of the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribes;
14. On Trafficking: Government must consider to bring a Comprehensive Bill in human
trafficking which is a process leading to commercial sexual exploitation and labour exploitation.

proper procedures in handling, recording and filing complaints; provision of adequate safety
measures and amenities in all public transport vehicles with security guard, GPS and CCTVs;
a public emergency response system with one central ER No. and medico-legal guidelines to
perform a medical examination of a victim of sexual assault, etc. The Additional Secretary also
stated that such recommendations had been referred to the concerned Ministries for actions.
5.1 As regards the recommendations regarding amendments to Criminal Law, the Additional
Secretary informed that Justice Verma Committee had agreed to most of the provisions of the
Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2012 and there was a broad convergence between the provisions
in Bill and recommendations of Justice Verma Committee.
5.2 He mentioned that in addition to the provisions in the Bill, Justice Verma Committee had
recommended certain other things such as Right to private defence of body, sexual harassment,
disrobing of a woman, voyeurism, stalking, etc., which have been accepted and incorporated in the
Ordinance. Regarding punishment for a public servant for knowingly disobeying any direction of
law, Justice Verma Committee recommended for five years, but the Government had agreed to one
year by keeping the provision of the Bill intact.
5.3 Regarding compensation to the victim of acid attack under section 326 of IPC, Justice
Verma Committee recommended that the compensation should be adequate to meet, at least, the
medical expenses incurred by the victim. However, the Government considered that the fine of
Rs.10 lakhs was better and adequate and accordingly retained the same. Clarifying the issue
whether compensation would be from the State or from the perpetrator, in case the accused does
not have the means to pay the fine or the compensation, the representatives of the Ministry
submitted that under Section 357A of Cr.P.C. victim compensation is provided and ‘to the extent
possible’, the Government will do it under compensation scheme. The perpetrator will undergo
additional punishment or imprisonment in case he fails to pay the compensation. The Committee
was not convinced and felt that the expression ‘to the extent possible’ was a very vague term
which should be omitted and Centre and the State Governments must together come to the rescue
and rehabilitation of victim and ensure compensation. The Chairman also observed that the States
also do not have adequate resources. Therefore, the Central Government must evolve a scheme to
compensate the States to share the financial burden. Clarifying the issue of compensation in case
of attempt to throw acid, the additional Secretary maintained that since there would not be any
injury and medical expenses in that case, the recommendation of Justice Verma Committee in this
regard was redundant.
5.4 With regard to Section 354 of IPC, the legislative Secretary submitted that the Verma
Committee wanted it to be replaced with an offence of sexual assault and punishment for sexual
assault. After examining the Verma Committee Report, the original Section 354 has been retained
but with increased inprisonment from one year to five years. In addition, new offences, which
were recommended by the Verma Committee with regard to sexual harassment, voyeurism, stalking
and disrobing of women, have been created on the basis of recommendation of Verma Committee,
which were earlier not there in the Bill.
5.5 Commenting on Section 370 of IPC, the Legislative Secretary submitted that it existed
since 1860 and was very restrictive in nature dealing with buying or disposing of any person as
a slave. The new proposal sought to substitute it with new Sections 370 and 370A to deal with
trafficking of persons including the slavery as well as making it gender neutral. The chairman
observed that exploitation should include sexual exploitation only and other aspects should be
taken care of separately. However the Joint Secretary, MHA informed that it was actually
universal definition of ‘human trafficking’ and the country is a signatory to the U.N. Convention
on Organised Crime.

71
5.6 A new offence under Section 370A for employing a trafficked person has been added in
the Ordinance on the basis of the recommendation of the Verma Committee. The Chairman
however observed that such provisions could be misused in the rural areas, where farmers hire
people. If somebody files a complaint, they would be arrested. Therefore ‘trafficking’ should mean
trafficking for sexual purpose. Another member also opined that this could also be against those
people across the country who employ domestic helpers. Another Member opined that it includes
bonded labour which deserved a specific law by itself. The Joint Secretary, MHA submitted that
trafficking was a large scale phenomenon happening in the country in all types. He cited practices
in Haryana where the brides were being imported at a particular cost. The Additional Secretary
stated that the concern of the Committee was noted and assured to re-examine it.
5.7 The Legislative Secretary informed that the Verma Committee wanted to retain the offence
of rape under 375. However the Legislative Department thought to make the offence of rape as
gender neutral with the word ‘sexual assault’ to make it wider and including the offence of rape
also. One Member of the Committee questioned the intention of making the offences gender neutral
in view of the increasing atrocities and violence against women in the country.  However, other
Members reacted to this and opined that it should be gender neutral as it covers wider ambit of
the entire issue. The Legislative Secretary clarified that the Government has created two types of
offences. One is sexual harassment which is of a lower level. However, the other one, sexual
assault, is a substitute for the existing rape, is a serious offence.
5.8 Regarding Sections 375, 376, 376A, 376B, 376C, 376D and 376E of IPC, the Legislative
Secretary informed that the offences had been made gender neutral and in two Sections 376A and
376E which deal with death penalty in case the action of accused leads to death or vegetative state
of the victim or in the case of repeat offenders, though Verma Committee did not recommend. The
Verma Committee also had not made any recommendation on Section 376B dealing with sexual
assault by husband upon his wife during separation.
5.9 Under  Section 509 of IPC dealing  with modesty of a woman,  the punishment has been
increased from one year to three years and also with fine. The Committee wanted to know the
experience of Delhi Police and safeguards against misuse of this Section as well as reasons for
retaining it when Justice Verma Committee has recommended for its repeal. Responding to the
queries, the Additional Secretary submitted that the Government has retained as a deterrent against
increasing eve teasing and the offence has been made cognizable to have zero tolerance society
with respect to crime against women; and this is the starting point of all crimes against women.
The Committee opined that ragging was also needed to be brought under it as inhuman things,
including sexual assault, removal of clothes and then walking naked were being done under it. It
sometimes led to suicide and murder.
6.0 Regarding amendments of Section 54A of Criminal Procedure Code, The Legislative
Secretary pointed out that existing Section 54A of Cr.PC was being modified to take care of
procedural aspect to make it more convenient for identification of the person. The Chairman of the
Committee suggested that the videography, should be mandatory.
6.1 With regard to proviso to Sections 154 and 161 of Cr.P.C., the  Legislative Secretary stated
that the Verma Committee has also made a similar recommendation. The Committee desired that the
words “as far as possible” may be deleted and recording of the statement could be entrusted  to
a woman Government officer in the absence of a woman police officer.
6.2 Section 160 Cr.P.C. provide certain protection to the physically disabled person or persons
who are below the age of 18 years or above the age of 65 years or women to see  that those
people are not summoned unnecessarily. The Chairman observed that the upper age of 65 years
should be reconsidered. He also felt that the age of juvenile should also be revisited.

72
6.3 The Section 164 of Cr.P.C. deals with recording of the confessions and the statements. A
new sub-section is being added for recording of the statement of the person against whom such
offence has been committed as soon as the commission of the offence is brought to the notice
of the police. The Legislative Secretary further stated that if the victim is disabled, then the
assistance of an interpreter or a special educator is to be provided when the statement is recorded
and the same may be videographed. The Committee felt that the videography should be mandatory.
6.4 With regard to Sections 198B and 273 and 327 of Cr. P.C. and  Section 53A  of the
Evidence Act, the Committee agreed to the provisions made there under. Regarding Section 119 of
the Evidence Act, the Committee felt that videography should be made mandatory.
7.0 The Chairman also asked the representatives to furnish information on the issues not
respond orally in the meeting.
8.0 A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept.

3. The Chairman welcomed the witnesses and asked the Home Secretary to respond to the
issues/queries raised by the Members of the Committee during the last sitting.
4. On the issue pertaining to trafficking, the Home Secretary expressed agreement with the
view of the Committee that the Bill should limit itself to sexual aspects or sexual violence and not
tread into areas which could be covered by other Acts. On the issues of compensation to be given
to the victims, he informed that the Central Government was urging all the State Governments to
bring schemes for compensation under the relevant provisions of the law. However on the point
of payment of compensation to victim by Government in case of inability of the convict to pay
fine,  he stated that the Government would not be able to agree because if Government accepts
this, then it would have to be applicable to all IPC crimes and the State cannot afford. Using the
taxpayers’ money for compensating crimes committed by a particular person would not be
sustainable. The Chairman, however, was not convinced and mentioned that the Committee would
make its recommendation in this regard after discussing among Members.
5. With regard to use of word ‘intercourse’ under Section 376B of IPC as it could give a
wrong signal, the Home Secretary clarified that the words ‘sexual assault’ had not been used
because after  inducing or seducing, the consent had been obtained and if it amounts to sexual
assault, then this section will not apply.
6. Regarding section 509 of IPC which related to insult to the modesty of a woman, the
Chairman enquired about the safeguards against the misuse of this Section and the experience of
Delhi Police. The representative of Delhi Police informed that under section 509, 229 cases in 2011
and 236 cases in 2012 were registered. In the year 2013, in the first month only, Delhi Police had
registered 306 cases as more women were coming forward. He further submitted that under this
section, the chargesheet is filed on the basis of the statements of the girl and sometimes, it
becomes difficult because a complaint may be with some ulterior motive also. The Home Secretary

75
submitted that eve teasing was the most common problem and most girls try to swallow it. As it
was a non-cognizable offence with simple imprisonment of one year and if the case was forwarded
to the Magistrate, he may or may not take action or may take years to decide the case. In that
circumstance, the boy might be back on the roads doing the same thing again, exposing the girl,
to more hazards. The Government therefore was proposing to make the offence cognizable with
enhanced punishment to three years. Commenting on the possibility of the provision being misused,
the Home Secretary clarified  that kind of probability was not so much because before the Courts,
mens rea  is an essential element to a crime which has to be established. Regarding necessity of
having Section 509 when Section 354A covers “unwelcome and explicit sexual overtures” and
“non-verbal conduct of sexual nature” under it, the Committee observed that while Section 354A
straightaway deals with sexual harassment in gender neutral way, whereas Section 509 deals with
most common offences being committed on the streets, in schools, colleges.
7. With regard to amendments in Cr.P.C., the Home Secretary agreed to the suggestion of the
Committee and informed that Government was planning to do away with the words ‘as far as
possible’ and putting the words ‘should be recorded by a woman police officer, or, if the woman
police officer is not present, by any other woman officer.’
8. Regarding proposed exemption of attendance to a male witness of under 18years in Section
160 of Cr.P.C., the Home Secretary submitted that the Government had no objection in retaining
the original provision of 15 years.
9. With regard to Section 53A of the Evidence Act, the Chairman, while taking note of the
legal status of prostitution, asked about the remedy available in case a prostitute files a complaint
after changing her mind. The Home Secretary admitted that this kind of hazard was there, and,
it would always be there in all cases of sexual relations.  Responding to a query regarding changing
of mind by lady due to non fulfilling of promise after living together for years or for a considerable
time, the Home Secretary opined that in such case, sexual assault may not be made out but a case
of breach of promise could be made out because for making out a case of sexual assault, she
would have to prove that there was no consent. When the chairman drew attention to the fact that
Consents were not given in writing, the Home Secretary admitted existence of grave hazard in this
regard.
10. With regard to sexual harassment during ragging, the Home Secretary submitted that ragging
would come under section 509 and it could not be any excuse to exempt any person. A crime will
be a crime, whether it is in the course of ragging or whatever. On being pointed out that the
Section 509 was woman specific and what about safeguards available to boys, the representative
of Delhi Police drew attention of the Committee to the gender neutrality of Section 354A. However,
the Home Secretary differed and stated that Ragging was not covered in the Section as requirement
of sexual undertone must be there.
11. Responding to the concerns of the Members regarding Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act,
the Home Secretary clarified that the Act gave no protection to any member of the Armed Forces
if he or she commits a sexual offence. The Act provided for requirement of sanction only in case
of acts done or purported to be done in the course of discharge of their duties. Sexual offences
cannot be in the course of discharge of duty and there was unnecessary controversy by saying
that Armed Forces had been left out. He further mentioned that not in a single case, the court had
asked for sanction under Section 197 or Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act, 1958 in case of
sexual offence. Responding further to the Chairman’s observation regarding non registration of FIR
in such cases, the Home Secretary stated that non-registration of FIR was another problem which
happens, not only in sexual offences but also in other offences because of  the normal tendency
of the officer-in-charge to avoid registration of FIRs to keep the crime graph low. But, in case
of sexual assault, if FIR is not registered, that police officer will be liable to criminal action. With

76
regard to issue concerning court martial, the Home Secretary submitted that the Army had an
option for trial and if the Army conducts a court martial, it will have to tell the same to the court.
However, with regard to trial of sexual offence in normal courts under the IPC or under the court
martial in the military courts, he assured to revert back on this issue.
12. On the issue of reducing the juvenile age from 18 to 16 in view of their involvement in
heinous crimes and need for differentiation in this regard, the Home Secretary opined that  a boy
of 16 years could be like an adult and commit as heinous crime as anybody could do. The
Legislative Secretary submitted that it was possible to reduce the age of juveniles under the existing
law, but a policy decision in this regard had to be taken. In some other countries like UK, the age
group between 15 and 18 is treated differently, in case they commit heinous crimes, then they are
tried by the normal courts, not by the juvenile courts.  In spite of the International Convention that
the age of the juvenile should be 18 years, these laws have been amended keeping in view the
crimes being committed by persons in the age group of 15 to 18 years.

of the Committee. The Home Secretary assured to consider those suggestions.

2.0 At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members to the sitting of the Committee and
apprised them the agenda of the day i.e., clause-by-clause consideration of the Criminal Law
(Amendment) Bill, 2012.
{At this stage witnesses were called in}
2.1  The Chairman welcomed the Home Secretary and Legislative Secretary and representatives of
Department of Legal Affairs to the sitting of the Committee and asked the Home Secretary to give
replies on the issues raised by members  during the last meeting before  taking  up clause-by-clause
consideration of the Bill.
2.2   The Chairman, then, clarified that except Sections 100 and 370 of Indian Penal Code all other
Clauses of the Bill were to be amended as per Ordinance, therefore, the Committee should take
into account the provisions of the Ordinance and recommendations of Verma Committee Report,
if required. The Chairman asked the Home Secretary about the fate of the Bill and introduction of
a Bill replacing Ordinance.
2.3 Responding to the Chairman’s query Home Secretary informed that Government will
withdraw the present Bill and it has drafted a Bill replacing an Ordinance which would be
introduced in Parliament as soon as possible, however, Government would try to  incorporate most
of the suggestions given by the committee. The Chairman suggested that the Government should
wait for the Committee report on Bill. The Home Secretary assured that he will discuss the matter
with Home Minister.
3.0 The Committee, thereafter, took up the existing provisions for  consideration in the light of
the provisions of the Ordinance promulgated by the Government and Verma Committee Report.
3.1 Section 100 of IPC
3.1.1 The Committee took up the amendment to Section 100 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC),
which is provided in the Ordinance and not there in the Bill. The Home Secretary informed the
Committee that they had discussed with the Ministry of law and came with a slightly better
formulation, which reads as under:
“After sixthly, the following shall be inserted:
An act of throwing or administering acid, which may reasonably call apprehension that
grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such act.”

79
3.1.1 The Committee decided to go ahead with the new formulation of the Ministry.
3.2 Section 166 of IPC
3.2.1 The Committee took up amendment to Section 166 A of the IPC. The Chairman informed
the Committee that the Committee may accept the Section 166A as provided in the Ordinance,
however, he suggested that the imprisonment may be made rigorous.
3.3 Section 326A of IPC
3.3.1 Section 326A deals with voluntarily causing grievous hurt by use of acid, etc. A Member
suggested that the fine imposed under this section shall be given to the person on whom the acid
was thrown or to whom the acid was administered i.e. the fine money has to be used for treatment
of the victim. The Committee accepted the provision of Ordinance.
3.4 Section 326B of IPC
3.4.1 In Section 326B, some Members suggested that instead of the words ‘attempts to
administer’, there should be the words ‘administers or attempts to administer’. The Home
Secretary agreed with the view of the Members.
3.5 Section 354B of IPC
3.5.1 Section 354B provides punishment of imprisonment of not less than three years, extend-
able up to seven years. Some Members felt that this punishment is insufficient and should be
increased. They also suggested that it could be made life imprisonment. The Committee, however,
decided to increase it to five years extendable upto ten years. The Committee also felt that the
victim has to be a woman and the perpetrator can be anybody. Some Members felt that in certain
occasions there may be crowd which cheers and applaud the disrobing of a woman publicly, and
in such cases, entire crowd should be held responsible. The Committee, however, felt that only
those participating in the act can be held liable and holding the entire crowd watching could be
stretching too far.
3.6 Section 354C of IPC
3.6.1 Regarding Section 354C, which provides for voyeurism, some Members felt that the
punishment of one year for the first offence is not sufficient; it should be increased.  The
Committee, however, felt that it is already one year to three years for first offence and three to
seven years for second offence,  therefore, it will not be appropriate to increase the punishment
for the first offence.  Some Members again raised the issue of making accused or perpetrator
gender specific.  The Committee, however, decided to go with the present proposition as provided
in the Bill and Ordinance.
3.7 Section 354D of IPC
3.7.1 While discussing about Section 354D, some Members expressed doubts regarding the words
‘watches’ or ‘spies’ on a person and their implication. It was felt that though the word ‘spies’ on
a person can be understood but the word ‘watches’ may have wider ramification. On being asked
the Home Secretary clarified that watching has to be designed and it must result in a fear of
violence or serious alarm or distress in mind of such person or interferes with the mental peace
of the person. The Committee, however, felt that Home Secretary should discuss the issue with
Law Ministry and take a view in the matter.

80
3.8 Sections 370 and 370A of IPC
3.8.1 While discussing about trafficking in Section 370 and Section 370A, some Members
expressed the doubt about the use of the words ‘forced labour’ or ‘services’ in the present law.
It was felt that since the law specifically belonged to criminal assault, all provisions relating to
labour, forced labour, etc., should appropriately be dealt in different laws. The Home Secretary
agreed with the view of the Committee.
3.9 Section 375 of IPC
3.9.1    While discussing about Section 375, some Members felt that the word ‘rape’ should also
be kept within the scope of sexual assault. The Home Secretary clarified that there is a change
of terminology and the offence of ‘rape’ has been made wider. Some Members also suggested that
somewhere there should be some room for wife to take up the issue of marital rape. It was also
felt that no woman takes marriage so simple that she will just go and complain blindly. Consent
in marriage cannot be treated as consent forever. Several Members of the Committee, however, felt
that the marital rape has the potential of destroying the institution of marriage. The Committee felt
that if a woman is aggrieved by the acts of her husband, there are other remedies of approaching
the court. In India, for ages, the family system has evolved and it is moving forward. The
institution of family is able to resolve the problems. It was, therefore, felt that if the marital rape
is brought under the law, the entire family system will be under great stress and the Committee
may perhaps be doing more injustice.
3.9.2 Some Members also suggested that the age mentioned in the exception to the Section may
be raised to 18 years from 16 years. The exception provides that sexual intercourse or sexual acts
by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under 16 years of age, is not sexual assault. The
Home Secretary, responding to this suggestion, stated that by doing so by one stroke, thousands
of marriages in different States would be outlawed.
3.10 Section 376 of IPC
3.10.1   While discussing Section 376, the Committee felt that in sub-Section (1) of Section 376,
the liability of the accused to pay compensation to the victim, which shall be adequate to meet at
least medical expenses incurred by the victim should also be included. The Committee, accordingly,
decided to add this in sub-Section (1) of Section 376. Some Members also mentioned that the State
needs to take care of the medical expenditure, treatment, etc. of the victim.
3.10.2 In Sub-Section 2 of Section 376, the Chairman brought to the notice of the Home Secretary
that in item (1) of sub-Section 2 of Section 376, the word ‘political’ has been deleted in the
Ordinance whereas it is there in the Bill. The Committee decided to accept the version of the Bill.
One Member felt that there should be a clause providing for punishment when a person has a
medical condition that can be transmitted through sexual intercourse and that person knowingly
commits such intercourse without use of protection devices and that act should also be brought
under aggravated crime. The Home Secretary stated that Section 270 of the IPC provides for
punishment for this though it is slightly less. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that
punishment under Section 270 may be increased suitably.
Section 376 A
3.10.3 While discussing Section 376A, some Members felt that the Government will have to take
a decision regarding death penalty. It was stated that several countries have abolished the death
penalty whereas India is still continuing with it. However, the majority of the Members felt that
the issue of abolishing death penalty is totally a different matter and needs to be discussed and

81
decided separately. The Committee took note of the fact that the death penalty being proposed
under Section 376A is only in the extreme case where the victim has died or goes in a vegetative
state and under Section 376E in the case of a repeat offender. Accordingly, majority of the
Members agreed to the view of accepting present provision for death.
Section 376B
3.10.4 The Committee, then took up Section 376B i.e. Sexual assault by husband upon his wife
during separation and Section 376C relating to Sexual intercourse by a person in authority for
discussion and agreed with the provisions of the Ordinance.
3.10.4 While taking up Section 376D relating to Sexual assault by gang, where, the punishment
is the imprisonment for life thereby meaning imprisonment for the remainder of that person’s
natural life, the Chairman of the Committee sought to know the reason for variation in
provision for punishment in Section 376A  where there is provision for death penalty and 376D
where punishment for imprisonment for life for the offence of sexual assault by one or more
persons. Responding to that the Home Secretary stated that for sexual assault by gang not
causing death the punishment has been kept for imprisonment for the remainder of that
person’s natural life.
3.11 Section 509 of IPC
3.11.1 The Committee then took up Section 509 for discussion. The Bill originally provides for a
fine of Rs.1,000/- besides simple imprisonment for a term up to three years but the Ordinance does
not contain the amount of fine. The Committee, however, decided that the amount should be
included in the provision and it should be increased to Rs. 2,000/-.
3.12 Section 54A of Cr.P.C.
3.12.1    The Committee then took up Section 54A of the Cr.P.C. This provision is in the
Ordinance whereas the Bill does not contain this. The Section, originally, as in the Ordinance,
provides that if a person identifying the person, arrested, is mentally or physically disabled, the
identification process may be videographed. The Committee felt that the word ‘may’ should be
changed to ‘shall’ and decided to make recommendation accordingly.
3.13 Section 154 of Cr.P.C.
3.13.1 Some Members felt that the use of words ‘as far as possible’ should not be there because
whenever a statement is taken from a woman, a woman officer should always be there. The
Committee, accordingly, decided to delete the words ‘as far as possible’. The Committee also felt
that whenever a woman police officer is not available, any woman Government officer could be
made available to record the statement. Similarly, in Clause (b) of the Second Proviso, the words
‘may be recorded’ may be changed to ‘shall be recorded’.
3.14 Section 160 Cr.P.C.
3.14.1 In this clause, Section 160 of the Cr.P.C. is proposed to be amended by providing that no
male person under the age of 18 years and above the age of 65 years or a woman shall be required
to give personal attendance. As of now, a male person below 15 years and a woman is not required
to give attendance to a police man. The Ordinance includes physically or mentally disabled person
also. The Committee also feels that the words ‘fifteen years’ as prescribed in the proviso of the
Section 160 of Cr.P.C. may be retained.

82
3.15 Section 161 Cr.P.C.
3.15.1 Section 161 of Cr.P.C. regarding the statement by a woman about alleged offence under
Sections 354, 375, 376, 376A, 376B and 509 shall be recorded as far as possible by a woman
officer. The proviso in the Bill and the Ordinance also contain the words ‘as far as possible’. The
Committee felt that the words ‘as far as possible’ may be omitted and the words ‘or in her absence
other woman Government officer’ may be added at the end.
3.16 Section 164 Cr.P.C.
3.16.1 Section 164 Cr.P.C .  provides for recording of statement of the victim for crime committed
against victim under certain Sections of the IPC along with provisos.  The Ordinance has an
amendment to Section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code proposing that while recording of the
statement by a magistrate of temporarily, permanently physically, mentally disabled, the magistrate
shall take the assistance of an interpreter or a special educator in recording the statement.
3.17 Section 198 B Cr. P.C.
3.17.1  The Ordinance also provides for insertion of a new Section, viz., Section 198B which is
not there in the Bill. Section 376B of Indian Penal Code provides for making the offence for ‘sexual
assault by a husband upon his wife during separation’ as cognizable. The Home Secretary clarified
that the Verma Commission has recommended for doing away with it on the pretext that the same
punishment should apply here that applies to a stranger having sexual relationship. However, the
Government is not doing away that provision  but the cognizance of crime would be taken on the
complaint of wife, not on the complaint by a third person.
3.18 Section 273 of Cr.P.C.
3.18.1 The proposed Amendment seeks to insert a new proviso to Section 273 of Cr.P.C. so that
court would be required to make appropriate measures to ensure that a person below the age of
18 years and who is alleged to have been subjected to sexual assault etc. is not confronted by the
accused although the right of cross examination would still be there. The Committee accepted the
proposition.
3.19 Section 327 of Cr.P.C.
3.19.1 Section 327 of Cr.P.C.  says, “trial of sexual assault or offence under section 376 shall be
conducted in camera. ” The proposed Amendment seeks to amend Section 327 of Cr.P.C.
substituting the words, figures or letters “trial of rape or an offence under Sections 376, 376A,
376B, 376C and 376D of the Indian Penal Code”, by the words, figures or letters “trial of sexual
assault or an offence under Sections 354, 376A and 376B of the Indian penal Code”. However, the
Ordinance contains three additional Sections, viz., 376C, 376D and 376E of the IPC. The
Committee acceded to the amendment.
3.20 Section 53A of the Indian Evidence Act
3.20.1    The amendment seeks to insert new Section namely, Section 53A after Section 53 of
the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 regarding evidence of conduct or character of the victim or previous
sexual experience with any person. The Committee accepted the amendment.
3.21 Section 114A of the Indian Evidence Act
3.21.1   Section 114A of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 provides for presumption as to absence
of consent in certain prosecution for sexual assault. Ordinance includes additional Clause (m) and

83
has the words ‘such person’ in the place of the words ‘he or she’. The Home Secretary clarified
that it is an existing section which provides that where sexual intercourse by the accused is proved
and the question is whether it was without the consent of the one alleged to have been raped and
she states in her evidence before the court that she did not consent, the court shall presume that
she did not consent. It shifts the burden of proof on the accused, which is normally not there in
jurisprudence but the burden of proof shifts when the victim says that her consent was not there.
Her statement by itself is taken at its face value. The Government is proposing to replace the word
‘rape’ with the word ‘sexual assault’.
3.22 Section 119 of the Indian Evidence Act
3.22.1 The Ordinance provides for substitution of Section 119 of the Indian Evidence Act which
is not there in the Bill. This replacing Section deals with witness who is unable to communicate
verbally. The Ordinance contains the words ‘may be video graphed’ but the Committee felt that
it may changed to ‘shall be video graphed’.
3.23 Section 146 of the Indian Evidence Act
3.23.1 The Committee took note of the text of the new proviso, as drafted in the Ordinance which
includes consequential changes due to addition of new Sections in IPC connected with sexual
assault. The Home Secretary clarified that  where the question of consent is an issue, it shall not
be permissible to adduce evidence or to put questions in the cross-examination of the victim as
to his or her general immoral character, or as to his or her previous sexual experience with any
person for proving such consent or the quality of consent. The Committee sought to know way
out in case of false accusation to which the Home Secretary acceded to examine the issue in detail.
4.0 The Chairman, then, made general observations of the Committee which inter-alia  include:-
4.1 Government must make arrangements for recruitment of women force in police to facilitate
establishment of women cells in each police station of the country and the Union Ministry of Home
Affairs must impress upon the State Governments to take suitable measures to enhance the strength
of the women police force to the level of, at least, 33 per cent of total police strength.
4.2 The registration of FIRs should be made mandatory. Any dereliction of duty on the part of
any particular officer of not registering an FIR will be punishable. The Committee sought  that
once the FIR is lodged, it must be passed on to the higher police officer for information and
necessary direction in the matter ensuring time-bound investigation. The Committee further felt that
investigation should be completed within a period of 60 days.
4.3 The Government should make suitable arrangements for installation and enforcement of
Global Positioning System (GPS) in police vehicles and Surveillance Cameras at all strategic
locations. The GPS would not only enhance the functional and operational efficiency of the Police
but would also inject transparency in the system besides smooth and easy tracking of crimes in
the country.
4.4 There should be restriction upon the media showcasing women in poor light and effective
measures should be enforced to prohibit film industry from showing obscenity, vulgarity and
violence against women and pornography denigrating women folks.
4.5 Tragic events in the recent past and the continuing trend of crimes, especially rape and
gang rape have shaken the country making significant erosion of people’s faith due to delay in
investigation, prosecution, under-trial, making the people disappointed with the system. The
Committee, therefore, strongly felt that the time has come to undertake the process of introspection
and take up judicial reforms immediately. The Government must undertake policy and legislative

84
changes for re-engineering of procedure and court process. The Committee felt that there was an
urgent need to take steps towards strengthening judicial system for ensuring speedy justice for all
in the real spirit of democracy and the rule of law. The Committee viewed  that adequate
infrastructure development at subordinate as well as higher judiciary level with sufficient budgetary
provision is necessary for achieving the goal of pendency reduction.
4.6   The Committee, therefore, strongly opined  that Government must create special fast track
courts for handling cases of rape and gang rapes including domestic violence in all parts of the
country or at least one court in each district wherever there is the need.
4.7 The Committee also discussed the issue that the definition of juvenile accused has to be
revisited in view of the fact that in the recent past it has been reported that a number of crimes
are committed by the boys of the age between 16 and 18 years. However, consensus could not
emerge on the issue.
4.8 The Committee observed  that education system has far reaching and lasting impact on the
mindset of growing children and integration of social  and moral values imbibing Indian culture,
customs and traditions during the school life is necessary to establish ethical and moral
development coupled with deep regard for human values. The Committee, therefore, concluded
that the school curriculum and management, classroom atmosphere and overall education system
must aim at imbibing and integrating moral development with values of family system, respect for
women and preservation of life and peaceful environment amongst children.
4.9 Coming to compensation to victims of acid attack, the Committee was of the view that in
case the convict is not in a position to pay fine to the victim, both the Union Government and
the State Government should take steps to rescue the victim.
5.0 The Chairman directed the Secretariat to prepare draft Report on the Bill for consideration
and adoption at its next meeting on 26
th February 2013.
6.0 A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept.
7.0 The Committee then adjourned at 6.05

th, 166 th and 168 th Reports of the Committee and  invited Members to give this

3. The Committee, thereafter, took up the 167 th Report on Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill,
2012 for consideration and adoption. He informed that the Home Secretary had been invited to give
clarification, as and when required. He also mentioned that some women’s organisations
approached him and offered some suggestions and he would discuss those suggestions while taking

discussed various issues threadbare in the earlier meetings and would not take up fresh issue for
discussion.
[At this Stage, witnesses were called in]
3A. The Chairman welcomed the witnesses and asked the Home Secretary to respond on the
issue of making the perpetrator male only and constraints in accepting this proposition. The Home
Secretary responded that our culture was evolving on the lines of the Western culture and people
in authority, whether they are men or women, can misuse their position of authority. There had
been instances of this nature in the West but fortunately, the Government had not come across any
such instances in our country. Some Members felt that the law should be gender neutral as law
was made for posterity and there was no harm in keeping it gender neutral. After some discussion
the Committee finally concluded that perpetrator should be gender neutral.
4. The Committee therefore took up clause wise adoption of the Bill and then adoption of the
Report.
4.1 Clause 1A ( Section 100 of IPC)
(Insertion of new Clause in the Bill)
4.1.1 This Clause seeks to amend Section 100 of IPC which deals with the right of private
defence of the body. The Committee noted that the Ordinance contained an amendment to Section
100 of IPC whereas such an amendment was not there in the Bill, which was under consideration
of the Committee. The Home Secretary, clarified that they have got better formulation after
consulting the Law Ministry. The Committee agreed with the view point of the Home Secretary.
Accordingly, the following Clause was inserted in the Bill before Clause 2:–

87
“Clause 1A In the Indian Penal Code (hereafter in this Chapter referred to as the Penal
Code), in Section 100, after the clause sixthly, the following shall be inserted:
Seventhly- An act of throwing or administering acid which may reasonably cause
apprehension that grievous hurt will otherwise be the consequence of such act.”
4.1.2 The Clause 1A was inserted.
4.2 Clause 2 (Section 166A of IPC)
4.2.1 This clause seeks to insert a new section 166A in the Indian Penal Code regarding public
servant disobeying direction under law.
4.2.2 The Committee took note of addition of Clause (c) in the Ordinance which was missing in
the Bill and felt that the same may be added in the Bill. The Committee also felt that the provision
of simple imprisonment is not sufficient in view of the gravity of the crimes committed under
Sections 354, 354A, 354B, 354C, sub-Section (2) of Section 354D, Sections 376, 376A, 376B,
376C, 376D and 376E. The Committee, accordingly, recommended for the insertion of the word
“rigorous” punishment in the Section and crimes could also be made cognizable and non-bailable.
4.2.3 S ubject to the above recommendation, the Clause was adopted, as amended.
4.3 Clause 3 (Sections 326A and 326B of IPC)
4.3.1 This clause seeks to insert new Sections 326A and 326B to make acid attack or attempt
to throw acid specific offence. The Committee took note of the amendments made in these
Sections 326A and 326B in the Ordinance which widened the nature of the crime and also added
two explanations in Section 326B. The Committee agreed to the changes made in the Ordinance
and felt that the same may be incorporated in the Bill.
4.3.2 The Committee took note of unregulated sale of highly concentrated acid in open
market and recommended for its regulation to ensure its sale to the genuine end-users.
4.3.3 Subject to the above observation, the Clause was adopted, as amended.
4.4 Clause 4 (Section 354 IPC)
4.4.1 This clause seeks to amend section 354 to enhance the punishment for assault or criminal
force to women with intent to outrage her modesty.
4.4.2 The Committee recommended that the minimum fine of one thousand rupees should be
increased to five thousand rupees.
4.4.3 The Clause was adopted, as amended.
4.5 Clause 4A (Sections, i.e., 354A, 354B, 354C and 354D of IPC)
(Insertion of new clauses)
4.5.1 This new clause seeks to cover various aspects pertaining to sexual harassment and related
matters. The Committee noted that new Sections of  354A, 354B, 354C and 354D have been added
in the Ordinance in this regard.
4.5.2 Section 354A of the Ordinance provides for sexual harassment and punishment therefor.
Section 354B provides for assault or use of criminal force to woman with intent to disrobe her.
Sections 354C and 354D deal with voyeurism and stalking respectively.
4.5.3 W ith regard to the Section 354B, the Committee felt that the punishment is not sufficient
for the crime and should be increased to five years, extendable to ten years with fine. The

88
Committee recommended for incorporation of the above said Sections in the Bill accordingly on the
suggested lines.
4.5.4 The Clause was inserted.
4.6 Clause 4B (Sections 370 and 370A of IPC)
(Insertion of new Clause)
4.6.1 This new clause seeks to substitute Section 370 of IPC (buying or disposing of any person
as a slave) with Sections 370 and 370A to deal with trafficking of persons and employing them
for exploitation. These new Sections were provided in the Ordinance, which were not there in the
Bill and the Committee felt that they be incorporated in the Bill.
4.6.2 The Committee observed that labour-related issues had been included in both the Sections
370 and 370A of the Ordinance, which were equally important. The Committee felt that since this
law being exclusively for sexual assault and related issues, labour and other related issues should
be dealt in a separate law.  The Home Secretary during the discussion agreed with the view point
of the Committee and assured to look into the matter on these lines. The Committee recommended
that both Sections 370 and 370A may be relooked in the light of the above observations.
4.6.3 The Committee also noted that forced prostitution and induced prostitution should also be
brought under the ambit of the expression ‘exploitation’ and ‘sexual exploitation’. The Committee
recommended that the Ministry of Home Affairs may look into the matter and bring both forced
prostitution and induced prostitution under the ambit of ‘exploitation’ and ‘sexual exploitation’.
4.6.4 Subject to the above observations, the Clause 4B was inserted.
4.7 Clause 5 (Sections 375, 376, 376A, 376B, 376C 376D and 376E of IPC)
4.7.1 This clause seeks to substitute Sections 375, 376, 376A and 376B by Sections 375, 376,
376A, 376B, 376C and 376D of the Indian Penal Code replacing the offence “rape” by “sexual
assault” to make the offence gender neutral and also to widen the scope of the offence.
Amendment to Section 375 proposes to raise the age for consent from 16 years to 18 years in
sexual assault as well as the age of wife from fifteen to sixteen years in the exception for sexual
assault. The Committee took note that the Ordinance made further amendments to the provisions
as contained in the Bill and also brought in some new Sections. The new Sections in Ordinance
provide for punishment for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of the victim,
punishment for sexual assault by gang, and punishment of deaths for repeat offenders.
4.7.2 The Committee noted that the definition of ‘sexual assault’ has been revised drastically in
the Ordinance to widen the ambit of sexual assaults of various natures, which has more far
reaching implications than envisaged in Section 375 of the Bill. The Committee felt that the
provisions contained in Section 375 in the Ordinance needed to be incorporated in the Bill. The
Committee, however, felt that in the Exception provided after clause (e) of section 375 should not
cover clauses (a) & (d) of the Bill. The Committee recommended for a review in this regard while
bringing the new Bill.
4.7.3 Section 376 provides punishment for sexual assault. Sub-Section (1) of Section 376
provides punishment for sexual assault with not less than 7 years imprisonment, extendable up
to life with fine. The Committee was not in agreement with the imposition of fine for some
specified amount without mentioning about the intricacies involved in attending to the medical
needs of the victim. The Committee, therefore, recommended for paying adequate compensation
to the victim, to meet at least the medical expenses incurred by the victim in place of the word
“fine”.

89
4.7.4 The Committee also noted that the Ordinance contained ‘rigorous imprisonment’ whereas in
the Bill, it was only ‘imprisonment’. The Committee recommended that the word ‘rigorous’ may
be added before the word ‘imprisonment’ to make the punishment more tougher.
4.7.5 Sub-Section (2) of Section 376 deals with punishment for aggravated sexual assault. The
Committee noted addition of an item relating to armed forces in the Ordinance and inclusion of the
words “guardian or teacher” in Section 376(2) (e) of the Ordinance. The Committee further noted
a sub-clause dealing with gang rape has been deleted as the Ordinance has dealt with the issue of
gang rape in a separate Section comprehensively. The Committee also notes that in the Ordinance,
a new clause regarding sexual assault on a person incapable of giving consent has been added. The
Committee also noted deletion of the word ‘political’ in clause (i) of the sub-Section and
recommended for its retention.
4.7.6 The Committee further noted that the definitions of “police officer” and “armed forces”
have been added under the Explanation 1 of the Section 376(2) in the Ordinance which was not
there in the Bill. The Committee recommended for its addition. The Committee also noted that the
Explanation 2 at the end of the Section 376 (2) was redundant in view of the new Section 376D
dealing with sexual assault by gang and accordingly, recommended for its deletion.
4.7.7 Section 376A is a new Section in the Ordinance which is not there in the Bill. This Section
prescribes punishment of rigorous imprisonment not less than 20 years, extendable up to remainder
of natural life or death for causing death or resulting in persistent vegetative state of the victim.
The Committee recommended for its insertion in the Bill before the present Section 376A of the
Bill.
4.7.8 The Committee noted that some persons convicted for rape and murder cases were given
clemency by the President of India. The Committee also noted a case wherein the accused died
well before the clemency was given. The Committee felt that application for clemency should not
be considered in rape and murder cases. The Committee also felt that mercy petitions should be
disposed of within three months and reasons for granting clemency should also be made public.
4.7.9 The Committee recommended that Sections 376A and 376B of the Bill may be re-numbered
as 376B and 376C. The re-numbered Section 376B of the Bill deals with sexual assault by husband
upon his wife during separation. The Committee made no change in this Section. The re-numbered
Section 376C of the Bill deals with sexual intercourse by a person in authority. The Committee
noted certain changes made in the Ordinance and recommended for changes accordingly. The new
sections 376D and 376E created  in the Ordinance which were not there in the Bill. Section 376D
deals with punishment for sexual assault by gang and 376E deals with punishment for repeat
offender. The Committee recommended for the addition of those Sections after the re-numbered
Section 376C.
4.7.10 Subject to above observations and recommendations, the Clause was adopted, as
amended.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
On the basis of the recommendations of the Law Commission
of India in its One Hundred Seventy Second report on ‘Review of
Rape Laws’ as well as the recommendations of the National
Commission for Women for providing stringent punishment for the
offence of rape, a High Power Committee was constituted
consisting of the representatives of the Ministry of Women and
Child Development, Ministry of Law and Justice, National
Commission for Women, Law Commission of India and the Ministry
of Home Affairs to examine the matter considering the suggestions
of various quarters on the subject. The Committee submitted its
report along with the draft Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2011
and recommended to the Government for its enactment. The draft
Bill was further examined by the Government.
2. The Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2012 seeks to amend
the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973
and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, inter alia, so as to—
(a) substitute sections 375, 376, 376A and 376B by
replacing the existing sections 375, 376, 376A, 376B, 376C
and 376D of the Indian Penal Code, and replacing the word
‘rape’ wherever it occurs by the words ‘sexual assault’, to
make the offence of sexual assault gender neutral and also
widening the scope of the offence of sexual assault;
(b) include sections 326A and 326B in the Indian Penal
Code to make acid attack a specific offence;
(c) enhance the punishment under sections 354 and 509
of the Indian Penal Code, making the offence more stringent;
(d) amend sections 154, 160 and 161 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 for providing women and male
person under the age of eighteen years or above the age of
sixty-five years more protections;
(e) amend the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 by way of
inserting a new section 53A wherein evidence of the character
of the victim or of his or her previous sexual experience shall
not be relevant or questioned.
3. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objectives.

STANDING COMMITTEE ON HOME AFFAIRS INVITES SUGGESTIONS ON THE
CRIMINAL LAW (AMENDMENT) BILL, 2012
The Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill, 2012 as introduced in the Lok Sabha on 4 December
2012 and pending therein, has been referred to Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Home Affairs, headed by Shri M. Venkaiah Naidu, M.P.  Rajya Sabha  for
examination and report. The Bill seeks to amend the Indian Penal Code, 1860, the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872. The Bill provides for:
(i) making the offence of sexual assault gender neutral and also widening the scope of
the offence of sexual assault;
(ii) making acid attack a specific offence;
(iii) making the punishment for offence more stringent;
(iv) providing women and male person under the age of eighteen years or above the age
of sixty-five years more protections; and
(v) providing that the evidence of the character of the victim or of his or her previous
sexual experience shall not be relevant or questioned.

the public/associations/women organizations/civil societies, etc, on the provisions of the Bill.
