1.8 The Ministry further apprised the Committee with the relevant observations and
recommendations of Administrative Reforms Commission’s 7
th Report titled “Capacity Building For
Conflict Resolution” and Government’s decision thereon which is reproduced as below:–
“12.6.4.1.1 The most significant ‘supra State’ institution of the region is the North Eastern
Council (NEC) set up in 1972, following the enactment of the North Eastern Council
Act,1971. Its creation was necessitated by the reorganisation of the region into five States
and two Union Territories and in response to the twin needs of effecting better inter-State/
UT coordination, for maintenance of internal security and for facilitating planned,
integrated development of the North East. While the aspect of security coordination received
adequate consideration by the NEC in its initial phases – the Inspector General of the
Assam Rifles acted as ex-officio Security Adviser – this responsibility was subsequently
resumed by the Ministry of Home Affairs and the NEC is now primarily an agency to
prepare and finance development schemes of inter-State importance. It also runs a number
of educational and training institutions catering to the requirements of the region.
12.6.4.1.2 NEC initially consisted of the ‘common Governor’ of the North Eastern States as
its Chairman with the Lieutenant Governors of the UTs and all the Chief Ministers as
members. After the appointment of separate Governors (1981), the practice of either the
Governor of Assam or the senior-most Governor acting as its head was followed. Following
an amendment in the NEC Act in 2002, Sikkim has been added as a member and, due to
its non-contiguity with other member-States, ‘stand alone’ schemes can be sanctioned for this
State. Through this amendment, provision was also made for nomination of the Chairperson
of the NEC by the President and for positioning some full-time members. In pursuance of that
provision and on the recommendations of an expert Committee (2003), it was decided that
normally, the Union Minister for Development of the North Eastern Region shall preside over
the NEC. Two full-time members have also been inducted to the Council.
12.6.4.1.3 In the absence of a systematic overall organisational appraisal of the NEC so far,
it is difficult to be categorical about its successes and failures. It is, however, a fact that like
many other high level bodies, transaction of purposive business by the NEC has been
hampered, as its proceedings tend to be dominated by rhetoric with limited time devoted to
deliberations. Similarly, increasing State plan outlays, coupled with ever increasing central
subventions through statutory transfers, centrally sponsored schemes and ad hoc allocations
have resulted in a ‘shift of attention’ of the member-States from this regional institution. It
must however be acknowledged that NEC sponsored schemes have contributed significantly to
improve inter-State road and air connectivity, substantially augment power distribution and
harmonious regional cooperation. It is agreed by all that the inter-State institutions of
medical, dental, technical and paramedical education established and maintained by it in
different parts of the region have not only added to the development of human resources but
have also enhanced better understanding between different areas within the region.
12.6.4.1.4 To review the role of the NEC in conflict reduction, reference may first be made
to the mandate given to it originally under Section 4 of its Act, and the present position.

4
Initially, the Council had a three-fold mandate of (a) considering issues in which two or
more States of the region had an interest and to advise the Central Government in the
matter; (b) preparation of regional plans and (c) security coordination in the region.
Following the amendments, its present charter is:
(a) To function as a regional planning body;
(b) To finance and implement projects of benefit to two or more States (except
Sikkim);
(c) To review the pace of development in the region particularly in the context of
the regional development plans; and
(d) To review measures taken by the States to maintain security and public order
in the region.
12.6.4.1.5 For the purposes of this Report, the role of the NEC in conflict resolution may
be studied in three contexts – NEC as an inter-State coordinating body; NEC as a Regional
Planning body and role in ensuring maintenance of Public order. These aspects are briefly
considered in the succeeding paragraphs.
12.6.4.1.6 One of the primary functions of the Council is to act as a forum to review the
pace of development in the region. The amendment in the mandate of the Council which
withdrew the power to discuss ‘issues of common interest to two or more States and to advise
the Union Government thereon’ has already been referred to. The ‘withdrawn responsibility’
was identical to the mandate given to the Zonal Councils under the States Reorganisation Act,
1956. While the Commission is not recommending the rejuvenation of the Zonal Councils in
other regions for the reasons mentioned in Chapter 14, it is clear that in matters like
movement of supplies, including food-grains and passengers, local taxation policies and
border disputes etc, a coordinating and problem solving forum is still highly relevant for the
North Eastern Region. It is, therefore, imperative that the original provisions for inter-State
coordination with its direct nexus with conflict resolution is restored.
12.6.4.1.7 The amendments to the NEC Act of 2002, as noted earlier, while somewhat
narrowing the scope of the advisory jurisdiction of the Council more explicitly states its
responsibility to review maintenance of security and public order. Earlier, this responsibility
devolved only indirectly as part of the coordinating and advisory role of the NEC, it
nevertheless found adequate reflection in the agenda of the Council. Explicit introduction of
this responsibility through the 2002 amendment, creates problems for the DoNER, as the
‘administrative Ministry’ for the NEC. DoNER has been assigned no role in the sphere of
security in the region. NEC, therefore, has to directly deal with the Ministry of Home Affairs
in discharging this responsibility. The larger issue is how to work out the modalities of
discharging this responsibility. It is clear that if the ambit of ‘internal security reviews’ has
to extend even a little beyond holding meetings, the NEC secretariat will need to be more
actively involved in security coordination issues. To facilitate meaningful reviews, the Council
secretariat must involve itself with the emerging developments in the field. Ministry of Home
Affairs (MHA) also needs to take a view whether ‘security and public order reviews’ under
the aegis of the NEC offer benefits which cannot be had by the MHA’ s own reviews. MHA
must further consider whether special empowerment of the NEC entailed by this responsibility
will result in increased administrative burden on the agencies normally involved in monitoring
the law and order scenario in the region. To effectively coordinate or even assist in
deliberations on internal security related issues, the Council secretariat would need suitable
augmentation. In short, adequate preparatory arrangements are necessary if the renewed
mandate of the NEC for internal security reviews is to be meaningfully discharged.”

1.9 The Committee was further apprised of the recommendations contained in the 7th Report
of Second ARC which are enumerated below:
(a) The NEC Act, 1971 may be suitably amended to restore the original ‘conflict resolution
provision’ requiring the Council to ‘discuss issues of mutual interest to two or more states
in the region and to advise the Central Government thereon’.
(b) To enable the Council to assist effectively in the discharge of its responsibilities for
reviewing the measures taken by the member-States for maintenance of security in the
region, Ministry of Home Affairs should keep the Council Secretariat regularly within its
‘security coordination loop’. The Council Secretariat would also need to be suitably
strengthened to effectively assist in security coordination.
(c) The Planning Commission needs to lay down a framework for preparation of integrated
regional plans, with priorities and not as an assortment of schemes by the NEC. The
regional plan should focus on areas with a bearing on intra-regional, inter-State priorities
which have the potential of avoiding conflicts and promoting regional integration.
(d) Planning Commission should ensure the association of the NEC in the State plan
formulation exercise by suitably amending their guidelines.
(e) The responsibility of sanctioning funds from the ‘Non Lapsable Central Pool of
Resources’ (NLCPR) should be entrusted to the North Eastern Council (NEC). NEC should
work out mechanisms for scrutinising proposals for funding from the ‘pool’ and their
funding in coordination with the Ministries concerned.
(f) It is desirable that a 10-year perspective plan is prepared for the entire region
encompassing areas like development of human resources and infrastructure. A governance
reform agenda should also form part of this plan. This comprehensive plan needs to be
reviewed by the Prime Minister regularly with the Chief Ministers for speedy follow-up.
(g) The Ministry for Development of North Eastern Region (DoNER) may be abolished and
the responsibility for the development of the region, including the infrastructure sectors, and
utilisation of the non-lapsable fund should be restored to the subject matter Ministries, with
the MHA acting as the nodal Ministry.
1.10 Explaining about the action taken on the recommendations of the 7
th Report of ARC, it was
stated that the Government accepted in principle empowering NEC with the conflict resolution
provisions and it was decided that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take up this matter with
NEC. The Government also accepted in principle that Ministry of Home Affairs should keep the
Council Secretariat regularly within its ‘security coordination loop’ and MHA should examine the
issue in consultation with NEC. The Government accepted the role of Planning Commission in
laying guidelines for formulation of integrated regional plans and ensuring the association of the
NEC in the State plan formulation. The responsibility of sanctioning funds from the ‘Non Lapsable
Central Pool of Resources by NEC was not accepted on the ground that NEC is a planning body.
Recommendation regarding Ten-year perspective plan was accepted by the Government. The
recommendation regarding the abolition of the Ministry of DoNER and restoration of responsibility
for Development of region to the concerned line Department/Ministry has not been accepted on the
plea that Ministry of DoNER provided undivided attention to development of North East. However,
it was decided that a review of functioning of NEC and DoNER could be undertaken to make these
bodies more effective.

2.0 Mandate and Working of Ministry of DoNER
2.1 The Committee took into cognizance the recommendations of Seventh Report of Second
Administrative Reforms Commission regarding the abolition of the Ministry of DoNER and
restoration of responsibility for development of the region to the concerned line Department/
Ministry. The Committee noted that the Government has not accepted this recommendation on the
plea that Ministry of DoNER provides undivided attention to development of North East and that
a review of functioning of NEC and DoNER could be undertaken to make these bodies more effective.
2.2 It would be worthwhile to mention that the Committee, in its 170
th Report on Demands for
Grants (2013-14) pertaining to Ministry of DoNER, as presented to the Rajya Sabha on 25 th April,
2013 commented on the dismal achievements of the Ministry. The Committee noted the Ministry’s
confession about its weakness in advocacy and coordination role, inadequate technical support,
inadequate over all staff support, inadequate space and absence of field offices. The Committee was
of the strong view that the purpose for which the Ministry was set up, has not been fulfilled and
it seems that the implementing ministries do not pay heed to the requests or suggestions of the
Ministry of DoNER. The Committee, therefore, strongly, recommended that Government should
consider the handicaps of the Ministry of DoNER in a very serious manner and devise way out either
by placing the Ministry of DoNER under PMO directly or evolve some other mechanism so that the
Ministry of DoNER could get its decisions implemented by the line Ministries/Departments/agencies.
2.3 In regard to the working and the mandate of the Ministry of DoNER, the Committee in the said
report felt that it failed to understand that a Ministry, which was carved out to focus and expedite
development in the North East Region, after more than a decade of its existence, has realized that it
lacks sufficient power and necessary infrastructure to carry out its mandate, and is completely
dependent on various Line Ministries/Departments for execution of projects. The Committee took a
serious view of the situation and felt that a holistic view at the functioning and powers of the Ministry
should be taken. The Committee not being impressed with the functioning of the Ministry felt that the
line ministries are not supporting or paying heed to the suggestions/ requests of the Ministry.
2.4 The Committee, while reiterating its recommendations as made in its 170
th Report,
feels that it is the high time the Government review the functioning of the Ministry and
devise a mechanism to strengthen Ministry of DoNER for its effective functioning so that
the projects and schemes meant for NER are completed in time and the line agencies/
Ministries/Departments while implementing those projects co-ordinate with the Ministry of
DoNER. The Committee also reiterates its decision as indicated in its 170
th Report that it
would hold discussions with the Cabinet Secretary, Planning Commission and other
stakeholders in the matter.
3.0 Presentation by the Secretary, Ministry of DoNER
3.1 The Secretary, Ministry of DoNER during the course of presentation before the Committee
in its sitting held on 22 nd April, 2013 dwelt upon the background and provisions of the Bill as under:–
“there are three nominated Members of the North-Eastern Council, but, unfortunately, their
tenure has not been fixed. So, the present incumbents are there for around last eight years,
since March, 2005. So, it is considered necessary to restrict their tenure to three years,

7
which can be extended to a maximum of five years so that new blood is infused into the
Council. This is one point. The second point is, most of the Member States of the North-
Eastern Council have issues relating to each other, like boundary disputes. This Bill seeks
to empower the Council to discuss those kinds of issues among themselves and try to sort
them out without the interference of the Government of India. That is the main purpose.
The third one is, if the emoluments are fixed in the Act itself, it will be difficult to change
it and every time when the emoluments need to be changed, we will have to amend the Act.
So, we are seeking to empower the Government through a subordinate legislation to fix the
emoluments... earlier DoNER was a Department under the Ministry of Home Affairs. Now
it is a full-fledged Ministry. Now we just want to change the nomenclature. ”

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
The North-Eastern Council (NEC) was set up in 1972 by the
North-Eastern Council Act, 1971 for securing balanced and
coordinated development and effecting coordination among States of
the north-eastern area viz. Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur,
Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and Tripura. The Governors and
Chief Ministers of constituent States are members of the Council.
2. The North-Eastern Council (Amendment) Act, 2002, inter-
alia, added Sikkim as the eighth member-State of the Council;
envisaged functioning of the Council as a regional planning body for
the north-eastern area and provisioned for three members and
Chairman of the Council to be nominated by the President.
3. The nominated Union Minister, Governors and Chief
Ministers of the constituent States are members of the Council as
long as they hold the office. Since establishment of NEC, being a
statutory body, is of permanent nature, therefore, tenure of
nominated members of the Council should be specified in the Act.
Therefore, the Bill, inter alia, seeks inclusion of (a) one member of
the Planning Commission of India, being in charge of the north-
eastern region; (b) two non-official members nominated by the
President for three years period extendable for a further period not
exceeding two years.
4. Second Administrative Reforms Commission, in its
7th Report on ‘Capacity Building for Conflict Resolution,’ inter alia,
recommended for suitable amendment in the Act of 1971, to restore
the original ‘conflict resolution provision’ requiring the Council to
discuss issues of mutual interest of two or more States in the
region and to advise the Central Government thereon. This
recommendation was in-principle approved by the Group of
Ministers headed by the then Finance Minister in the meeting held
on 8th December, 2009, NEC should be used as forum for
discussion on matters of common interest to the Region and make
recommendations. The Bill seeks amendment in the Act that will
enable the Council to perform this function.
5. Department of Development of North-Eastern Region was
formed in 2001 within Ministry of Home Affairs and subsequently
upgraded to full-fledged Ministry in 2004. The Bill also seeks
amendment in the Act to that effect.
6. The Bill seeks to acheive the above objects.

working of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy, Hyderabad. The One Hundred Sixty-
third Report was presented to Rajya Sabha/laid on the Table of Lok Sabha, on the 30

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS WHICH
HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
RECOMMNEDATION
FIELD VISIT
1.1 The committee is of the view that the basic training modules of the Academy must consist
of the courses keeping in view stark reality of society and the aim of the training programme
should be to impart knowledge and skill to face the ground challenges of the country. The
Committee also feels that training on management and administration should also be provided.
When the officers grow higher up the ladder, they are also required to handle administration and
finance. Training needs to be given on these aspects as well and some module may be prepared
for these aspects.
(Para 2.4.1 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.1.1 The present syllabus of Basic Training course of IPS probationers includes numerous
modules which have been designed to impart knowledge and skills and also requisite sensitization
keeping in view the ground realities of the society so as to prepare them to face the challenges
in the field. Field visits to acquaint them with the problems of vulnerable sections of the society
such as juveniles, marginalized communities, and weaker section of the society are organized.
1.1.2 While basic inputs on management and administration is provided during Phase-I training,
the probationers after their return from District Practical Training are given additional inputs on
aspects of supervision and financial management.
1.1.3 Furthermore, officers are given inputs on management and administration during their Mid
Career Training Programme.
1.1.4 In addition to above, the Academy has set-up a model police station which is a forum for
the officers to understand the running of the police station and the challenges being faced by the
Station House Officer. A model police station provides the experience in police station
administration, as well as public order management against crime investigation through simulation.
However the suggestion made by the Parliamentary Standing Committee has been noted.
RECOMMENDATION
MID CAREER TRAINING PROGRAMME (MCTP)
1.2 The Committee is of the opinion that exposure to best policing practices should also be
imparted at training stage, if feasible, preferably in countries with similar democratic political set
up. The Committee believes that training modules consisting of foreign collaborations having police
agencies of the country having similar political and economic condition as that of India would
immensely impact so far as their policing skill is concerned. The Academy may consider this aspect.
(Para 2.5.10 )
2

3
ACTION TAKEN
1.2.1 In the MCTPs our police officers are travelling to developed democratic countries like UK
and Australia and are exposed to modern democratic methods of policing. Now for selecting new
foreign collaboration for MCTP training their tie up with police agencies of foreign countries is
being insisted. A proposal for sending IPS probationers for foreign experience under Phase-II
training is being examined in consultation with Min. of Finance.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.2.3 The Committee may be apprised of the final decision taken in regard to sending IPS
probationers for foreign experience.
RECOMMENDATION
SPECIAL TACTICS WING
1.3 The Committee notes the initiatives and activities taken by NP A in imparting special
tactical training to police officers. The Committee, however, also takes note of the fact that STW
is having its manpower on ad-hoc basis. This will not help in better functioning of the work.
Efforts may be made to put in place dedicated manpower at the earliest. Directional level tactics
course for senior officers of the rank of DIG and above be started at the earliest. Fund
requirements of NP A for developing allotted land for tactical training, separate STW building,
procurement of equipments and weapons may be looked into promptly so as to make the Special
Tactics Wing par excellence. This level of excellence may further be used for revenue generation
by imparting such training to the police officers of other countries.
(Para 2.6.7 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.3.1 Tactics course for senior police officers has been introduced after the visit of the
Committee. This course is called the ‘Management of Tactical Operations’ Course and was
conducted from 30.04.2012 to 05.05.2012. Another course in the present calendar year is
scheduled to be held from 11.12.2012 to 20.12.2012. Second course has been re-designed
keeping in view the feedback from the first course, as this is an on-going process of making
the course relevant for officers on directional level. For developing of allotted land, the initial
plans have been prepared. The Special Tactics Wing has already developed a level of competency
to run courses for Police Officers of other countries and such courses may be planned, in
future.
RECOMMENDATION
TRAINING PROGRAMMES : INDOOR VS. OUTDOOR TRAINING
1.4 Tie up with foreign police agencies would definitely give an opportunity to the trainee
officers to understand the nuances of working of police agencies in other countries. The
Committee is of the considered view that the faculty exchange programmes with other foreign
police agencies and training institutes would give an opportunity for exchange of views among the
faculty and to refresh their knowledge. The committee, therefore, recommends that tie-up with
foreign institutes for both trainees and faculty may be organized for better exposure.
(Para 2.8.7 )

4
ACTION TAKEN
1.4.1 To understand the working of police agencies of other countries till now there was tie up
with following three foreign Universities under MCTP Programme:
(i) Australia – Charles Stuart University in collaboration wit the Indian School of Business,
Hyderabad.
(ii) London, UK – Cambridge University, UK in collaboration with the OP Jindal Global
University, Gurgaon.
(iii) London, UK – London Business School - IIM, Ahmadabad in collaboration with the
London Business School, London, UK.
1.4.2  Whenever, MCTP programmes conducted abroad, two faculty members of NPA are also
deputed abroad which helps improve the ties with foreign institutes and trainees.
1.4.3  The officers of NSG/BSF/CRPF/NIA/CBI etc. are deputed to France/USA/Israel/Japan etc.
to attend various training programmes/ seminars.
RECOMMENDATION
COMPARATIVE STUDY OF POLICE STRUCTURES AND POLICE SYSTEM
1.5 The Committee feels that teaching of a comparative study of police structures and police
system over the world at NP A at the inducting stage also would enable the probationers to have a
much wider horizon and a much larger perspectives, and would further enable them to introduce small
improvement in police working on the basis of their knowledge of the overall police system and
police structures. There should be a course on comparative police systems. NP A may look into this.
(Para 2.10.1 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.5.1 Recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee shall be implemented for the
training of IPS probationers from 65 RR (2012) batch onwards.
RECOMMENDATION
TRAINING ON ADMINISTRATIVE, FINANCIAL AND SOCIAL ISSUES.
1.6 The Committee desires that NP A may have a relook at the present modules and incorporate
specific aspects on administrative and financial management if they are not sufficiently covered.
(Para 2.11.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.6.1 The present syllabus of Basic Training course of IPS probationers includes numerous
modules which have been designed to impart knowledge and skills and also requisite sensitization
keeping in view the ground realities of the society so as to prepare them to face the challenges
in the field. Field visits to acquaint them with the problems of vulnerable sections of the society
such as juveniles, marginalized communities, and weaker section of the society are organized.
1.6.2 While basic inputs on management and administration is provided during Phase-I training,
the probationers after their return from District Practical Training are given additional inputs on
aspects of supervision and financial management.

5
1.6.3 Furthermore, officers are given inputs on management and administration during their Mid
Career Training Programme.
1.6.4 In addition to above, the Academy has set-up a model police station which is a forum for
the officers to understand the running of the police station and the challenges being faced by the
Station House Officer. A model police station provides the experience in police station
administration, as well as public order management against crime investigation through simulation.
However the suggestion made by the Parliamentary Standing Committee has been noted.
RECOMMENDATION
LAW AND JURISPRUDENCE IN TRAINING MODULES
1.7 The Committee agrees that an in-depth understanding of jurisprudential principles would
inject legal insight to the IPS officer which would certainly help them solve the legal issues
involved in the case. The Committee, therefore, feels that there is further scope for enhancing the
module on law and jurisprudence in the training curriculum of IPS officers. Therefore, the entire
module on law and jurisprudence may be revisited involving some legal experts.
(Para 3.1.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.7.1 The Academy has initiated steps to have a committee involving legal experts to revisit entire
module on Law and Jurisprudence in the training of IPS probationers.
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
1.7.2 The DRSC on Home Affairs may be apprised of the conclusions arrived by the
committee involving legal experts, set up to revisit training module in Law and
Jurisprudence for IPS Officers and the action proposed.
RECOMMENDATION
CASE STUDY
1.8 The Committee hopes that the introduction of integrated Training format would enable the
IPS officer to have in-depth understanding of rejoinder of crimes. The format may be thoroughly
assessed after one year.
(Para 3.2.7 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.8.1 Since integrated training method has been adopted in 2012, follow-up study in the form of
evaluation of the efficacy of the method will be undertaken in July-August, 2013. By that time 64
RR Probationers would also complete their district training as well.
RECOMMENDATION
ETHICAL AND MORAL VALUES AND INTEGRATION
1.9 The Committee is of the view that since policing does have a bearing on the lives of
individuals and, therefore, Police Personnel, particularly officers should possess high moral and
ethical values so as to arrest the declining trend in quality and standard of public life. The
Committee believes that when the pursuit of social commitment and integrity is effectively imbibed
into police personnel irrespective of rank and file, the malaise and qualms of corruption could be
eradicated from public life to a large extent. Transparency and public accountability is a pre-requisite

6
for good governance. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the training modules prepared
for probationers and also for in-service officers must cover the lessons on ethical traits and moral
behaviour.
(Para 3.3.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.9.1 The Academy is committed to prepare leaders for Indian Police who will lead the force with
high integrity, uprightness and a strong sense of service to the people. The emphasis on ethics and
moral values is not only reflected in the inputs given on the subject during the training but also
permeates through curricular and extra- curricular activities at the Academy. The strong sense of
values, the practical dimension of courage and uprightness is imparted not only through class room
training but also through outdoor training, team activities and individual exposures. The emphasis
is laid on strengthening the inner moral compass in individual probationers so as to enable them
to withstand pressures that they might face in the field.
1.9.2 Eminent persons of impeccable integrity from all walks of life including police are invited
as expert speakers to interact with the IPS probationers and inspire them by their personal example.
In addition, field visits and experience sharing modules also help in this regard.
RECOMMENDATION
ETHICAL AND MORAL VALUES AND INTEGRATION
1.10 The Committee observes that Officer is generally vested with the power which extends at
times to taking life and liberty of the people but what matters is how he exercises his power.
Therefore, emphasis should also be given as to how to use the power. The Committee is also given
to understand that in other countries like Japan training curriculum contain the constant emphasis
on ethical aspects in policing so that while doing a particular job, a set of principles has to be
adhered to. The Committee, therefore, recommends that adequate emphasis should be laid in the
training programme of Officers Trainee and NP A should teach probationers good policing practice
which is practicised globally. Modules on ethical values and morality should also be included in
the MCTP programmes as it is equally required at that stage as well.
(Para 3.3.3 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.10.1  Focus of the Academy training is not only to acquaint the IPS Probationers with the
powers vested in the police by law but also on the judicious exercise of those powers. Issues of
Police Legitimacy are covered as part of exercises of power by the police in various professional
aspects. During Basic course Trainee Officers are sensitised on ethical and social aspects through
‘composite code module’ and ‘Rights based policing’ which cultivate correct ethical and social
attitudes. Researches on issues of police legitimacy and best practices being followed in other
countries are shared with the IPS Probationers.
1.10.2  Committee’s suggestion of including Modules on ethical values and morality in MCTP
course has been accepted. SVP NPA will be instructed accordingly.
RECOMMENDATION
TRAINING MODULES ON LEFT-WING EXTREMISM AND TERRORISM
1.11 The left wing extremism is spreading its tentacles across the country and a well prepared

7
module needs to be prepared for training on dealing with this. The Greyhound of Andhra Pradesh
Police has been successful in dealing with this and they can be a role model in regard to this
training. If possible, the probationers may be attached with Greyhounds for some period. NP A
should become centre of excellence in giving training on dealing with left wing extremism.
(Para 3.4.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.11.1  The basic training at the Academy takes into account the seriousness of the problem and
spread of the LWE. The Academy has adapted its training to equip the probationers with necessary
skills in Jungle Field Craft and Tactics. The Tactical Wing of the Academy provides extensive basic
inputs in this regard which are supplemented by a week-long attachment with the Greyhounds of
AP and another attachment with Central School of Weapons & Tactics (CSWT), BSF Indore.
1.11.2  The emphasis is not only in imparting skills in Field Craft and Tactics but also ‘Winning
Hearts and Minds’ of the local population. The success stories in this field are shared by the
officers who have successfully implemented these strategies on the field with demonstrable
results.
1.11.3 The Academy through its robust Special Tactics Wing is conducting a large number of In-
Service training courses to deal with the problem of Left-Wing Extremism and is striving to
become a Centre of Excellence.
RECOMMENDATION
ETHICAL AND MORAL VALUES AND INTERATION
1.12 The Committee desires that the message of the Preamble to the Constitution of India, being
“Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic” should not only be read and understood by
the police personnel but should also be imprinted into their ‘hearts and minds’ to be reflected into
their actions while dealing with actual incidents. Keeping in view the fact that India is a vast
country with complex social structure i.e. multi-lingual, multi-ethnic, multi- religious, training
modules must give emphasis to these aspects. A sense of justice and sensitivity towards the people
particularly of weaker sections should be initiated by them.
(Para 3.3.5 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.12.1 In order to enable the probationers to imbibe the values of Democracy and Secularism
enshrined in the preamble of the Constitution, modules on National Integration and Communal
Harmony are regularly conducted at the Academy. The endeavour of the Academy is to
inculcate in the probationers the concern for Rights of the Citizens as against Authority of
the police.
RECOMMENDATION
PSYCHOLOGICAL PROFILING
1.13 The Committee desires that psychological profiling may be made use of for better
counselling and de-stressing. Yoga is a good tool for de-stressing and to rein in the mind and this
may be used to the maximum extent.
(Para 3.5.2 )

8
ACTION TAKEN
1.13.1 The Academy uses technique of Psychological Profiling for individual and group counselling
of IPS probationers. The domains of measurement through psychological tests include:–
· Personality correlates of leadership
· Cognitive and problem-solving styles
· Interpersonal orientation
· Psycho-socio correlates of stress
· Conflict Management Style
· Emotional Intelligence
· Team Building Competence
· Creativity
1.13.2 On case-to-case basis, intensive individual counseling is also given.
1.13.3 Y oga is an important part of Outdoor Training curriculum. Trained Yoga Instructors impart
Yoga training not only to IPS Probationers but also to other in-service course participants.
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
1.13.4  The Committee hopes that ‘Psychological profiling Module’ as used by NPA for
training to probationers and in-service police officer would go a long way in counseling and
de-stressing management.
RECOMMENDATION
PEOPLE-FRIENDLY POLICING
1.14 The image of Government depends more on the reaction of the rank and file of the law
enforcing agencies particularly police officers towards the common man, when the common man
approaches them in the hour of need. The Committee, therefore, feels that police being at the
cutting edge level needs to adopt courteous behaviour and friendly temperament so that people may
approach them without fear and with faith to have redressal of their grievances. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that training modules and practical training courses as imparted by NP A
must be included all behavioural and attitudinal aspect and the Academy should work on this. The
Ministry should oversee the implementation of the Mission. An early decision may be taken in this
regard.
(Para 3.6.5 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.14.1  As part of the training, a Model Police Station is being run at the Academy. It has a
distinct reception area to highlight to the probationers the need for courteous and empathetic
behaviour by the police while receiving complainants, victims of crime, witnesses, etc. The
simulated exercises are conducted to train the probationers in empathetic dealing with victims of
crime.
1.14.2 In order to train police officers at the cutting edge level in States for courteous and friendly
behaviour, a project is already being implemented by BPR&D under the guidance of MHA.

9
RECOMMENDATION
ACCESS OF SUB-ORDINATES TO SENIOR POLICE OFFICER
1.15 The Committee firmly believes that open access of constabulary to higher police personnel
and hassle-free communication among them would ensure higher degree of trust and faith amongst
each other which would not only lead to redressal of grievances of constabulary but would also
help in taking strategic decision, formulation of pragmatic plans based on the situation and
experience at grass root level and execution thereof to achieve set objectives. This will improve the
efficiency of the forces. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the training modules should
invariably emphasise this. This needs to be done both in the NP A as well as the training courses
of States and District Training Centres.
(Para 3.7.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.15.1 The Academy training lays emphasis on leadership and team building both of which require
great amount of trust and faith from the constabulary which forms more than 90% of the police
human resources. To promote open access of constabulary to senior police leadership and also for
effective grievance redressal, the IPS probationers are exposed to various traditional platforms like
weekly parade, orderly room, surprise visits, Sainik Sammelan etc. In addition, forums such as
‘KhulaManch’ which introduces democratization to the officer trainees and ‘Pre-dinner talk’ which
allows free and frank discussions between officer trainees and luminaries visiting the Academy. In
addition to this, they are also exposed to modern technological tools like SMS, mobile phones,
e-mails etc for open and better access to the constabulary. The important role played by
constabulary and subordinate officers in strategy formulation, pragmatic solution and execution of
set objectives is emphasized in the training.
1.15.2 As suggested by the Committee greater emphasis shall be laid on this by the Academy in
its various training modules. For doing the same at State and District Police Training Centres, MHA
will also direct the BPR&D to issue an advisory to all the States in this regard.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.15.3 The Committee would like to be apprised of the action taken by BPR&D in regard
to issuing guidelines to States and District Training centers.
RECOMMENDATION
TRAINING ON COURT PROCEDURES
1.16 Though moot court proceedings at the Academy are good and give theoretical aspect but do
not give the true picture of the courts. Dealing with court cases is an important aspect of the
policing. The actual procedure of the courts is not only complex but cumbersome also, and the
attachment of the probationers for a period of seven days does not appear sufficient. The committee,
therefore, recommends that probationers should be given sufficient actual court exposure so that
inadequacies on the part of the agencies of the Government do not become a stumbling block in the
disposal of the case. NPA should, therefore, consider to give sufficient emphasize on this.
(Para 3.9.1 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.16.1 In view of the recommendations made by the Committee, the Academy has enhanced the

10
duration of attachment of the IPS Probationers with the Public Prosecutor and District Court as
part of their District Practical Training with a view to give them greater exposure to the court
procedures. In addition a ‘Çourt Craft’ module has been introduced in the basic training.
1.16.2 NICFS, New Delhi conducts various joint training courses on court proceedings for police
officers, prison officers, judicial officers and prosecutors.
RECOMMENDATION
COMMUNITY POLICING
1.17 The Committee notes that one of the Police Mission set out by the Prime Minister is on
Community policing and the Ministry is considering the report of the Committee thereon. After it
is decided to implement it, NP A may take a cue from this and include it in the course. On the
basis of experience of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, NP A may prepare a manual on community policing
which can be useful for probationers of NP A and all other State’ s Police Organization. The
Committee views that community policing implies people’ s participation in local security
arrangement and, therefore, leads to much interaction between the police and people. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the mission on Community Policing should be included in
the State and District Police Training Centres of various States and literature procured at the centre
must also be disseminated.
(Para 3.10.1 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.17.1 Community Policing is part of the National Police Mission undertaken by BRR&D. The
Academy also provides in depth inputs into the concept of Community Policing. The trainees are
also acquainted with various community policing initiatives taken in different parts of the country.
The Academy utilizes the presence of police officers, academicians, eminent resource persons from
the different parts of world, who visit the Academy in connection with Mid-Career Training
Programmes, to interact with and share their experiences on community policing with the trainees.
As suggested by the committee, the Academy shall undertake the task of preparation of Manual on
Community Policing.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.17.2 Manual on community policing may be prepared at the earliest and circulated to the
State and District Police Training Centers.
RECOMMENDATION
DEALING WITH THE CHALLENGES OF TERRORISM
1.18 Though after reviewing the police response to Mumbai attack and finding that there was
big gap between the training imparted and the actual requirement of tactical skill to combat the
potential menace of terrorism, a separate wing called Special Tactics Wing(STW) has been set up
in NP A with the objective of imparting training to State Police and Central Armed Police Forces
to enable them to conduct tactical operation against the terrorists in jungle and urban environment,
the efforts are not complete as yet. The urban intervention training infrastructure is likely to be
completed in 2013. This may be completed as per schedule.
(Para 3.11.3 )

11
ACTION TAKEN
1.18.1 The urban interventions training infrastructure will be completed as per schedule.

DEALING WITH THE CHALLENGES OF TERRORISM
1.19 NP A should think and act ahead of the terrorists on the possible techniques and
technologies likely to be used by terrorists and start training in advance. Government may provide
necessary infrastructure to NP A. Training on preventive steps to prevent the possible terrorist attack
is required. Lesson from USA are required to be learnt where 9/11 incident has not been repeated.
The Committee recommends that NP A has to take initiative to make headway in training in this
regard.
(Para 3.11.4 )

RECOMMENDATION
DEALING WITH THE CHALLENGES OF TERRORISM
1.20 The Committee is of the view that since the country is facing terrorist threats counter

12
Intelligence techniques and anti-terrorism operations need to be included in the curriculum so that
the officer who come out are well-versed in the counter-terrorism intelligence techniques.
(Para 3.11.5 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.20.1 During basic course, IPS Probationers are exposed to various intelligence techniques, latest
equipments and related exercises. They also remain attached with SIB, Andhra Pradesh for practical
exercises to understand intelligence operations.
RECOMMENDATION
INTELLIGENCE COLLECTION AND ANALYSIS
1.21 The Committee is surprised to find that although probationers are given elaborate training
on the intelligence collection and analysis but there is no dearth of intelligence failures which led
to massive incidents killing several innocent persons. Though, intelligence success is rarely reported
in the media it failure attracts immediate attention of the media besides immensely affecting the
lives of the people. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the training modules on intelligence
collection and analysis must be comprehensive and the same may be replicated at the State and
District Police Training Centre.
(Para 3.12.3 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.21.1  MHA agrees with the view of the Committee, and will take up with BPR&D to advise
states to replicate training modules on the intelligence collection and analysis at the State level
Police training centers.
1.21.2  Some of the training institutes conducting intelligence training courses are:
1. IB, Training School, 35 Sardar Patel Marg, New Delhi.
2. Maharashtra Intelligence Academy, Pune, Maharashtra.
3. G Training School, BSF, New Delhi.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.21.3 The Committee feels that intelligence collection and analysis is a significant course
of action during criminal investigation, and therefore, NPA management may think of
imparting ‘Specialized training course on intelligence collection and analysis to police
officers inclined towards criminal investigation. Due consultation in chalking out the
suitable training module can be taken from IB, CBI, NIA and BPR&D. Once the training
module is finalized, it should also be replicated at State and District Police Training Centers.
RECOMMENDATION
LAW AND ORDER
1.22 The Committee notes the doctrine of use of minimum force by the police personnel to deal
with the volatile and peaceful demonstration. However, the people in general have police-phobia
as the impression of colonial attitude of the police personnel persists in the minds of the public.
Some of the police outrages over incidents linger in the hearts of the people. The Committee,

13
therefore, strongly recommends that probationers and in-service officers should emphasize on
handling the peaceful and volatile demonstration with acute care and sympathy towards the people
because India is a democratic country and people of the nation have every right to express their
genuine demands thought peaceful demonstration within the parameters of the Constitution. The
officers when on duty required to take on the spot decision as there may not be time to consult
seniors. Therefore, emphasis should be laid in the training on dealing with such situations.
(Para 3.13.4 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.22.1 The underlying thread of training of IPS Probationers at the Academy is to instill in them
the role and responsibility of police in a democratic society. While training them in dealing with
demonstrations, the Fundamental Rights [under Article 19(1b) of Constitution] of the citizens are
emphasized. Parallel to authority-based policing, the training focuses on Rights (of citizens) based
policing. The Doctrine of minimum use of force forms the basis of training in Maintenance of
Public Peace and Order.
1.22.2 As part of the training, both probationers and in-service officers are exposed to newer less
lethal methods of crowd control. The Academy collaborates with DRDO in disseminating
information about new Less Lethal Crowd Control Technology.
RECOMMENDATION
NATIONAL SECURITY/INTERNAL SECURITY
1.23 India is a dominant player of the global economy and global politics and there are a lot
of geo-political and the national security issues which are of utmost concern, therefore training
modules covering National Security issues are indispensable. Therefore, training modules should not
only cover the course in terms of terrorism or left wing extremism but also in terms of security of
vital installations like Dams, Atomic Energy installations, Refineries and various other security
considerations with in the territory of the country.
(Para 3.15.2 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.23.1 Keeping in view the importance of National Security in globalized world, the curriculum of
IPS Probationers was amended in the year 2010 and a new subject titled Internal Security has been
introduced. As part of the subject, the trainees are not only given inputs on the importance of
security issues and its impact on economy but are also acquainted with the nuances of current
challenges to Internal Security especially Left Wing Extremism (LWE), Urban Terrorism, etc. The
special module is conducted to acquaint them in the important tasks of security of vital
installations.
RECOMMENDATION
NATIONAL SECURITY/INTERNAL SECURITY
1.24 The Committee is of the view that Officer Trainees should be imparted training to handle
the latest and sophisticated weapons to ensure that the police are always ahead of the criminals
in terms of handling guns and weapons. Early action may be taken to have the infrastructure for
urban intervention training.
(Para 3.15.7 )

14
ACTION TAKEN
1.24.1 The endeavour of the Academy is to acquaint the probationers with latest weaponry and
gadgetry available, to deal with the challenges of terrorism, insurgency, Left Wing Extremism etc.
The Academy procures the sophisticated weapons and gadgetry to train the probationers in their
use. The Special Tactics Wing of the Academy is constantly upgrading its capacity to impart
tactical training in jungle operations and dealing with urban terrorism including room intervention,
hostage rescue etc.
RECOMMENDATION
EMERGING AREAS OF CRIMES
1.25 In the modern world, police officers need training not only on cyber laws, but also the
nuances of hacking to decode encrypted e-mails and other messages. The Committee, therefore,
strongly recommends that NPA should give thorough training to the police officers to deal with
computer hacking and related cyber crimes.
(Para 3.16.4 )
1.25.1 The Committee understands that a lot of sophistication is being brought into the crime, and
therefore, corresponding modification in training modules to cover changing aspects of crime are
but natural. The Committee desires that there is an urgent need to reverse the general perception
“that the police are always behind the criminals in terms of training and knowledge as well as
the use of arms and weapons”. NPA may take a lead in this regard.
(Para 3.16.5 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.25.2 In order to enable the Officer Trainees to face the emerging challenges of Cyber Crimes,
extensive inputs on investigation of Cyber Crimes are given. Resource Persons, both from
Government and Private IT sector, are invited to expose the officer to the latest tools and
techniques in Cyber Forensics.
1.25.3 The Cyber Forensic Lab s at the Academy have been strengthened with latest Cyber Forensic
tools. Hands-on sessions on the use of such tools to investigate Cyber Crimes are conducted for
officer trainees.
1.25.4 The Academy also conducts the In-Service courses on ‘Cyber Crimes’ at two levels. One
at the Basic level and another at the advanced level. Simulated exercises that involve seizing of
digital evidence and analyzing digital data using cyber forensic tools are conducted for the officers.
Constant updating in this regard is emphasized at the Academy in order to keep the police officers
abreast with latest advances in digital technology so as to enable them to meet the challenges
thrown by sophisticated and tech savvy criminals.
RECOMMENDATION
KEY CONCERN AREAS OF WORKING OF THE ACADEMY AND ORGANIZATIONAL
DEVELOPMENT INTERVENTIONS(ODIS)
1.26 The Committee notes the key concern areas affecting the working of the academy and is
of the considered view that in order to over come key concern areas of the working of the academy,
specific Organizational, Development Interventions(ODI) are required to enable the Academy to
achieve its objectives and mission. Some of the issues such as staff/faculty, research wing and

15
foreign training have already been dealt, in detail, in the preceding paragraphs. The Committee,
however, recommends that the Ministry may consider all the issues and find solution to them so
as to strengthen the Academy. The Ministry may help NP A management undertake concerted efforts
to implement organizational development interventions to strengthen organizational structure and to
enhance the functional proficiency of the Academy.
(Para 3.17.1 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.26.1 The Academy has been continuously endeavouring for organizational development and
improvement. The recommendation of the DPSC for concerted efforts in Organisational
Development Intervention is welcome and the Academy is in complete agreement with the same.
The NPA shall prepare master plan for organizational development intervention and undertake efforts
in this direction.
FURTHER OBSERV ATION
1.26.2 The Committee may be apprised of ‘Master Plan’ as proposed to be prepared by NPA
for Organizational Development Intervention and steps/effort taken in that direction.
RECOMMENDATION
PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF NPA
1.27 The Committee hopes that the outcome of performance evaluation of NP A done by
Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI), Hyderabad would be of immense use for
strengthening NP A and its programmes. The Committee also desires that BPR&D may conduct an
independent evaluation of the basic and MCTP Training imparted at NP A.
(Para 3.18.3 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.27.1  The BPR&D has been requested for conducting an independent evaluation of the basic and
MCTP training imparted at NPA with the help of senior retired police officers. These retired and
senior police officers will also be asked to re-visit the existing training modules in NPA and suggest
ways and means to make them more field oriented by introducing practical exercises, case studies,
simulation exercises, field visits etc so that the training becomes more relevant for the field. The
outcome of the above evaluations will be sent to MHA after receipt of the reports.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.27.2 The Committee would like to be apprised of the report on independent evaluation of
the basic and METP Training imparted at NPA when submitted by BPR&D and further action
taken thereon.
RECOMMENDATION
SWOT-ANALYSIS OF THE WORKING OF THE ACADEMY
1.28 The Committee has dealt most of the issues in preceding paras and gave its
recommendations. One area of concern for the Committee is lack of priority for training for police
in the States. This is a big challenge and needs to be addressed. The Ministry of Home Affairs

16
may start new scheme for strengthening police training in the States. On making Academy more
relevant and reducing gap between rules of law and field reality, existing modules may be revisited
with more field orientation.
(Para 3.20 )
ACTION TAKEN
1.28.1 (a) Based on the training gap analysis done by BPR&D for the various States and UTs in
2008-09 and on MHA’s recommendations, the 13
th Finance Commission has sanctioned Rs.2266
crores for strengthening the training infrastructure in various States. (b) A meeting was held with
the ADG (Trg)/IG (Trg) of all the States and UTs in BPR&D Hqrs., on 09.11.2012 wherein the
States have been requested to re-assess the training capacity gap taking into consideration the basic
training, the pre-promotional courses and the regular refresher courses for the various ranks in the
police. The above data will be analysed in BPR&D Hqrs. (c) The Government has also sanctioned
a Training Intervention Plan in which HRD studies will be carried out in 20 States/UTs and
recommendations will be made on training interventions.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
1.28.2 The Committee hopes that the amount of Rs. 2266 crore sanctioned by 13
th Finance
Commission would go long way for strengthening the training infrastructure in various
States. After the HRD studies are completed, a road map may be prepared for training
intervention in the State Police at the earliest.

RECOMMENDATION
SELECTION OF FACULTY
2.1 The Committee feels that since the nature and style of crimes are changing due to
technological development, modernization and sophistication, faculty needs to be chosen with great
care. Stringent yardsticks have to be laid down for the selection of faculty not only at the teaching
staff level but also at the level of Assistant Directors and Deputy Directors. The teaching staff
from all fields viz, law, business management, human resource management, police science, forensic
sciences, criminology, sociology, psychology, etc. must be selected with due care keeping in view
the requirement of the academy and also taking into account its role and the responsibility. The
Committee also understands that the post of the Assistant Directors, is very important and their
selection should be done through a stringent selection procedure. High caliber, integrity and
efficiency should be the criteria for selection.
(Para 1.7.6 )
ACTION TAKEN
2.1.1 As per present practice, Director of the Academy selects the faculty who meets the
essential criteria and recommend his/her name for posting to the Academy. Appointment of the
recommended officers are made on their services being made available by the State Government.
In addition, Director NPA is authorised to invite specialists from the fields of law, business
management, human resource management, police science, forensic sciences, criminology,
sociology, psychology, etc as guest faculty.

RESEARCH WING OF NPA

(NIAR) was established by LBSNAA, Mussorie in 1995 as a Training and Research Wing of the

Research’ instead of a Centre for Applied Research on the line of National Institute of
Administrative Research (NIAR). An early decision may be taken and sufficient infrastructure may
be created near the campus of the Academy for the purpose.
(Para 1.11.6 )

consultation with Ministry of Finance.

BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS

AUDIT OBJECTION

RECOMMENDATION
INDOOR VS. OUTDOOR TRAINING
2.6 Though the quantum of the indoor and outdoor training cannot be fixed in terms of
percentage, however, sufficient outdoor training must be imparted to have the physical fitness of
the police personnel while indoor training should be so adequately imparted to ensure that the
police personnel possess requisite understanding of law and jurisprudential knowledge. The NPA
may have a relook at the present curriculum and reviewed with experts.
(Para 2.3.4 )
ACTION TAKEN
2.6.1 A comprehensive review of the Indoor and Outdoor training was carried out in Workshops
held in the year 2009 in the Academy in which police officers from all over India and other experts
took part. After extensive deliberations, the recommendations of the Workshop resulted in
formulation of new IPS Probationers’Final Examination Rules 2012, in which not only two more
new papers- (1) Internal Security and (2) Investigation-II were incorporated but also the weightage
of Outdoor subjects like Field Craft and Tactics was increased from 50 marks to 200 marks. The
outdoor syllabus was updated to deal with the new challenges posed by Urban Terrorism, Left-
Wing Extremism, Insurgency and other complex Law and Order problems taking place in the field.
2.6.2 The present syllabus of Outdoor Training not only takes care of the physical fitness of the
IPS probationers but is also designed to equip them with necessary skills in police tactics along
with understanding of law and jurisprudence. In addition to the above, Academy had asked ASCI
to conduct “Quality Audit” for faculty of the NPA for further improvement.
RECOMMENDATION
MID-CAREER TRAINING PROGRAMME (MCTP)
2.7 The Committee notes that the Academy is collaborating with some of the foreign universities
of reputation viz Cambridge, Charles Stuart and London School of Business for conducting its
pioneer Mid-Career Training Programme for senior Police-personnel. However, the Committee feels
that the Academy should also explore collaboration with institution in other countries having
expertise in Police Training and Development (T&D for police) with the purpose of not only
improving capabilities and skill among serving police officers to combat effectively the ever
changing wide ranging challenges of terrorism, naxalism, caste and communal conflict, drug
trafficking, accidents, natural calamities and other disasters, but also to evolve different training
modules concerning standard policing practices to make the Academy a centre of excellence. The
committee, in this regard, recommends that NP A management should prepare a comprehensive
strategy in this direction for further foreign collaboration and seek the requisite approval from the
Government for implementation. Besides different phases of MCTP programmes, need based
refresher courses may also be organized for a week at regular intervals.
(Para 2.5.8 )
ACTION TAKEN
2.7.1 (a) Besides Mid Career training Programme various other training programmes are organised
in collaboration with other countries like USA, France, Germany. During last three years 36 such
courses have been organised and 572 police officers have been trained. However further
possibilities of foreign collaboration will be explored.

20
(b) NPA is already conducting regular specialized and refresher courses at regular
intervals, as a part of senior courses.
RECOMMENDATION
FACULTY AND LINKAGES
2.8 The Committee notes that the Academy does not invite faculty or resource persons from
abroad and the main reason is lack of incentives and remunerations. However under institutions
tie up for MCTP , foreign resource persons are also involved. The Committee is of the view that
whenever any foreign experts come to India, such visits may be made use of by organizing their
sessions for both basic training and MCTP .
(Para 2.8.5 )
ACTION TAKEN
2.8.1 At present when foreign experts visit the Academy for MCTP their services are utilized for
Basic Course also as per their availability.
2.8.2 The courses offered by foreign agencies are organized at SVP NPA as per suggestion of
Bureau of Police Research & Development (BPR&D). The last course offered by Federal Bureau
of Investigation (FBI), USA ‘Interview and Interrogation Training’ was conducted at SVP NPA
Academy, Hyderabad from April 16-20, 2012 and 35 Police officers attended this course.
RECOMMENDATION
TRAINING SCHEDULE
2.9 The Committee is not satisfied with the cryptic reply of the Ministry. The Committee is,
therefore, of the view that there needs to be some institutional safeguards to the syllabi and
curriculum. Attempt to derail the training schedule should not be allowed.
(Para 2.12.1 )
ACTION TAKEN
2.9.1 The overall working of the Academy is supervised by the Academy Board, headed by the
Union Home Secretary as Chairman and other members comprising of CPOs, State Police Chiefs,
other eminent experts from the fields of management, social science, media etc. Any change in the
syllabi of Basic Training Course can be carried out only with the approval of the Board and MHA.
Similarly, the ultimate performance of how the training has been carried out is judged through the
examinations in both indoor and outdoor subjects which are assessed by outside examiners.
Therefore, there are inbuilt safeguards to not allow derailment of training schedule of IPS
probationers.
RECOMMENDATION
PREPARATION OF CHARGE SHEET
2.10 The Committee recommends that IPS probationers as well as the in-service officers must
be imparted adequate training to enhance their supervising skill so that FIRs and charge sheets must
be prepared in a comprehensive manner. The probationers should be made fully conversant with
the procedure of preparation of charge sheet and framing charges.
(Para 3.8.1 )

21
ACTION TAKEN
2.10.1 In order to ensure better supervision of cases especially investigation and preparation of
charge sheet, the Academy conducts a number of simulated exercises comprising to criminal cases
of different nature. This effort has been further strengthened by effectively utilizing the Model
Police Station platform. As part of these simulation exercises for the probationers are given hands
on experience in preparing charge sheet. In addition, the supervisory skills are imparted through
the module on scrutiny of case files. In order to improve the quality of investigation and charge
sheet, matter will be taken up with State govts by the BPR&D so that these are incorporated in
the training of NGOs by the S tate Police Training Academies.
