41
OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
OF THE COMMETTEE — AT A GLANCE
Declaration of Kashmiri Migrants as Internally Displaced persons
The Committee desires that the Ministry should ensure that Migrants be provided all
the facilities for rehabilitation as are provided to a displaced community. (Para 2.1.9)
Conducive Environment for Return to the Valley
The Committee is of the view that after so many years since the exodus took place
and especially after declaration of ambitious packages for the return of Migrants,
improvement on the ground has been scanty and just one family has returned to the Valley
since the announcement of the package. There can be two explanations for such an
extremely poor response from the community: either (i) the package is not attractive
enough; or (ii) the environment is not safe for them to return. The Committee also notes
that other components of the PM’s Package except the employment and transit
accommodation component, could not be initiated as they can come into force only after the
Migrant families return to the Valley. This has resulted in a strange situation where the
families refuse to return as the environment is not conducive enough while the government
refuses to pass the benefits to them as return is a precondition for availing the benefits.
The Committee also refuses to buy the Ministry’s explanation that lack of consensus among
various Migrant organizations for permanent return and settlement is the main reason
behind non-return of Migrants to the Valley. While there may be difference of opinion
between the organizations, the perception in the community is that the situation on the
ground is not at all conducive for return which is the main reason for the failure of the
plan rather than lack of consensus among the organizations. The Committee is therefore
of the opinion that some more components of the PM’s package should be opened up for
the Migrants without the conditionality of their return. This, in the view of the Committee,
will serve as a confidence building measure encouraging the families to return to the Valley.
(Para 2.1.11)
The Committee feels that the decision in the matter brooks no delay. The Committee
recommends that revision in the package may be sympathetically considered for early
implementation. (Para 2.1.13)
The Committee is saddened by the plight of Migrant families of Budgam who have
been forced by the circumstances beyond their control to live in resettlement camp in their
home State. The Committee, therefore, feels that the least the government can do is to
provide them enough housing units for settlement. The Committee therefore impresses
upon the Government that 505 units of transit accommodation may be allotted to them on
priority basis. (Para 2.1.16)
The Committee advises the Government to be extremely cautious in clearing the
names of militants for surrender. Militants who have shown signs of change of heart may
only be accommodated. (Para 2.1.18)
The Committee is of the opinion that strict action should be taken against
perpetrators. The Government should also send a message to the affected persons with

42
assurance that if their cases had not been filed, they should come forward to lodge their
cases without any fear. The Committee would also like to be apprised of the status of filed
cases along with conviction of perpetrators. (Para 2.1.20)
Condition of Pandits Living in the Valley
The Committee notes that more than 600 families are still residing in the Valley.
The Committee also notes that about 31 families had to be shifted to a transit camp due
to security reasons. The Committee in view of the prevailing conditions, desires that the
courage of such Kashmiri Pandit families still residing in the Valley should be appreciated
and they should be provided appropriate security. They may also be provided other facilities
as may be required. (Para 2.1.22)
Grant of minority status
The Committee notes that according to the State Government, the Kashmiri pandits
belong to Hindu religion and as such do not qualify for grant of minority status. However
the State Government feels that the issue of granting minority status needs to be examined
by the State Government from all angles. The Committee feels that the State of J&K has
a special status in Indian Constitution. The government of J&K should look into the
demand of the Kashmiri Pandit for confering on them minority status keeping in mind their
pitiable condition. (Para 2.1.24)
The role of Ministry of Home Affairs
The Committee is of the view that the situation of Migrants still remains neglected
several years after the exodus started. It may be due to extreme difficulty in resettlement
or wrong policies, but whatever may be the case the situation on the ground remains grim.
The Ministry of Home Affairs being the nodal agency cannot shirk away its responsibility
for not being able to improve the situation on the ground. The Committee exhorts the
Ministry to look for different solutions if the previous policies have not worked.
Implementation of Recommendations of the Inter-ministerial Team. (Para 2.1.26)
The Committee recommends that the remaining posts may be filled soon so that the
approved benefits are not unduly delayed. (Para 2.1.28)
White Paper on Exodus of Migrants
The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry of Home Affairs. The
Committee however feels that though all information on militancy in J&K may have been
well documented, but all the facts should be brought out in the form of a White Paper
covering all the developments in the matter in a single document for public information.
Unregistered families (Para 2.1.30)
The Committee notes that several Migrants’ associations have complained that there are a
large number of families of the Migrant community who remain unregistered. Though the
Ministry has claimed that all families which fulfil the criteria have been registered, the
Committee is of the view that since there are complaints of organizations of non
registration of a large number of families, the Ministry of Home Affairs should examine the
complaints in this regard and draw up a mechanism whereby families fulfilling the criteria
be registered without much hassle. (Para 2.1.32)

43
The Committee feels that keeping in mind the practical difficulties being faced by the
Migrants, the demand may be looked into. (Para 2.1.34)
Reasons for Failure of Schemes
The Committee strongly recommends that interaction with the representatives of the
Migrant groups should be frequently conducted in order to get the relevant feedback. In the
light of dismal response to the schemes, such feedback would be of immense importance for
focused implementation and course correction of the policy. (Para 2.1.38)
PM’s Package
The Committee is disappointed to note that even the 3000 posts provided by the
Central government are still to be filled, leave aside the other 3000 to be provided by the
State Government. The situation looks even more disappointing when seen in the light of
the fact that the other components of the PMs Package have not even taken off. Out of
the two components, i.e.  employment and accommodation, the targets of employment
component have not been even half met. (Para 2.1.43)
The Committee is also extremely disappointed by the response of the State
Government. It is the responsibility of the State Government to fulfil its share of the
promise. Amending the rule position and convincing the majority community about the need
for minority welfare schemes is in line with the welfare objective of the Government.
Hence, the State Government should move ahead and take positive steps by filling 3000
posts from Kashmiri Migrants. (Para 2.1.44)
The Committee is of the opinion that the State Government’s approach should be
flexible enough to consider transfer requests on compassionate grounds from any part of
the State to any other part of the State especially in the case of female employees. As far
as possible, female employees should be posted in areas close to the areas of their
husbands’ posting. The Committee is further of the opinion that the 21 requests of inter-
district transfers of female employees, close to their husbands’ workplace may be considered
positively on priority basis. (Para 2.1.46)
The Committee is of the view that though the objective of the Government to help
Migrants return to the Valley may be very noble, but the results on the ground have been
dismal. There can be no other reason than the security threats which looms large over them
for their not returning to their native places. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
the Government should show more flexibility in implementing the Package for better
results. (Para 2.1.47)
Slow implementation of PM’s package
The Committee feels that the required modifications in the PMs Package may be
carried out on priority basis so as to make the Package more attractive for the Migrant
community. The Committee is, however, not convinced by the reply of the Government, as
against a comprehensive package of Prime Minister amounting to R1618.40 crore in
April, 2008, only R104.52 crore till May, 2013 has been expended by the State Government
and since 2009 only four meetings of the Apex Committee have been held. In view of the
Committee, these open facts do not reflect committed, sincere and sympathetic approach
and course of action on the part of a responsive Government towards an aggrieved group
of people of the State. (Para 2.1.51)

44
Neglect of Jammu Region in PM Package
The Committee is of the opinion the compensation should be given where it is due
and no discrimination in this regard should be made. The State Government should look
into the issue so that the grievances of the affected people from outside the Valley may also
be suitably addressed. (Para 2.1.53)
Protection of Migrants’ Properties
The Committee is not satisfied with the evasive reply of the Government. The
Ministry of Home Affairs or the State Government have evaded the reply to the number of
complaints received and attended. The Ministry may discuss the matter with the
representatives of Migrants, get the details from them and get them verified from the State
Government. (Para 2.1.60)
The Committee recommends that the Central Government should look into the
proposal submitted by the State Government on priority basis so that the Migrants of the
hilly regions of Jammu may be adequately compensated. An early decision may be taken in
the matter. (Para 2.1.62)
Encroachment of Temple and Shrines
The Committee hopes that the Temples and Shrine Bill would address the grievances
of the Hindu community in the State. Efforts should be made to get the Bill passed in the
State Assembly at the earliest. It also recommends that the State Government should
seriously look into specific cases of grievances so that the confidence of the Migrants could
be won back. Migrant organizations may be asked to give details of specific cases.
(Para 2.1.67)
Educational Concessions to the Wards of Kashmiri Migrants
The Committee recommends that the Ministry of HRD should make an effort to
keep centralised data of the students belonging to the Kashmiri Migrants for better
implementation of its policies and keeping track of benefits reaching the wards of the
Migrants. The Committee understands that there is no special package to the Jammu
Migrants and it is for the State Government to grant the same. The Committee also notes
that scheme of scholarships to minorities is not being extended to Kashmiri Migrants and
the suggestion for extending the scholarship scheme to Kashmiri Migrants is being
considered by the Ministry of HRD. The Committee feels that the Migrants who have been
displaced due to hostile environment are not only religious minority in the State but also
have been economically deprived. Education is the only means that can improve the lot of
their future generations. The Committee therefore recommends that the suitable
scholarship scheme for such deprived J&K Migrants may also be evolved and extended to
the affected Migrants in J&K, while extending the present scheme. (Para 2.1.72)
Financial Assistance for Unemployed Youths
The Committee is disappointed to note the fact that there are no takers for the self
employment package of the Government. First, the conditionalities attached are stringent.
Secondly, the amount is not sufficient for starting an enterprise. The Committee is also of
the opinion that in today’s world it may not be possible for the Government to create jobs
for everyone. The youth should therefore look for self employment avenues. The
Committee feels that since the offtake of the scheme is very little, the option of increasing

45
the funds per individual for self-employment may be explored. This may be done to make
the scheme more attractive. The Government should be more realistic in its approach if it
does not want to remain satisfied with schemes just on paper. (Para 2.1.74)
The Committee recommends that the State Government should formulate a policy
instead of considering their cases on case to case basis, to assist the militancy affected
entrepreneurs to revive industrial activity among the affected community. (Para 2.1.76)
Employment in Central Government Services
The Committee recommends that the feasibility of the proposal of one job per
Migrant family may be looked into and an early decision may be taken. The Committee
recommends that the proposal of creating 1000 class-IV posts for unemployed Migrant
youths, who could not study beyond matriculation, may be sympathetically considered for
early implementation. (Para 2.1.82)
Issues related to teachers
The Committee recommends that the cases of 221 teachers who have been deprived
of employment due to overage may be sympathetically looked into as the people from the
Migrant community are suffering from various handicaps and therefore deserve sympathy
for the same. (Para 2.1.84)
Regularization of Contractual Teachers in Delhi
The Committee is saddened by the fact that after long years of services in the
teaching profession, teachers still have to go through the ordeal of appearing in
examinations, though with age relaxation, and are bereft of social security benefits
admissible to regular teachers till they are appointed on regular basis. In view of the
Committee, this seems to be a inhumane approach on the part of the government, whether
it be a State or Union. The Committee recommends that these teachers being from the
displaced Migrant community, may be given some extra points as may be decided, along with
age relaxation during the recruitment process of Delhi Subordinate Services Selection Board
for recruitment of teachers. (Para 2.1.87)
Relief to Migrants at Par with J&K rates
The Committee recommends that all States should provide relief to J&K Migrants at
par with J&K State so that they do not feel disadvantaged or discriminated. (Para 2.1.90)
Problems of Migrant Shopkeepers in INA Market, New Delhi
The Committee desires that action in regard to rehabilitation of displaced
shopkeepers from the migrant community in INA market, New Delhi may be taken on
priority basis. People from the migrant community who have left their native places due to
conditions beyond their control should not face undue delays in the allotment of Stalls.
(Para 2.1.92)
The Committee is of the opinion that the pretext given that Kashmiri Migrants are
not Indians for not allocating shops in INA market is highly objectionable. The complaint
may be looked into and action may be initiated against people involved in such blatant
discrimination. (Para 2.1.94)

46
Reimbursment of medical expenses
The Committee is surprised to note that out of a corpus fund of R5 crore for the
welfare of the Migrants for reimbursing medical expenses, the reimbursement has been
made to the tune of only R57.14 lakh since its creation i.e. 2007 and only around 200 claims
had been received. This looks unbelievable considering the fact that the Migrants are living
in poor financial conditions. The Committee is of the opinion that surely there are many
more genuine members of the community who are in need of medical aid. The Committee
recommends that the government should look into the reasons for limited coverage of the
scheme. It is also of the opinion that when the money is available, it must be cobwebs of
rules and procedures as well as formalities which are behind such limited coverage. The
Committee recommends that the procedure should be simplified by removing bottlenecks so
that maximum bonafide beneficiaries can take the advantage of this fund.
(Para 2.1.96)
The Sub-committee, during the visit to different Migrant camps in Srinagar and
Jammu learnt that several members of the affected community were suffering from deadly
diseases like cancer, kidney failure, etc. and need immediate help. The Committee strongly
recommends that the Ministry should provide additional facilities in the health centers
established in the camps for treating such deadly diseases. It also hopes that the Ministry
would also provide health insurance cover to Migrants for which budget has already been
earmarked. (Para 2.1.98)
Cash Relief
The Committee is extremely dissatisfied by the logic given by the Ministry for
limiting enhancement of the relief by Rs.400 per soul. The Committee notes the claim of
the Government that the thrust of its policy has been to ensure that the difficulties and
hardships of the Migrants are minimized and the needy families are provided an amount,
enough for sustenance and support. The Committee in this background fails to understand
how a meager enhancement of R400 per soul would be able to fight the inflationary
pressures in a big city like Delhi. The Ministry’s decision to totally disregard State
Government’s recommendation for enhancement of the relief to R10000 per family is
unfortunate. It, therefore, recommends that the recommendation of the State Government
may be accepted. (Para 2.1.102)
Problems and Delay in Verifications
The Committee recommends that all issues related to the verification process may
be resolved at the earliest so that request for cash relief made by genuine claimants may
be addressed. (Para 2.1.104)
Housing Assistance
The Committee recommends that the verification process for allotment of remaining
dwelling units may be conducted soon so that they can be allotted soon as there has already
been considerable delay in allotment. (Para 2.1.106)
The Committee is of the opinion that housing assistance under PM’s Package for the
Migrants has remained a non-starter as just one family has availed it. This again highlights
the fact that the most of the PM’s Package has not even taken off. Since the Government
is pinning its hopes for rehabilitation of Migrants on the PM’s Package, the outcome has
been extremely disappointing to say the least. The Committee feels that there is a need for

47
serious rethink on the policy. The Committee in this connection would like to suggest that
the demand of certain organizations that building reconstruction grant should not be a static
quantity and it should be on actual cost of construction and should vary from case to case
may be looked into. (Para 2.1.109)
The Committee also feels that the Package also needs financial revision so that the
few components of the Package which have been availed could be made more attractive.
(Para 2.1.110)
The Committee recommends that the construction of the rest of the accommodations
may be completed soon. If needed, more such units with proper amenities and connectivity
may be created in proportion to the number of people from the Migrant community joining
the work force in the State as presently these units are being shared by the employees in
a very congested manner. (Para 2.1.111)
The Committee also recommends that the Government should positively consider the
demand for provision of one unit of transit accommodation in the Valley on acceptance  of
employment. It is of the opinion that this would serve as a strong incentive for the Migrant
youths to take up jobs in the Valley. (Para 2.1.112)
Satellite Towns and Cluster Accommodation
The Committee welcomes the idea of creating cluster accommodations for the
Migrants in different districts. Keeping in mind the fact that the PM’s package in the
present form has not found many takers, innovative ideas like creating cluster
accommodation can fulfill the twin needs of the Migrants: (i) returning to their native
place; and (ii) returning in a safe environment. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that suitable land may be identified and acquired for the purpose and the scheme be
implemented in a reasonable time frame so that the objective of Migrant’s return does not
remain on paper but sees light of the day. (Para 2.1.115)
Construction of Additional Two-Room Tenements at Jammu
The Committee is of the opinion that since the number of families that have shown
interest in returning to the Valley in present circumstances has remained negligible, the
demand for construction of additional two-room tenements at Jammu may be looked into
if a substantial number of families are interested in staying at Jammu so that the
rehabilitation process could be taken forward in due course of time. (Para 2.1.117)
Problems of Jagti
The Committee is of the opinion that while there are no free lunches, and all
resources have a cost, the Government should look into the purchasing capacity of the
residents. Since they are displaced people who need Government help they should be made
to pay according to their capacity. The Committee, therefore, recommends that electricity
may be provided to them at a price they can pay. (Para 2.1.120)
The Committee recommends that the State Government should look into the
feasibility of setting up of Notified Area Committee for providing civic amenities in Jagti.
(Para 2.1.122)
The Committee recommends that the medical facilities in the upcoming hospital may
be started as soon as possible so that the hardships faced by the residents are mitigated.
(Para 2.1.124)

48
The Committee recommends that allotment of the remaining flats in Jagti may be
done on priority basis and the verification process for the same may be completed as soon
as possible. (Para 2.1.125)
Improvement of Living Conditions in Transit Accommodation in the Valley
The Committee feels that the grievances of the Migrant people residing in Jagati and
Talwara are quite genuine. The Committee strongly recommends that the State Government
should take all necessary steps required to improve the living conditions in the Migrant
camps at Jagati and Talwara. (Para 2.1.129)
Political Empowerment
The Committee is of the view that migration of a large number of people had been
an extraordinary incident in a democratic country, whose Constitution guarantees every
citizen to live at the place of his desire. Hence, this unprecedented incident deserves
appropriate political empowerment of this community by taking recourse to suitable steps
by the Central Government as well as State Government of J&K. The Committee
hopes that its suggestion will be taken in right perspective with positive approach.
(Para 2.1.133)
Updation of Voters List of The Migrants and Issue of Photo I-Cards
The Committee recommends that the issues of updation of voter lists and
simplification of voting procedures for the Migrants may be appropriately taken up with the
Election Commission so that the Migrants are not made bereft of their voting rights as
citizens of the State. (Para 2.1.137)
The Committee is surprised by the cumbersome nature of the electoral process
designed for the Migrants. No wonder that they allege the whole system has been instituted
to discourage them. While that may not be the case, simplification of the process is
obviously required. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government may take
up the matter with Election Commission so that the Migrants can rightfully take part in
the electoral process like rest of their fellow citizens. (Para 2.1.138)
The Committee during its deliberations with the Migrants was informed by several
representatives that they face tremendous difficulties in getting various certificates for
establishing identity, residency etc. The Committee is of the opinion that since the
representatives have complained about the cumbersomeness of the process, the same may
be simplified and made Migrant friendly. The entire procedure may be re-looked.
(Para 2.1.141)
Issues related to Special Police Officers (SPOs)
The Committee is of the opinion that the honorarium for SPOs may be increased
from R3000/- per month as the sum is too meager. Keeping in mind the tough nature of
their job, and in order to keep them motivated, the demand for increase may be
sympathetically considered. The Committee also recommends that the policy for absorption/
conversion of SPOs as Constables/Followers may also be implemented so that it may serve
as an incentive for SPOs and keep them motivated. (Para 2.1143)
Appointment on Compassionate Ground
The Committee is not satisfied with the routine reply given on a significant issue of

49
giving employment to a family member of a Government employees/civilian/member of an
armed Forces or para military forces, who dies as a result of militancy related action or due
to enemy action on the Line of Actual Control/International Border within the State of
Jammu and Kashmir. The Committee strongly feels that such cases deserve due attention
and disposal on priority. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that all cases of
appointment on compassionate grounds should be decided at the earliest in a time bound
manner, with proper monitoring at higher level. (Para 2.1.145)
Issues related to Village Defence Committees (VDCs)
The Committee is of the opinion that keeping in mind the strategic nature of role
being played by the VDCs to thwart terrorist acts and despite the volunteer nature of the
job, the Government may look into the feasibility of paying honorarium to further motivate
them. (Para 2.1.47)
Non-payment to Migrants
The Committee takes a serious note of the fact brought before it. The Committee
is of the firm view that decisions of Courts should be honored without delay, if not appealed
in higher Court or for review by the same Court. The Committee therefore strongly
recommends that the all the issues related to payment as well as arrears thereof may be
cleared/settled at the earliest, keeping in mind their challenged financial condition. The
Committee desires that status in this regard should be monitored at the appropriate level
in the Union Ministry of Home Affairs. (Para 2.1.149)

REPORT 
I, the Chairman, Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee, present this Eighteenth Report relating to the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 
1995•. The Bill seeks to make special provisions for the prevention of, and for coping with 
terrorist and disruptive activities and to supplement the criminal law. 
2. In pursuance of the rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred .. the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya 
Sabha on the 18th May, 1995 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and 
report within two days. 
3. Accordingly, the Committee considered the Bill in its meeting held on the 19th May, 
1995 and also heard the Home Secretary. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report in its meeting held on the 22nd 
May, 1995. 
5. Some Members of the Committee gave amendments/suggestions on the Bill which 
are appended to the report. 
6. In his presentation, the Home Secretary stated that the following provisions under 
TADA which were either misused or had the potential of being misused are proposed to be 
dropped in the new legislation:-
(i) Section 5 of TADA Act makes unauthorised possession~f arms in a notified area 
an offence. The Arms Act provides for deterrent punishment for possession of 
certain classes of unauthorised arms. Therefore, there is no need to repeat the 
provision in the new legislation. 
(ii) Section 15 of T ADA Act provides that confessions made to a police officer are 
admissible in evidence. This is against the grain of the normal provision of the 
Indian Evidence Act, 1872 whereunder statements made to the police are not 
admissible as evidence. 
(iii) Section 21(1)(c) and (d) lays down certain presumptions relating to confessions. 
This section provides that if it is proved that one of the accused makes a confession 
that the other has committed the offence, it shall be presumed that the other 
(accused) has committed the offence. It also provides that if it is proved that an 
accused has made a confession to any person other than a police officer, it shall be 
presumed that he has committed such an offence. 
(iv) Section 20(8)(b) provides that a court shall not grant bail unless it is satisfied that

**Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part-II, dated the 18th May, 1995. 

there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused is not guilty Of an 
offence under T ADA. This provision made it extremely difficult to obtain bail in 
TADA cases. 
The Home Secretary also enumerated the following safeguards in the proposed 
legislation to check its abuse:-
(i) Presently under TADA Act an appeal from the designated court lies to the 
Supreme Court. It has been argued that under Indian conditions , with prevailing 
poverty, it is difficult for poor people to approach straightaway the Supreme Court . 
In the new legislation, an appeal has, therefore, been provided to the High Court . 
(ii) As suggested by the Supreme Court, a provision has been made -that investigation 
in the cases relating to terrorist and disruptive activities should be done by an 
officer not below in rank than that of a Deputy Superintendent of Police. This 
would cut down the misuse substantially. 
(iii) A provision has been made that for vexatious , malicious or corrupt actions by the 
police whereby any person is wrongly arrested or threatened to be arrested , are 
made punishable with an imprisonment upto one year or with fine, or with both. 
(iv) In a normal case any police officer can 1egister a case, make an investigation , and 
file charge-sheet . But, in the new legislation there are three stages. Firstly, no 
information about the commission of an offence shall be recorded by the police 
without the prior approval of the District Superintendent of Police . Secondly , the 
investigation of an offence shall not be done by a police officer below the rank of 
Deputy Superintendent of Police/ Assistant Commissioner of Police. Thirdly , no 
court shall take cognizance of an offence under this new legislation without the 
previous sanction of Inspector-General of Police/Commissioner of Police . 
7. Among the salient feature s of the present Bill, the Home Secretary mentioned the 
setting up of the Special Courts for speedy disposal of the cases, because if the cases relating 
to terrorism are also to be dealt with by the ordinary courts , it woufd take years together 
•before the case would come up for hearing or it may not come up for hearing at all. 
Secondly , the police custody is for thirty days as against sixty days under the TADA Act . 
The judicial custody which was earlier one year (six months divided into two parts) has been 
reduced to six months (in two parts of three months each). If the investigations are not 
completed within this period; the court has to be approached again. 
8. Several Members were of the view that the opposition to TADA today is based on 
thousands of T ADA cases made out against thousands of innocent persons and that the new 
legislation does not provide any relief to these! persons. The Home Secretary clarified that a 
criminal law had always prospective effect and not -applied retrospectively . The proposed 
legislation would come into force after it becomes an Act of Parliament and would apply to 
the offences committed thereafter. He further added that in respect of the old TADA cases, 
there_ is already a provision in sub-section (4) of section 1 of the TADA Act , according to 
which the old cases would continue ~o be dealt with as per the existing law of the land. The 
Home Secretary, however, apprised the Committee that the cases of T ADA detenues are 
being reviewed administratively at the Central and the State level as per the direction of the 
Supreme Court. Under this direction, high level administrative committees are to be 
constituted. At the Central level, the Committee is headed by the Home Secretary, and the 
Law Secretary and the Director, CBI as its members. At the State level, these Committees 
would consist of the Home Secretary, the Law Secretary and the Director-General of Police . 
In some cases, these Committees are beaded by Retd. High Court Judges. These 

Committees review the cases to see whether the T ADA provisions have been applied 
properly or not. As a result of this system of review, thousands of cases have been 
cancelled/withdrawn/filedlfADA provisions dropped benefiting a very large number of 
persons. In this context, the Home Secretary stated that these review Committees were 
being made more powerful and vigorous and they were also meeting regularly. 
9. In reply to another query regarding the need for statutory review Committee in the 
Bill, as in the case of National Security Act, Maintenance of Internal Security Act etc., the 
Home Secretary clarified that under the National Security Act and other preventive 
detention laws, there is no court and there is no trial. The detenue does not go to the court 
and the court has only wni jurisdiction. But in the present case a charge-sheet is filed, trial 
takes place and the court decide the case. The idea of statutory review C~mmittee would, 
therefore, be meaningless. So, there is a wide difference between the two. It is for this 
reason that the Supreme Court has observed that as regards pending T ADA cases, these 
should be admin'istratively reviewed. 
10. Some Members expressed the appreh&nsion that the new legislation might be 
misused against political opponents, trade unionists and workers. They were of the firm view 
that adequate safeguards should be there in the proposed fegislation to check its misuse. In 
reply to a quer y whether the proposed legislation has been brought after consulting the 
Chief Ministers, the Home Secretary stated that discussions had taken place with them and 
their views had been ascertained and the Bill has been prepared reflecting their views. 
11. Prior to considering this Bill, the Committee had occasion to discuss the TADA in 
its meetings held on the 4th and lOth May, 1995 and hear the Home Secretary in the matter. 
After deliberations, the general view which emerged in the Committee was that the T ADA 
Act should be repealed and either a separate legislation should be enacted to counter 
terrorism or the essential legal requirements to fight terrorism be incorporated in the normal 
laws of the land, with in-built safequards against misuse. The view of the Committee and the 
connected papers were forwarded to the Government for consideration. 
12. In view of the above and after hearing the Home Secretary and taking into 
consideration the views expressed by the Members on 19th May, 1995 the following views 
emerged while adopting the Report on the Bill on 22nd May, 1995:-
- The present bill was uot necessary as the existing laws of the land were adequate to 
curb the menace of the terrorism. 
- The bill in necessary to counter terrorism and disruptive activities. 
- The bill should be criculated to all Chief Ministers for their views and public opinion 
should also be elicited. 
- The present law should not be a permanent statute and should be periodically 
reviewed after every three years. 
- Compensation should be given to innocent victims of the TADA. 
- The direction of the Supreme Court regarding Review Committees should be made a 
part of the new legislation. 
- An integrated view should be taken of the whole situation and that the existing Jaws 
such as N.S.A., D.I.R etc. were quite adequate to meet the problem of terrorism 
and disruptive activities. So, there was no need to incorporate some of the· provisions 
of the T ADA in the new legislation. 
- The definitions in the new .legislation should be modified and made specific to check 
its misuse. 

In the light of the suggestions, views, observations and amendments made by the 
members, the Committee adopts this Report on the Bill for consideration of the House.

Dear Sir, 
I propose the following amendments to the Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1995:-
1. The Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1995 seeks to replace the 10 year old Terrorist 
and Disruptive Activities (prevention) Act (TADA). Even though TADA was 
draconian the saving grace was that it was time-bound, unlike the present Bill which 
would become a permanent law in our statute book. There is no need for making 
this law as perpetual. I suggest three-year time limit for the operation of the law 
after which it may be reviewed according to the needs of the times. 
2. Oauses 3 and 4 define terrorism and disruptive activities. These definitions are not 
precise but nebulous and capable of misuse. Clause 3 contains .15 independent 
offences. It is nothing but rearrangement of offences against the State as enumerated 
in Macaulay's Penal Code. This clause should be made precise so as to exclude trade 
union activities and political activities like peaceful 'hartal' etc. Otherwise a country 
made bomb or a gelatine stick can easily be planted and false charges may be cooked 
up. 
3. Oause 4 deals with disruptive activity. It enumerates several independent offences 
and is a mere restatement of provisions dealing with the public tranquility in the 
Indian Penal Code. We find in some of these provisions the Kafkaesque dimensions. 
For instance under sub clause (3) of clause 4 'prophecy' 'prediction' 'pronouncement' 
have been made offences. The astrologers and god-men that the members of the 
Cabinet at Delhi frequent may qualify for being contingent terrorists should the~ 
dilate on their longevity. 
4. Oause 8(7) says the judge or the additional judge of the Special Court may continut 
in service even after superannuation i.e. until the case is over. This will give place t1 
picking up of selective judges and therefore this provision should be deleted. 
5. Oause 14 provides for keeping the identity and address of a witness as secret an 
permits avoidance of their names and addresses in the Special C'...ourt's orders c 
judgements or in any records of the case accessible in public. Probably it is due t 
the apprehension that the said witness may be harmed. Yet, it is not fair. TI 
identity should be known to the accu&ed and cross-examination of the witness is 
must for any fair trial. Therefore, this obnoxious provision ~ould be deleted. 
6. Clause 18(2) :xtends the remand period. One of the factors that caused the misuse 
T ADA was the difficulty in getting the bail for the accused. The present provisi• 
may likewise tempt the authorities to misuse the said Act and therefore I comme 
for its deletion.

THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT BILL, 1995 
NOTE 
The Criminal Law Amendment Bill, 1995 has been introduced on 18th May, 1995 in the 
Rajya Sabha. In the Statement of Objects and Reasons (Para 4) given for the present Bill, it 
has been mentioned that Chief Ministers and Governors of States have been consulted "and 
in the light of views expressed by the Chief Ministers and Governors as also the Leaders of 
various political parties, the Government have decided not to extend the life of the Terrorist 
and Disruptive Activities (Prevention) Act." This seems to be far from the truth. The 
consensus in the Chief Ministers' Conference was in favour of the retention of the TADA 
Act with some modifications to provide safeguards against its possible misuse. 
Section 17 - Bail 
The provisions for granting bail have now been diluted to the extent that even hardened 
terrorists would be able to get bail easily. This will have serious repercussions particularly in 
J & K where terrorism is at its extreme. Under the T ADA, an appeal from the designated 
court lies with the Supreme Court. This should continue. 
Section 24(2) - Punishment of Police Officials 
Under the proposed sub-section (2) of Section 24, punishment of imprisonment upto J 
year has been provided for policemen or corruptly or maliciously proceed or threaten t< 
proceed against any person for an offence under the new Jaw. This provision of actim 
against policemen would totally demoralise the police force and no police officer would lik• 
to proceed under the new law for fear of prosecution. When the proposed law alread 
provides for registration. of a case with the approval of the SP and launching of prosecutio 
only with the sanction of the IG, Police, there is no need at all to provide for prosecution c 
policemen. Hence, this sub-section should be deleted. 
Strengthening the Bill 
As pointed out above, the Criminal Law Amendment Bill as it has been drafted seen 
to have no teeth to deal with the threat of terrorism and disruptive elements. The curre· 
situation in the country requires a stringent law to deal with the anti-national elemen 
seeking to spread terrorism in the country. The proposed law would be ineffective in dealiJ 
with the menace of terrorism.

CHAPTER-I
DADRA AND NAGAR HA VELI
1.1 INTRODUCTION
1.1.1 Dadra and Nagar Haveli was born on 17 th December, 1779 as a result of a treaty between
Portuguese and Marathas. The Marathas assigned 72 villages to Portuguese in return of their
friendship and the group of 72 villages came to be known as Dadra and Nagar Haveli. The
Portuguese ruled this territory until its liberation on 2
nd August, 1954. After its liberation, the
Administration was carried on by local body known as Free Dadra and Nagar Haveli Administration
till its merger with the Indian Union on 11
th August, 1961. Consequently, the Free Dadra and Nagar
Haveli Administration was succeeded by formal statutory Administration headed by an Administrator.
1.1.2 This UT has an area of 491 sq.km. and comprises of two enclaves viz. (1) Dadra and
(2) Nagar Haveli. Five villages in the UT viz. Dadra, Naroli, Samarvarni, Masat and Rakholi are
treated as statutory Census Towns in population Census 2011. Besides, this UT has 65 villages, one
District Panchayat, 11 Village Panchayats and one Municipal Council. Silvasa is the capital city of
this UT.
1.2 PRESENTATION BEFORE THE SUB-COMMITTEE
1.2.1 The Sub-Committee on Administration of UTs in its sitting held on 21
st October, 2013 heard
Joint Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs along with Administrator, UT of Daman & Diu and Dadra
& Nagar Haveli on various aspects of administration of UTs in order to take stock of the
implementation of projects/schemes and programmes undertaken by the UT Administration.
1.2.2 The Administrator holding charge of two UTs of Daman & Diu and Dadra & Nagar Haveli
made power point presentations on UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli. The highlights of the
presentations were as follows:
● The population of UT is about 3.44 lakh consisting of about 1.94 lakh male and
1.5 lakh female with 1.8% and 52% SC and ST populations. The sex ratio is 774
against the national average of 940. However, the sex ratio in the 0-6 years age group
is 926 against national average of 914.
● The literacy rate is 76.20% as against 74.04% of India. The male and female literacy
rates of UT are 85.20% and 64.30% respectively. The SC literacy rate is 78.25%
against 54.32% national average; however, ST literacy rate is lower at 41.24% against
47.08% national average.
● Budget allocations to the local bodies and municipalities have been on increasing trend,
it has been increased from R41.00 crore and R13.03 crore in 2008-09 to
R156..35 crore and R36.90 crore in 2013-14. However Committee notes that the
allocations in percentage terms have dwindled down from R48.66 in 2008-09 to R28.74
in 2013-14.

2

R6907 in 2013-14. The total allocation in 2012-13 and 2013-14 has been R564.70 crore

62% has been utilized upto September, 2013.
● In Dadra and Nagar Haveli, 98 per cent power is utilized by the industries and
100 per cent recovery of charges is made. Silvassa is basically the marble capital of
the country as all the Italian marble imported in raw form is cut and polished for being
supplied to the rest of the country. Since T&D losses are lower than Daman and Diu,

construction of six high level bridges, computerization of V AT, study of science

● Cost of construction of six high level bridges has been estimated at R54.17 crore and
cost of construction of nine new bridges has been pegged at 49.67 crore. A ring road

● Water Supply/irrigation projects comprise Integrated Management Plan with Estimated
cost of 
R255 crore and construction of several Check Dams at several locations in

Starting of MRI services and setting up of Medical College and Nursing College is

professional courses.
● For tourism, several projects like Lake Front Development at Dudhani, River Front
Development on Daman Ganga River at Silvassa, development of Silvassa Haat,
construction of State Museum at Silvassa, Development of Butterfly Park and Prakruti

● About 9000 old age, disabled and widow beneficiaries are getting Pension. Bicycles
have been given to 3500 girl students. 14000 students are covered under
Supplementary Nutrition Programme and free text books, stationery and uniforms are
provided to all SC and ST students.
● New initiatives such as Sankalp- development of model village, other rural

1.2.3 The UT Administration also raised the following issues/demands for attention of the sub-
Committee:
● Opening of Passport Seva Kendra at Silvassa/Daman is required
● Clearance of the proposal of construction of Ring Road pending with MoRTH is
required.
● SFC clearance for Integrated Water Management Plan is pending with Department of
Drinking Water.
● SFC clearance for 220 KV Electric Sub Station is pending with Ministry of Power; and
● Allocation of Power has been reduced by the Ministry of Power, which needs to the

1.2.4 The Committee notes the submissions made by the Administrator of the UT and
makes following recommendations:
● The Ministry of External Affairs should consider for opening of a Passport Seva
Kendra either at Silvassa or Daman to cater to the needs of people of both the UTs.
● The construction of ring road in Silvassa Town area is necessary as there has
been fast increase in population growth in recent period. The Ministry of Road
Transport and Highways should accord early clearance for proposed construction
of Ring Road. Besides, the UT Administration should also make endeavour to
improve existing road networks as well as construction of new
roads for improving connectivity which will help best flow of goods and services.
● The Committee is of the view that UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli in tandem with
Government of India should address the issue of water supply on priority basis.
This integrated water management plan with a cost of R255 crore should be
implemented as soon as possible as it would help solve the problem of drinking
water throughout the UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli. The Committee is of the
considered view that the Standing Finance Committee clearance for Integrated
Water Management Plan pending with Department of Drinking Water, Ministry
of Rural Development of Government of India should be prioritized.
● The Ministry of Power should give clearance for 220 KV Electric SubStation at
Waghchhipa. The Committee also recommends that allocation of Power which
has been reduced by the Ministry of Power should be restored as the present
allocation is not adequate for the full requirement of the industries.

1.3 ISSUES
1.3.1 The Sub-Committee on Administration of UTs made study tour to the UT of Dadra and
Nagar Haveli on 5 th November, 2013. During its tour the Sub-Committee visited new circuit house
building, Daman Ganga River Front Development Project, Municipal Drinking Water Supply Project,
Vinobha Bhave Civil Hospital (VBCH) in Silvassa. The Sub-Committee also visitied Integrated Dairy
Development Scheme in Masat, New Hospital Building at Khanvel, SANKALP project at Kalsunpada
and proposed school building at Mandoni.
New Circuit House Building at Silvassa
1.3.2 The Sub-Committee noted that the new circuit house building was under construction. The
Sub-Committee noted the building plan of the proposed circuit house, the proposed amenities, etc.
there.
1.3.3 The Committee desires that the construction of new circuit house building at Silvassa
will be completed soon without time and cost overrun.
Daman Ganga River Front Development Project
1.3.4 Daman Ganga River Front Development Project is being undertaken on river Daman Ganga
at Silvassa. The objective of developing the River Front along River Daman Ganga is to develop
the place as one of the major tourist attractions and to provide an appropriate place for recreation.
A master plan for the River Front for a stretch of about 3.00 km. on the bank has been prepared
by the DNHPDA. According to the UT Administration, work order has been issued for construction
of retaining wall 1
st Phase (entire stretch of retaining wall which is approximately 3 kms.) for an
amount of R12.89 crore. The UT Administration has informed that the project will be completed
in June, 2015.
1.3.5 The Committee recommends that Daman Ganga River Front Development Project on
river Daman Ganga at Silvassa may be completed as per schedule. The Committee also
recommends that the UT Administration should make all out efforts to project Daman
Ganga River Front as an important tourist destination and give due publicity to it so that
tourist flow to the UT could increase.
Municipal Drinking Water Supply Project, Silvassa
1.3.6 The Administration is making efforts to provide drinking water supply in all habitations of
the territory throughout the year. Besides, the Administration has initiated long term plans like
Integrated Water Management Plan, Urban Water Augmentation Plan and water harvesting
structures, the piped water supply schemes in interior area of Mandoni and Dudhani in 2011-12
and so far 85% of work has been completed.
1.3.7 The existing scheme is designed for 40000 souls while population as per 2001 census itself
is 50,456. Thus the present system is not adequate. The tax concession given to industry in 1994
has increased industrial activities in Silvassa and there is manifold increase in population. Present
house connection is 2,000 against required 15,5000 connections. As drainage system is to be
implemented in near future, minimum 135 lpcd flow rate is required. Thus the present system
cannot match with present requirements. The existing distribution network laid in is not
commensurate with requirement, leading to uneven distribution of water. The UT Administration is
implementing water supply scheme for Silvassa and Amli Township in UT of Dadra and Nagar
Haveli. The project is to be implemented within Silvassa municipal area.
1.3.8 The work of water supply scheme in UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli has been entrusted
to OIDC as deposit work from Silvassa Municipal Council (SMC) on 28/09/20011. The documents

5
regarding project and the fund for this project amounting to R26,63,00,000/- were transferred to
OIDC on 1 st November, 2011. OIDC after taking necessary approval and scrutinizing the tender
document and also following the CPWD guidelines published the Notice Inviting Tender (NIT) on
12th December, 2011 for the above work with an estimated amount of R23,93,10,745/-.The
Sub-Committee visited OIDC Water Treatment Plant.
1.3.9 The Committee recommends that a comprehensive study should be done to address
the issue of drinking water for the population as well as for industrial units. The
Committee recommends that the UT Administration should expedite completion of long term
plans like Integrated Water Management Plan, Urban Water Augmentation Plan and water
harvesting structures, the piped water supply schemes in interior area of Mandoni and
Dudhani without any procedural delays.
Vinoba Bhave Civil Hospital, Silvassa
1.3.10 As stated earlier, the public health services are provided through one 241 bedded District
Hospital at Silvassa, one 50 bedded Community Health Centre at Khanvel, six Primary Health
Centres (All 6 PHC are 24x7 with 1 MO, 1 AYUSH doctor, 3 Staff Nurses) and three Rural
Dispensaries. The Sub-Committee visited the VBCH hospital, a multispecialty District Hospital. The
Hospital is providing high quality, affordable and accessible health care services to the community
through timely, safe, effective, patient centered and efficient quality healthcare efforts.
1.3.11 The Sub-Committee made a round of the Hospital and visited several departments including
the Telemedicine Centre installed in the Hospital to see the patients being treated through video
conferencing with other specialist doctors of other States. It was informed that the reports like
blood reports, X-rays, ECG, etc. of the patients are scanned and are sent to the specialist
concerned. The specialist, after analysis of the reports and after having conversation with the
patient through VC, recommends treatment. In case they are suggested to see the specialist
personally for further treatment, they are referred to these doctors and they are treated on priority
basis.
1.3.12 The Committee was impressed with the modern medical facilities available in Vinoba
Bhave Civil Hospital using new technologies. However, the Committee recommends that the
existing infrastructure in the said hospital should be upgraded for treatment of chronic
diseases. Sufficient fund may be provided for this purpose. The Committee recommends
that the administration should further improve health infrastructure in the UT of Dadar and
Nagar Haveli so that people residing in the UT could avail best health facilities.
Integrated Dairy Development Scheme, Masat
1.3.13 Dairying is an important source of subsidiary income to small/marginal farmers and
agricultural labourers as agriculture is mostly seasonal and there is a possibility of finding
employment throughout the year for many persons through dairy farming. According to the UT
Administration, the scheme has been implemented during last financial year 2012-13 for exclusively
women beneficiaries. The pattern of Assistance is @ 35% (40% in case of SC or ST or BPL
farmers of the project outlay (capital outlay), subject to a ceiling of R1.75 lakhs ( R2.00 lakhs
for SC or ST or BPL farmers) for unit of 10 animals by UT Administration of Dadra and Nagar
Haveli.
1.3.14 Besides, financial assistance, hundred bags of cattle feed (concentrate of 50 kgs. bag each)
and 100 kgs. of mineral mixture (1 kg. bag each) per beneficiary are provided @ 50% of the actual
purchase cost of cattle feed and mineral mixture as one time initial benefit by UT Administration
of Dadra and Nagar Haveli, from its Annual Budget through Village Level Milk Co-operative

6
Societies. It was informed that 18 Dairy Units with 350 beneficiaries have been covered and it is
proposed to establish 20 Dairy units during current financial year 2013-14. Individual beneficiary
earns R3,500 to R4,000 per month as an additional income. There are sixteen Village Dairy Co-
operatives run exclusively by 465 women beneficiaries. Organization of five new Village Dairy Co-
operatives is under process. The Sub-Committee visited the Dairy farm and interacted with the
beneficiary women.
1.3.15 The Committee understands that Dairy Development is an important source to
enhance the level of income of small/marginal farmers and landless agricultural labourers
on a sustainable basis besides increasing milk supplies in the areas by increasing milk
production. The Committee recommends that Village Dairy Cooperatives should be opened
in every village of the UT which would help not only improve self sufficiency to the village
families but also enhance milk production and improve soil fertility and crop yields from
the manure obtained from animals. The Committee desires that more and more women
should be involved in the scheme as it would lead to their economic empowerment as well
as their participation in economic process.
Visit to new Hospital building, Khanvel
1.3.16 The Sub-Committee was informed that Khanvel is now developing as next capital town of
southern region of UT of Dadra and Nagar Haveli. The population of the town has to travel to
Silvassa to avail better medical facilities and therefore is facing hardships. Presently, these peoples
are availing medical facilities from existing 40 bedded Community Health Centre which remains
over crowded. Therefore, the UT Administration has decided to convert existing Community Health
Centre into a 100 bedded Sub-District hospital. The total built up area of the building will be
5756.00 sq. mt and the construction work has been awarded at the cost of Rs. 9.99 crores. This
work is proposed to be completed within 18 months and as per agreement, date of completion is
23
rd June, 2014.
1.3.17 The Committee notes the progress in the construction of 100 bedded Sub-District
Hospital to cater to the needs of people of Khanvel .The Committee desires that the
construction should be completed within stipulated time.
Visit to a village Kalsunpada adopted under CSR project ‘SANKALP‘
1.3.18 The Sub-Committee was informed that the UT Administration of Dadra and Nagar Haveli
has initiated CSR projects in the UT. The UT Administration under Corporate Social Responsibility
(CSR) has involved corporate sector and initiated a programme called “SANKALP” through which
all the tribal villages and hamlets have been divided into units and development of these tribal
villages has been entrusted to the industries which are coming forward under CSR.
1.3.19 According to the UT Administration, there are 70 villages and 515 Padas in the UT of Dadra
and Nagar Haveli and the work under the CSR activities started two year back in which one company
Jaicorp adopted a village named Sindoni to develop the basic facilities like Pakka Houses, Toilets, etc
and the work is under progress. Another 12 companies have shown their interest in the said scheme.
It was stated that there are more than 147 companies which are having turnover of more than 100
crores and are required to participate in the said project as per new Company Act.
1.3.20 In the village Kalsunpada, a company, Sterling Generators Pvt. Ltd., has taken up SANKALP
project Under CSR for transforming it as a model village by providing basic civic amenities,
community hall, etc. The nodal officer of the company explained about the local tradition and
attempts to change the lifestyle of the 90 houses of the village. The nodal officer also stated that
after a medical check-up in the village, it was found that some people of the village need extra

7
attention for their health. He apprised the Sub-Committee that they are facing problems in
convincing the villagers for their rehabilitation as villagers are reluctant to change their life style
and want to live in their kuchcha houses at the very same location with their animals. The
Company has therefore planned to build 6 pakka houses in first phase by demolishing some
kuchcha houses of the convinced villagers after shifting them to temporary accommodations to
construct pakka houses. They will be reverted back after completion of construction. He further
submitted that by observing them, other villages will follow and construction of more houses will
pick up. He further stated that they propose to complete the project within a period of three years.
1.3.21 The Committee understands that Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) can play an
important role in the socio-economic development of rural people. The vast majority of our
country’s poorest people live in villages and these villages are in a state of neglect and
underdevelopment. The problems of hunger, ignorance, ill health, high mortality and
illiteracy are most acute in rural areas. In this context, the business houses can supplement
the efforts of Governments.
1.3.22 The Committee while appreciating the efforts made by the UT Administration in
involving the industries through the Corporate Social Responsibility of adopting the villages
cautions that corporate should not be allowed to tamper with local culture, way of life, etc.
The Committee during the visit to the village noticed that most of the villagers are
accustomed to their way of life and in particular design of their houses which is proposed
to be changed. The UT administration should remain vigilant to check if CSR initiatives are
according to local needs and sensitivity. The Corporate houses involved in development
should also respect local sensitivity in terms of their culture, way of life etc.
1.4 ISSUES PERTAINING TO INDUSTRIES
1.4.1 The Sub-Committee during its study visit interacted with representatives of trade and
industry associations and Trade Union and other Associations of UTs of Daman and Diu and Dadra
and Nagar Haveli at Silvassa. During the interaction, following issues emerged before the Sub-
Committee:–
Tax Exemption
1.4.2 According to the UT administration, Dadra and Nagar Haveli is predominantly a backward
area both economically as well as industrially. After liberation from Portuguese regime in 1954 and
merger with the Union of India in 1962, the industrial development made a low key start in the
year 1965 by establishing a industrial estate under co-operative sector namely Dan Udyog Sahakari
Sangh Ltd.
1.4.3 The Sub-Committee was informed that in the beginning there was no sales tax leviable as
it was backward territory inhabited by Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. However, with the
increase in Industries, trade and commercial activities in the U.T., there was persistence from the
neighbouring States to discontinue the exemption of tax to avoid unhealthy competition of prices
among the neighboring States; it was decided to impose sales tax in the UT of Dadra and Nagar
Haveli. Thus, Sales Tax regime came into force from 1983 and the Industrial Units who so ever
established were eligible for sales tax exemption for the period of 15 years. This Scheme was in
force upto 1998. At present the newly established Units are getting the benefit of Central Sales Tax
exemption which is available upto the year 2017.
1.4.4 Further with the implementation of V AT Policy at all India level, the Dadra and Nagar Haveli
Regulation 2005 and Dadra and Nagar Haveli Value Added Rules 2005 were enforced with effect
from 01.04.2005. Thus at present following tax laws are in force.

● The Central Sales Tax Act, 1956
● The Central Sales Tax (Dadra and Nagar Haveli) Rules, 1983
● The Dadra and Nagar Haveli Value Added Tax Regulation, 2005

Industrial establishments in their profit and gains, for the 1st five years and the same were available

or before 30th March, 2002 were entitled for 100% income tax holiday for the 1st five assessment

CHAPTER-II
DAMAN AND DIU
2.1 INTRODUCTION
2.1.1 For over 450 years, the coastal enclaves of Daman and Diu on the Arabian Sea coast were
part of Portuguese India, along with Goa and Dadra and Nagar Haveli. Goa, Daman and Diu were
incorporated into the Republic of India on 19 th December, 1961 by military conquest. Portugal did
not recognize the Indian annexation of these territories until 1974. The territory of “Goa, Daman
and Diu” was administered as a single Union Territory until 30
th May, 1987, when Goa was granted
statehood, leaving Daman and Diu as a separate Union Territory.
2.1.2 Daman is on main land on sea-shore near southern portion of Gujarat State. Diu is an island
near Una Taluka of Junagarh District in Gujarat State. For administration purposes, there are two
Districts namely, Daman and Diu, two tehsils, two blocks, two towns, fourteen Village Panchayats
and twenty six villages in the UT with Daman as the Head Quarter of the UT with 100% of grant
from the Government of India in the form of Central assistance.
2.1.3 There is one parliamentary constituency and one District Panchayat in the UT. The
Committee was informed that Daman and Diu has the oldest history of urbanization as it has oldest
Urban Local Bodies viz. Municipal Councils. The total population of the UT is 2,42,911 with
Literacy rate at 91.48 per cent. The UT has total urban area of 24.26 sq. kms. with 36.25% of
the total population. There are two Municipal Councils one at Daman and the other at Diu. UT of
Daman and Diu does not have its own power generation. 93% of the electricity is consumed by
Industries. JERC determines the tariff for all classes of consumers.

CHAPTER-III
CHANDIGARH
3.1 INTRODUCTION
3.1.1 Chandigarh city recognized as the well planned, maintained, cleanest and greenest city of
the country is one of the best experiments in urban planning and modern architecture in the
twentieth century in India. Chandigarh derives its name from the temple of “Chandi Mandir” located
in the vicinity of the site selected for the city.
3.1.2 Since the medieval period through modern era of Indian history, the area was part of the
large Punjab Province which was divided into East and West Punjab during partition of the country
in 1947. The city was conceived to be made the capital of East Punjab and to resettle West Punjab
refugees coming from Pakistan. In 1948, Punjab Government, in consultation with the Government
of India, approved the area of the foothills of the Shivaliks as the site for the new capital. The
location of the city site was a part of the erstwhile Ambala district. The foundation stone of the
city was laid in 1952. Subsequently, at the time of reorganization of the State in 1966 into Punjab,
Haryana and Himachal Pradesh, this city was made the capital of both, Punjab and Haryana and
was declared as a Union Territory in the direct control of the Central Government.
3.1.3 After reorganization of Punjab in 1966, the Administration of the UT was under the Chief
Commissioner. From 1
st June, 1984, the Governor of Punjab took over the direct Administration of
the UT and the post of Chief Commissioner was re-designed as Adviser to the Administrator. The
Union Territory Administration is headed by the Administrator who is appointed by the President
of India under Article 239(2) of the Constitution of India. The Administrator is assisted by the
Adviser to the Administrator who usually happens to be an IAS officer of the AGMU cadre. The
Administration of Chandigarh follows the Punjab Municipal Corporation Law (Extension to
Chandigarh) Act, 1976 following which the Municipal Corporation of Chandigarh came into
existence in May, 1994.
3.1.4 The master plan of Chandigarh was prepared by the French architect Le Corbusier as
analogous to human body, with a clearly defined head (the Capitol Complex, Sector 1), heart (the
City Centre Sector-17), lungs (the leisure valley, innumerable open spaces and sector greens), the
intellect (the cultural and educational institutions), the circulatory system (the network of roads, the
7Vs) and the viscera (the Industrial Area). The concept of the city is based on four major
functions: living, working, care of the body and spirit and circulation. Residential sectors constitute
the living part whereas the Capitol Complex, City Centre, Educational Zone (Post Graduate Institute,
Punjab Engineering College, Punjab University) and the Industrial Area constitute the working part.
The Leisure Valley, Gardens, Sector Greens and Open Courtyards etc. are for the care of body and
spirit. The circulation system comprises of 7 different types of roads known as 7Vs. Later on, a
pathway for cyclists called V8 was added to this circulation system. Tree plantation and
landscaping has been an integral part of the city master plan. Different types of flowering and
various species of evergreen have been planted along the roads, in parking areas, shopping
complexes, residential areas and in the city parks.
3.1.5 According to UT Administration, Chandigarh was planned for a population of half-a-million.
In Phase I, 36 sq. km. of land was acquired by the city administration for construction of
25

26
30 sectors. Land for seventeen additional sectors (Sector 31 to 47) was acquired and developed
during the second phase to cater for a population of 350,000. The predominance of multistoried
apartments in the second phase provide for higher population dimension. However, Chandigarh has
now grown beyond its planned capacity. Hence, development in the third phase has started in
Sectors 48 and beyond. By 2021 the population of Chandigarh is projected to be around 19.5 lacs
(at current rate of growth) almost four times for which it was originally built.

firsthand assessment of some projects/schemes.

Smart School
3.2.5 The Sub-Committee visited a Smart school of UT of Chandigarh. This smart school in the
UT of Chandigarh has led to the classroom teaching going beyond the confines of text-books. The
Chandigarh Administration has conceptualized such schools with the objective of making learning
an enjoyable experience, integrating students with society and preparing them for future challenges,
developed a visionary plan for the roll out of ‘smart school concept.
3.2.6 According to the UT Administration, the educational content in smart school solution is
strictly mapped to NCERT books and can be easily customized to any State boards. In these
schools, emphasis has been given on the use of information and communication technology. The
class rooms in such schools are proposed to be equipped with Plasma Screens and other
peripherals. All educational services of the school will be interconnected and centralized with the
Principal, who will act as Nodal Officer for all the activities.
3.2.7 The Committee understands that in this electronic age, integrated e-teaching and
learning methodologies in our schools have become imperative and through establishing
smart schools, UT Government can fulfill goals of bridging digital divide and empowering the
future generation of the country. The Committee appreciates the modernization process of
schooling system with emphasis on interactive boards, multimedia and maximum use of
e-contents. The Committee hopes that these smart schools will go a long way in terms of
achieving excellence in academics, co-curricular area and the educational management. The
Committee recommends that more and more schools with such facilities should be set up
in the UT and existing schools should be converted into smart ones. This project should also
be implemented in other UTs and States should also be advised to embrace technology in

development, integration and maintenance of web-portal for various Departments of the
Administration. The Sampark Project provides 23 G2C services like payment of utility bills, issue
of bus passes, senior citizen card, disability identity card, birth and death certificates, disbursement
of pension for old age person, widows and disable persons, submission of RTI application, public
grievances etc. and 5 B2C services like payment of telephone bills of various telecom operators
via 12 e-Sampark centres spread across the city and 13 Gram Sampark centres in the villages of
UT of Chandigarh. On an average, around 200,000 transactions are made annually at the Sampark

the citizens of Chandigarh by providing the facility of making payments for the services being

3.2.10 The Committee understands that e-governance is two-way communication process
where benefits/services are delivered to people without procedural delays. In any citizen-
centric democratic system, cutting down on unwanted processes of too many layers while

Rajiv Gandhi Chandigarh Technology Park (RGCTP)
3.2.11 The Sub-Committee visited RGCTP in the city of Chandigarh. The Sub-Committee was
informed that Rajiv Gandhi Chandigarh Technology Park (RGCTP) is an extremely important
project for the Union Territory of Chandigarh as it provides world class integrated infrastructure
necessary for the setting up of facilities/campuses by leading technology companies and other IT/
ITES/BPO companies for the first time in this region. Chandigarh has traditionally been a city
where not many multi-national companies had earlier set up their facilities and therefore a large
number of professionals had left Chandigarh in the past for other cities, in search of high level
employment. The level of educational facilities here had been much higher than the level of
employment opportunities available, especially in the knowledge sector and RGCTP is a major step
in the direction of plugging this gap.
3.2.12 According to UT Administration, the vision was to establish a world class IT Park with
state of the art infrastructure including the provision of 100% availability of power and broadband
connectivity. As the Tier I cities like Bangalore, Hyderabad, NCR of Delhi were getting choked
because of the IT boom in India, meticulous planning and aggressive marketing of Chandigarh as
an IT destination placed Chandigarh on the national map as an excellent Tier II destination which
started attracting the attention of a lot of IT multinational companies. As such, huge demand of
IT space started pouring in and the area of 123 acres started looking small.
3.2.13 According to UT Administration, the development of RGCTP has been anchored by
Infosys, which has completed its state of the art campus. DLF is also offering ready to use built
up space and is already housing 37 IT Companies. These state of the art buildings are already
providing directly employment to more than 6000 professionals. IT majors like Wipro, Bharti Airtel,
Tech Mahindra, alongwith 21 other companies are in the process of developing their respective
sites allotted to them.
3.2.14 Apart from a Hotel cum Convention Centre, a T ech Habitat Centre is also under
development on a 123 acre plot under PPP model. This project has been planned taking into

of facilities/campuses by leading Technology Companies and other IT/ITES/BPO companies
for the first time in this region will help increasing employment generation for IT
professionals as well as development of information technology infrastructure in the UT. The

should be completed and allotments made. The Committee would however like to suggest
that development of infrastructure like roads, sewerage, drainage, connectivity etc. should
