REPORT
CHAPTER - I
SITUATION IN J&K IN THE  AFTERMATH OF FLOODS AND LANDSLIDES
1.1 According to background note as received from the Ministry of Home Affairs, the State
Government of Jammu and Kashmir stated that due to continuous rainfall in the region during
the week ending 03.09.2014, severe damage to life and property was caused in several
locations in different parts of State. Of the 22 districts of Jammu and Kashmir, 10 districts
reported higher than normal rainfall during the week ending 03.09.2014. In the following week
from 04.09.2014 to 10.09.2014 also, with the exception of Poonch and Samba districts, all the
remaining districts reported higher than normal rainfall. The excess of rainfall was 2,953% in
Shopian district and 1,410% in Srinagar district. Because of the very high rainfall, breach of
embankments and landslides occurred in different locations devastating different districts both
in Jammu region as well as in Kashmir valley and in particular, the State summer capital,
Srinagar which bore the burnt of the nature’s fury. According to Ministry of Home Affairs the
primary responsibility of the disaster management rests with the States and the Central
Government supplements it by providing logistics and financial support.
1.2 Apprising the Committee about the extent of the damage, the Ministry of Home Affairs
submitted that the following damages have been reported as per preliminary information
received from the State Government of J & K:
Districts affected 10 Districts -
Kashmir Div:- Anantnag, Kulgaom, Pulwama, Srinagar,
Budgam.
Jammu Div: Jammu, Rajouri, Poonch, Udhampur, Reasi.
No. of villages affected 5642 (2469 Kashmir + 3173  Jammu)
No. of Human lives lost 287 (91 Kashmir + 196  Jammu)
No. of Houses damaged 2.54 lakh
Cropped areas affected 6.51 lakh hectares
1.3 In addition, the infrastructure including road communication, telecommunications,
power, health, fuel distribution networks and drinking water supply system were also affected.
1.4 The background note as furnished by the Ministry of Home Affairs further gave details
of rescue and relief measures taken in the wake of floods and landslides in the State. Search
and rescue operations included deployment of Indian Army, IAF, Navy, NDRF Personnel,
Central Forces. More than 2.90 lakh persons were rescued to safer places and 2.92 lakh people

2
were evacuated by all agencies to safer places. About 2.14 lakh people were rescued by the
armed forces alone. 50,815 persons were rescued by NDRF teams, while 27,420 persons were
rescued by CRPF. It was brought to the notice of the Committee that Army deployed 329
columns (approx. 30,000 troops) along with 224 boats. 30 transport aircraft and 53 helicopters
were deployed by the Indian Air Force. Army also deployed 17 helicopters. Three teams of
MARCOS of Indian Navy were also deployed. 15 engineers of Indian Army were deployed with
necessary engineer stores and equipments.22 teams of NDRF consisting of 955 personnel along
with the necessary equipment were deployed for assisting State Government in search and
rescue operations. During the period 6.9.14 to 25.9.2014, more than 3000 air sorties were
done by Indian Air Force/ Army.
1.5 Under the Relief Operations, essential commodities including food packets were air
dropped. Food packets, baby food, water and medicines were sent to the affected areas. Relief
camps were organised at different places. 1,67,300 blankets and 4226 tents were sent. 4500.25
tons material including 1492.4 tons food/ ready food Packets etc., 605 tons water 1,31,500
food packets were dropped up to by IAF 24.09.2014.Army established 6 relief camps in
Kashmir Valley and 13 camps in Jammu division. Indian Red Cross Society supplied 1664 tents.
In addition, they sent 750 tarpaulins and 1000 Kitchen sets. 17 dewatering pumps were
dispatched to Srinagar for use by the State Government. All depots in J & K had sufficient
stock of food-grains. FCI released foodgrains to the State Government as per its requirement,
without advance payment, on top priority basis. During the month of September 2014, State
Government of J & K lifted 43,873 tons rice and 997 tons wheat for distribution under PDS/
floods relief in Kashmir Division. State Government has sanctioned six months free ration to
the affected families.
1.6 As regards the supply of drinking water, State Govt. informed that around 80% of
water supplies has been restored in Srinagar city. About 90% water supply had been restored
in Jammu city (i.e.  40 MGD out of 45 MGD). 28 water purification plants having a total
capacity of purifying around 6 lakh litres per day had been airlifted and handed over to the
State Government.
1.7 The background note further stated that for medical assistance, oxygen cylinders were
sent by Army. Mobile oxygen generation plant was also sent by Army. 23 types of medicines
including ORS, IV fluid, paracetamol syrup, anti-pyretics, anti-diarrhoeal, antibiotics and
antispasmodic, etc. were sent. A total of 170 metric tonnes of medicines were supplied. In
addition, 35 lakh chlorine tablets, 13.25 lakh doses of measles vaccine, 7.5 lakh doses of Oral
Polio Vaccine, 30000 bottles of Vitamin-A, 3000 doses of anti- rabies vaccine, 500 vials of Anti
Snake Venom and 25 MT of bleaching powder and one lakh Sanitary Napkins were also sent
to the State of J&K. Total 51 Specialist doctors (22 Physicians, 13 Pediatricians, 10
Gynecologists & 6 Anesthetists) were deployed in different hospitals of Kashmir. 500 kgs of
Malathion (decomposer) were sent to the State from Bhatinda by road. 100 PPE have been
supplied. State Government informed that all district hospitals were functioning and health
services were restored.
1.8 The Ministry of Home Affairs also stated that Telecommunications connectivity has
been partially restored in the State. However, the telecommunications continue to be unsteady
in patches. Free access was arranged for stranded people to enable them to call their home

3
places. The Committee was further informed that power supply in the State has been restored
by and large. Power supply was restored in all Hospitals (Govt. and Pvt.), water supply
stations, and relief camps. All 17 damaged 33/11 kV Substations in Jammu have been restored.
Out of 36 damaged 33/11 kV substations in Kashmir, 34 substations have also been restored.
1.9 The Ministry of Home Affairs further informed the Committee that adequate fuel stock
(ATF/MS/HSD/SKO) was kept at Srinagar . However, additional motor spirit/ high speed diesel/
LPG were sent by road into the valley. Over 3.2 lakh LPG cylinders, 9943 KL MS and 21472
KL HSD have reached Srinagar, as on 04-10-2014 (at 0900 hrs). Over 3.5 lakh LPG cylinders,
6838 KL MS and 16580 KL HSD was also dispatched to Srinagar. Of the total 45 ROs in
Srinagar, 42 ROs are operational. According to the Ministry, State Government informed that
there was no shortage of petrol, diesel, LPG and Kerosene Oil in the Valley.
1.10 The Committee was also informed that in order to restore road Communications, BRO
deployed 1462 persons, 20-Dozers, 24 Excavator and 18 JCB in the State. Important roads had
been opened for traffic.
1.11 The background note also stated that of the total 745 bank branches in Kashmir Division,
708 branches were functioning. Out of the total 854 A TMs of Banks, 544 A TMs were
functioning. In Jammu and Ladakh Divisions of the State, all branches/ A TMs, except one,
were functioning.
1.12 The Ministry of Home Affairs further stated that after the visit of the affected areas in
the State, the Prime Minister announced an additional special assistance of `1000 crore to the
State for flood relief and rehabilitation. He also announced an ex-gratia amount of ` 2 lakh
each to the next of kin of the deceased and `50,000/ each to persons who were grievously
injured, from the Prime Minster Relief Fund. The State Government has `1105.6 crore available
in their SDRF for meeting the expenditure for rescue and relief works.

CHAPTER - II
PRESENTATION BY THE UNION HOME SECRETARY AND THE REPRESENTATIVES OF
THE STATE GOVERNMENT OF J&K
2.1 The Committee in its sitting held on 10th October, 2014 heard the presentation of the
Union Home Secretary and the representatives of Ministry of Home Affairs on the situations
in J&K in the aftermath of flood and landslides. During the course of presentation, a brief
account of the devastation and its impact was reiterated as was given in the background note
which has already been explained in the Ist Chapter.
2.2 Apprising about the monitoring mechanism over the situation, the Committee was
informed that National Crisis Management Committee under the chairmanship of the Cabinet
Secretary reviewed the situation in the State from 06.09.2014 to 16.09.2014 on a daily basis.
The National Executive Committee under the Chairmanship of the Home Secretary reviewed the
rescue and relief efforts on 22.09.2014 and 01.10.2014. Joint Secretary (DM) of MHA
alongwith officers from other Ministries was stationed at Srinagar from 08.09.2014 to
13.09.2014 to coordinate relief and rescue activities . The Chairman of the NEC i.e. Home
Secretary camped in J&K from 11.09.2014 to 17.09.2014 to co-ordinate the efforts of all
Central Ministries and the State Government.
2.3 Reiterating about various relief operations the Committee was informed that has issued
instructions to the Life Insurance Companies to expeditiously settle the claims in the State of
J&K in the wake of floods. LIC and 4 other public sector companies nominated their nodal
officers for co-ordinating and expediting settlement of the claims. All public sector insurance
companies were directed to convene special camps to facilitate easy reporting and settlement
of claims.
2.4 The representatives of the Government of J&K stated that due to excessive rains, four
tributary rivers of Jhelum, namely Vaishav, Sandran, Lidder and Brengi, overflowed causing
increase in water level of river Jhelum. At various locations, the Jhelum was flowing very high
above the danger level. The Jammu Division also got affected due to overflow of various
rivers. In SuranPoonch the discharge of the river was 2 lac cusecs as against the normal of
50,000 cusecs while in Chenab river, the level was 50 feet as against the danger level of 27
feet. In Tawi the water level reached 33 feet against the danger level of 14 feet and in Ujj the
discharge was 1.4 lac cusecs as against 60,000 cusecs. In Basantar the level was six feet as
against the normal of 2 feet.
2.5 The Committee further took note of the areas which were affected due to flood and
landslides. The Districts of Anantnag, Pulwama, Shopian and Kulgam in Kashmir division and
the Districts of Poonch, Reasi and Rajouri in Jammu division got affected on 3rd and 4th of
September 2014. Other Districts of both the divisions got affected due to floods subsequently.
Srinagar city also was affected due to floods. Most of the residential colonies and commercial
areas of the Srinagar got submerged. The Committee was informed that during monsoons,
4

5
normally some of the areas of Jammu division experience flood like situation, however, during
September, 2014 the situation was worst and has not been witnessed since last few decades.
In Jammu most of the areas were affected due to flash floods and the effect remained for two
to three days. Whereas such flood situation in Kashmir, particularly in Srinagar, has not been
witnessed since more than 100 years i.e. 1902.The effect of floods in southern Kashmir
remained for more than a week whereas the Srinagar city was the worst affected. Large parts
of Srinagar city remained submerged for more than three weeks.
2.6 Apprising about the impact of devastation, the representative of Jammu and Kashmir
Government stated that there was severe impact of floods across the State particularly in
Srinagar city. All the important institutions like Civil Secretariat, High Court, Police Control
Room, Five major hospitals in Srinagar and other important offices remained submerged for
more than three weeks. Due to the effect of floods and submergence of major institutions,
the people had to suffer and the functioning of the administration was also adversely
affected. Entire communication network such as Telephone, TV station, Mobile Network, and
the internet etc got totally disrupted. Road/Rail connectivity, power and water supply was
severely affected. Health care was also affected due to submergence of the major hospitals
in the city.
2.7 The Committee was further informed of challenge before the State Administration
which inter-alia  was carrying out assessment of damages/losses and immediate disbursement of
relief, restoration of public infrastructure, removal of garbage and animal carcasses, restoration
of supply of essential commodities, documentation/preparation of a special financial package.
2.8 The representative of State Government of Jammu & Kashmir further apprised the
Committee about the assessment of loss/damages and disbursement of relief to the affected
people. It was stated that the damages to the public infrastructure and losses to the private
property were very large. As per preliminary assessment, the loss to the public infrastructure
has been assessed to the tune of Rs 7000 cr. approx. As per the norms, amount eligible for
temporary restoration of public infrastructure works out to the tune of Rs. 1747 cr approx.
The temporary restoration of public infrastructure is being fast tracked. Losses to the private
property were being assessed by the Insurance Companies. The amount of relief admissible for
loses on account of private property as per SDRF norms has been worked out to Rs.1200 cr
approx. The representative also stated that the assessment was carried out by the teams of
officers in each district. The disbursement of relief to private individuals as per existing SDRF
norms has already started.
2.9 Apprising about restoration of Public Infrastructure viz.  health, it was stated that
Control Room was set up and advisories were issued to the public for taking various
precautions.110 medical centers were affected due to floods. 107 have been already restored
in the rural areas. Remaining 3 will be operationalized soon. 5 major Hospitals in Srinagar
which were submerged, have started functioning again partially or fully. It was further stated
that more than 60 metric tons of medicines were provided either through camps or through
the hospitals and medical institutions. More than 9.00 lac children were vaccinated against
measles. More than 25 lac chlorine tablets were distributed.The district hospitals were further
augmented to cater to the need of the people. 12 rapid response teams were constituted for
reporting any suspected outbreaks. Due to poor connectivity, heli-dropping of medicines was

6
carried out in rural areas. Damaged equipments in major hospitals are being replaced. Regarding
drinking water schemes, it was stated that out of nearly 5000 water supply schemes, 3000
schemes suffered partial and major damages. Restoration work was taken up on war footing
basis and water supply has been restored in nearly 90% areas. Tanker service is also being
provided as an additional support. In order to provide pure drinking water 60 R.O. pumps have
been installed at various locations. Process of permanent restoration of various schemes has
been taken up.
2.10 As regards the road connectivity, it was stated that due to damage to roads and
bridges, the connectivity between various areas had got affected. Immediately after the water
level receded, steps were taken to restore the connectivity. Due to major damages at some
places, the temporary restoration was not possible as such diversions were provided. All areas
are presently connected. But due to some major damages at various locations, people have to
reach destination through longer routes.
2.11 Apprising about the Power supply, the Committee was intimated that in view of the
damage to 4207 substations and damage to more than 11000 kms of cables, the power supply
across the State had got disrupted. With the receding of water level the process of restoration
was initiated. In some areas the restoration work got delayed as transmission tower had
collapsed. 95% of the areas have been provided electricity and the remaining areas are being
provided electricity shortly. At most of the places, the above restoration has been done on
temporary basis and the process for permanent restoration has been initiated.
2.12 Regarding the irrigation and Flood Control, the representative of the State Government
stated that nearly 6483 works of I&FC department had suffered damages. The damages on one
side has affected irrigation facilities and on other hand flood protection bunds have severely
been damaged. Temporary steps have been taken for restoration of the damaged works,
however permanent restoration shall need huge resources.
2.13 About removal of garbage and carcasses, the Committee was informed that though the
floodwater level had receded in Srinagar but most of colonies remained water logged for more
than three weeks. 200 pumps were arranged and pressed into service. The process of
removing floodwater by pump has been completed. Removal of garbage from various flooded
areas was a big challenge. 31000 metric tons of garbage had been removed from various areas
of Srinagar city.1646 animal carcasses have been disposed off. All areas were provided with
disinfectants and chemicals and people were provided phenyl solution also for cleaning of their
residential houses.
2.14 Regarding Higher Education, the Committee was informed that infrastructure of 13 colleges
in Srinagar, Anantnag and Pulwama have suffered losses to the tune of Rs. 135.00 crore. Buildings,
labs and libraries have got damaged due to which the functioning of colleges has got affected.
Temporary arrangements have been made to make these colleges operational after safety audit.
2.15 The Committee was also informed that supply of essential commodities was monitored
by the State Government. The stocking of essential commodities to Leh , Kargil and accessible
areas in the State was being done. Free ration for the month of September stands distributed
to all the flood affected families. Supply position of petroleum products had been streamlined;
buffer stock for 20 days supply has been created.

(i) While the losses are much more, the entitlement of the State under SDRF is to

(ii) The norms fixed for payment of ex-gratia relief to the private individuals are too

(iii) The business/trading community in the State has suffered huge losses.
(iv) Under the SDRF norms, there is no provision to provide any assistance.
(v) Similarly as against the loss of `7000 crore of public infrastructure, the

(vi) State Government is not in a position to provide funds for permanent

(vii) Therefore for the revival of the economy of the State, a special dispensation is

(viii) In order to meet the above requirements and to ensure rehabilitation of the

(ix) The State Government shall need liberal financial assistance from Central

2.17 The Committee wanted to know whether the State Government and the people of
Jammu & Kashmir ware satisfied with the rescue and relief operation work in the aftermath
of flood and landslides. Responding to the Committee’s query the Principal Secretary,
Government of Jammu and Kashmir stated as under:-
“In the present circumstances, this is something which was not expected, something
which happened after more than one hundred years. But the turn-around has been very
fast. We received excellent cooperation from the Government of India. Probably what
happened, .....was that with the snapping of the telecommunication line, anybody who
was marooned in his mohalla, he thought probably he was the only one who had been
in that kind of a situation and why everybody else was not coming to his rescue, while
the situation was that the entire capital city was under water. So, they took some time
to reach him. That is one initial anger which was there. Other than that, .....the State
Government is okay with the pace of rescue.”

8
2.18 The Committee sought to know whether the meteorological department had not
forewarned the State Government that the intensity of rain could be higher than the normal and
whether any kind of preemptive measures were taken by the State Government in respect of
evacuation or other issues. Replying to the query, the Principal Secretary, Government of J&K
stated that the State Government did receive the forecast that normal rain would be more than
heavy but it continued for almost six days.
2.19 The Committee is concerned to observe that the State Government of Jammu and
Kashmir received forewarning that State would receive heavier rainfall than the normal
rain but the kind of preemptive measures taken by State Government were not
sufficient to withstand the fury of the nature and the result was heavy casualties in
terms of human loss and properties including public infrastructure in the State. The
Committee notes that in the previous year when Phailin struck Odisha, the State
Government of Odisha had done a commendable job in terms of evacuation and other
facilities that were provided but comparatively, Jammu and Kashmir had more death
toll.
2.20 The Committee further sought to know as to why Jammu region received a huge death
toll in comparison to Srinagar. Answering the specific question of the Committee, the
representative of the State Government submitted before the Committee as under:-
“We did receive a kind of rain forecast, but we did not really anticipate that it will
be of that heavy nature. But, boats were mobilized,.... In Kashmir, people were
normally not evacuated. If we look at the areas which were submerged and which
remained submerged, water had never entered these areas, Sir. The colonies, which we
were speaking of, like Badami Bagh Cantt., where the Army Corps Headquarter is
located, Rajbagh, Mahjong Nagar and other colonies are located, these are basically
flood plains which were meant to serve as flood plains. But what has happened is over
the last one hundred years, they have come to be heavily populated. On the night of
6th, advance warnings were mounted from the mosques and all over the people with
loud speakers did go around, but people living in those areas probably did not believe
that it will come to that kind of a situation where it will be water of ten feet or fifteen
feet, depending upon the depression........as river Jhelum flows through Srinagar, the
way it was designed is that it was designed to spill over to one side, north side, as
the river flows. So, the embankments of the river were also put in such a way that right
embankment was always higher than the left. But since these houses and colonies had
covered the flood plain, they thought that probably this is not going to come and this
is what happened. But with the announcement, people did come out of the houses. If
you look at the death toll, in the entire Kashmir Valley, it is 91, of which in the
Srinagar city, which remained submerged, it is around 50 because people had moved out
of their houses. People who didn’t heed to the warnings and wanted to remain in their
houses, were the ones who had to be evacuated later .”
2.21 While the Committee would like to convey its gratitude to the many personnel
and the agencies of Central Government particularly, the Ministry of Defence who had
done a splendid work even at the risk of their own lives in this J&K flood. Over the
last fifteen years, the country has seen quantitative and qualititative development in

9
national capabilities in the matter of dealing with natural calamities viz ., handling
Phailin, wherein the death toll was limited. In the past, in a similar calamity in 1999
in Odisha, the country had lost almost 11,000 lives but in these last 15 years, in various
parts of the country, both at the national level and at the State level, the capabilities
have improved a lot which include early warning systems and efficient systems and
procedures of early mobilisation. The Committee is quite confident that the Disaster
Management apparatus could have done a much better job in the recent calamities in
J&K had there been an early warning followed by resilient set-up of systems and
procedures and smooth coordination and communication in place in the State of J&K
enabling the NDRF and the State Rapid Action Force to perform their entrusted task in
time. The Committee feels that it is not just about early warning systems, evacuation
system is also of paramount importance because, even if the state has an early warning,
evacuating people becomes very difficult in the absence of effective and efficient
evacuation system. In view of the heavy toll of human lives coupled with number of
missing persons, the Committee believes that there have been some lapses in this
regard on the part of the State Government. The Committee in this regard notes with
appreciation that except some hiccups initially, the delivery system after the devastation
was put in motion. The Committee here would like to caution that the duty of the
Government does not end here, as there is huge task of rehabilitation and
reconstruction before it.
2.22 The Committee would like the Government to ensure that the relief has reached
the needy on the ground level and the rehabilitation work has taken off. Since J&K is
a strategic and a sensitive State therefore, it needs to be rebuilt without any
procrastination. The Committee would like to be apprised of the planning and the
concrete steps to rebuild the State. The Committee is of the considered view that the
central Government should not shrug off its responsibility in re-building the state by
taking the plea that activities concerning the long term rehabilitation programme fall
within the jurisdiction of the State Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Central Government should extend all support to the State Government at the
time of unprecedented crisis. In the effort for rebuilding that State, Central
Government should extend the requisite financial assistance to the State Government
and in fact both the Governments should work intandem in rebuilding the State. The
Committee therefore recommends that rehabilitation of affected people and
reconstruction of the infrastructure along with revival of economy in the State should
be taken up on utmost priority.
2.23 The Committee takes note of the submissions made by the representative of State
Government that while the losses are much more, the entitlement of the State under SDRF is
to the tune of `2947.20 crore only. The norms fixed for payment of ex-gratia  relief to the
private individuals are too meagre and cannot help the affected families for rehabilitation and
the business/trading community in the State has suffered huge losses. The Committee also
takes note of the fact that under the SDRF norms, there is no provision to provide any
assistance.
2.24 The Committee feels that the compensation amount given to victims is very low
because the guidelines regarding compensation amount, etc. were framed in 2001. The

10
Committee observes that the unprecedented flood situation in Jammu & Kashmir led to
collapse of the entire economy of J&K and immediate steps are required to help the
people who have lost their businesses. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government should undertake assessment of loss of assets and prepare comprehensive
rehabilitation and reconstruction plan. Concerted efforts must be taken to do early
rehabilitation and put the economy on the right path to get back the confidence of the
people of J&K.
2.25 The Committee would like to point out discrepancies between the reported
feedback and the relief mechanism engaged in distribution of relief packages by the
Government agencies. The Committee has been given to understand that the food
packages were being distributed to the people of J&K on the basis of the 2001 census.
It is worthwhile to mention here that since 2001, the population has increased at a
considerable rate. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should
take into account the concern of the people and 2011 census be made as the basis for
executing the long term rehabilitation plan.
2.26 The Committee also desires to highlight the apprehension of affected people of
the Jammu & Kashmir regarding compensation against damages to buildings during the
flood. The Committee were given to understand that compensation was being given to
people whose buildings was completely damaged, whether it was concrete house or mud
house. It was brought to the notice of the Committee that there were a number of
buildings which were severely damaged and either started shattering or are on the verge
of collapse and the owners of such buildings apprehend that they would not get
compensation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take
into account the concern of people whose buildings are in dilapidated conditions caused
due to floods.
2.27 The Committee observes that the presentation of the Ministry of Home Affairs
and State Government contained the assessment of land loss but none of the
Governments took into account the loss of cattles. The Committee understands that the
main source of the means of livelihood of the people of J&K is cattle, therefore, the
State Government should take into account loss of cattles during the flood. The
Committee recommends that the rehabilitation policy and plan must also take into
account compensation for loss of cattles so that the economy of affected people must
return to support their livelihood.
2.28 The Committee also takes into account the loss of land and the standing crops
which were totally washed away, which the Government would take into account but
siltation due to accumulation of mud, sand and stones on the land made the land
uncultivable. The Committee feels that such land may not be cultivable for a long time
unless the Government takes timely intervention for making such land cultivable. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should prepare Action Plan in
this regard too in order to enable the farmers to sow the crops without losing the
cropping cycle.
2.29 The Committee notes that even when the State of J&K had an early warning, the
State had not enough satellite phones available which resulted into break down of

11
communication system and there was no way to contact the officials at district level.
Secondly, even with an early warning, the personnel available with the State
Government were not trained, making them incapable to mobilize resources sufficiently
in advance.
2.30 The Committee is, therefore, of the view that in order to combat the natural
calamities/furies, the Central Government needs comprehensive National planning with
resilient system for better disaster management throughout the country, irrespective of
the frequency of disasters in a particular area/ region. For combating the possible
onslaught of natural fury, there is urgent need for better coordination between national
and State agencies. The Committee, therefore, feels that at the national level, the
country should have a much better pre-emptive action from the Central authorities,
particularly for the States which are not used to this kind of disaster frequently. The
Central Government should apprise the State Governments some kind of advanced
planning and mechanism that the State Governments must put in place invariably
without any failure. The Committee believes that the State Government must realize
the consequences of nature fury and should not be complacent at any time and must
have comprehensive planning for enhancing capabilities at the time of natural
calamities.
2.31 The Committee feels that States like J&K are not well prepared to combat
natural disasters and such States should not be caught on sleeping mode at the time of
disaster. The Committee, therefore, desires that training and updating of State
Government machinery should be on continuous basis and it should always be on alert
mode.
2.32 W ith regard to declaring the flood and the landslides in Jammu and Kashmir a national
calamity, the Committee notes the views expressed by the Home Secretary who deposed before
it as below:-
“As of now, ...., the quantum of relief that has been sent to the State of Jammu and

give the State of Jammu and Kashmir to get back on its feet and start resuming
normalcy there, is enormous. Earlier if you r emember, ...., last time also the same

12
2.33 While appreciating the feelings of the Home Secretary, the Committee feels
that resource reach was not there in the interior valley, particularly in those villages

that apart from all the issues of preventive planning, the reach of relief to the people

is not merely a question of providing relief to the people who are victims of natural

people in J&K, the Government should ensure that all the loopholes should be
plugged.

2.37 The Committee takes into account the funds provided to the State Government
of J&K by the Central Government. The Committee feels that funds so released by the
Central Government must be utilized for the purpose and its utilization must be under
close supervision and monitoring. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should constitute Joint Team consisting of the representative of State
Government and the Central Government for better administration and implementation
of programmes with fair deal of justice and equitable distribution.
2.38 The Committee desires to highlight that so far as Srinagar is concerned, it was
patently obvious that flood pathways that have been in existence since Moghul times
have all been heavily populated. The Committee notes the submission of the
representative of the State Government that the colonies like Badami Bagh Cantt.,
where the Army Corps Headquarter is located, Rajbagh, Mahjong Nagar are basically
flood plains which were meant to serve as flood plains. The Committee was given to
understand that there was rampant encroachment on river banks and natural drains, for
instances, in Poonch near Sher-e-Kashmir bridge there was reportedly a colony of 250
buildings and in another area there was brick kiln which were washed away by the floods.
It has also been alleged that the real estate in Jammu and Kashmir, especially, the
Srinagar Valley, has been rampantly violating the established  norms and modalities.
Needless to say it is well established fact that fiddling with natural courses of rivers and
drains by constructing buildings, etc, whether legal or illegal, will, not only, have adverse
impact on the ecology and environment but will also invite natural disasters. Knowing fully
well that these are the traditional pathways for the outflow of water, the Committee
wonders as to how the State Government and the administration permitted
constructions in such areas. The Committee observes that on both the banks of
Jhelum River where the disaster has taken place and in the major areas of Srinagar
city, there was water for three weeks. The Committee believes that the accumulated
water was not just allowed to flow through its normal and natural route, as the same
was blocked. The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure as to why the
local authorities allowed such encroachments on a large scale which led to such
disaster. The Committee is, therefore, of the considered view that the Government
should bring into force building bye laws keeping in view the topology of the State so
that encroachments on river banks are avoided.
2.39 Another aspect which drew the attention of the Committee relates to the role of
deforestation in inviting floods. It was given to understand that a lot of deforestation
has taken place in Jammu and Kashmir, and the successive Governments have not
addressed this. The Committee, therefore, recommends that as a long-term measure,
the Government must ensure that deforestation does not take place. The Committee
feels that State Government should also consider whether the natural disaster had been
preceded by any ecological disaster because we have experienced the most gruesome
situation in Uttarakhand very recently.

15
2.40 Responding to the Committee’s query relating to carrying capacity of rivers, the
Principal Secretary of J&K stated before the Committee as under:-
“ the total carrying capacity of River Jhelum is around 35,000 cusecs and another spill
channel which has been constructed some time back to take care of the overflowing
waters in case such a situation is around, is another 20,000 cusecs. Taken together,
Jhelum and spill channel can take care of only around 55,000 to 60,000 cusecs. That
is the best optimum capacity. ...., ... With that in background, since the year 2010, Sir,
the State Government has been in correspondence with the Government of India for
deepening and dredging River Jhelum and creating another spill channel so as to
exactly take care of this kind of situation. …….. We will try and pursue with the
Government of India. This project which we have submitted is worth around `2,200
crores.”
2.41 The Committee notes that it has become normal to ignore dredging aspect of the
water bodies be it sea or rivers and the projects for deepening and dredging hang fire
for long, gathering dust in the shelfs. The Committee takes serious note of this and
desires that dredging proposals of the rivers submitted by State Governments
particularly flood prone States should be cleared at the earliest so that the work on this
is finished before next monsoon. The Committee also desires that the State
Governments should be asked to adhere to the time limit.
2.42 The Committee was given to understand that Central Government grants `60
crores to the Government of Jammu & Kashmir to clean drains and rivers by removing
silt and sand but the related work had reportedly not been carried out. The Committee,
therefore, desires that Central Government should regularly monitor the works under
the sanctioned money.
2.43 Ministry of Home Affairs in its subsequent written reply about Study on floods in
Jammu and Kashmir, mentioned that the Ministry of Water Resources has constituted a three
member Group comprising of Chairman, Central Water Commission, Commissioner (Indus) and
Director, National Institute of Hydrology Roorkee on 18.09.2014 to conduct an in depth study
and analysis of the recent unprecedented floods in Jammu and Kashmir, so as to make suitable
recommendation along with a detailed action plan to deal with such threat in future.
Representative from the State Government of J&K and India Meteorological Department were
co-opted in the Group. The Group has finalized their report.
2.44 The Ministry further informed that the Group in its conclusions has pointed out that
the exceptionally heavy rainfall during 4th-6th September was the main cause of heavy flooding
in Jhelum, Chenab and Tawibasisn of J&K. During the 4th-6th September 2014, a lot of run
off was contributed from the higher catchment to the Srinagar valley. Due to lack of steep
slopes, the runoff caused severe drainage congestion and inundation in Srinagar and adjoining
areas. Earlier low lying areas along the course of River Jhelum were functioning as natural
flood detention basin during floods and were absorbing flood water spilling over the banks of
river Jhelum. Subsequently, the same flood water used to get released slowly. However, during
the last 3-4 decades, maximum urbanization has taken place in these low lying areas due to

16
which there is no space for water to get stored during flood season. The situation in Jhelum
basin has got further aggravated due to siltation and encroachments/development of various
waterways like river, lakes, marshy land etc resulting in limited carrying capacity of Jhelum
and water bodies.
2.45 The recommendations include non structural measures like flood forecasting and
disaster management as well as structural measures as channel improvement and construction
of additional supplementary flood spill channel.
2.46 The Committee notes that siltation and encroachments have been identified as
one of the causes of flood in the State. The Committee also notes that the Group has
also recommended measures viz.  non structural measures like flood forecasting and
disaster management as well as structural measures as channel improvement and
construction of additional supplementary flood spill channel. The Committee desires that
lessons should be learnt from this disaster to avoid recurrence. The Committee hopes
that the Government would examine the recommendations of the study group and would
come forward with resilient disaster management mechanism. The structural measures
as recommended should also be addressed without any delay.
2.47 The Committee would further like to stress that the Government must examine
the situation arising in the Jammu region of the State where there have been severe
landslides and it is reported that villages have been washed away. The Committee feels
that in addition to excess rainfall, such immense landslide may have been triggered by
some other factors. The Committee, therefore, desires the Government to examine
other factors, particularly, seismic factors that could be involved in the unfortunate
incident. The Committee recommends that the Government should set up an expert
group of scientists and geologists for detailed study about the factors/reasons which
could contribute in major landslides with the instruction to submit the report within
stipulated timeframe.
2.48 The Committee understands that the economy in Kashmir is mainly based on
tourism and the rains and floods have destroyed the entire tourism industry there. The
Committee wishes to point out that the paradise on earth has collapsed due to the flood
and the Government has to rebuild the paradise in order to attract tourists not only
from the country but also from abroad. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends
that a special Action Plan or a project should be prepared both by the State Government
and the Central Government, covering all the aspects of tourism while rebuilding the
State.
2.49 The Committee is not quite satisfied with the preparedness of rescue and relief
machinery and disaster Management set up in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The
Committee is of the opinion that there is no use of referring to the provisions of
National Disaster Management Act 2005 and to reiterate that Disaster Management
Activities fall within the jurisdiction of the State Government and Central Government
only provides logistic support to the State Government. Therefore, the moot issue is the
actual implementation of the provision of the Act. The Committee therefore,

17
recommends that necessary steps may be taken to strengthen the National Disaster
Management mechanism. The Committee has already given its One Hundred and
Seventy Eighth Report on Disaster Management in the Country. The Committee is of
the considered view that actual implementation of the recommendations contained in
that report would definitely lead to better functioning of disaster management
machinery at the national and State level.
2.50 The Committee feels that there should be a comprehensive plan with sufficient
funds to rebuild the State, rebuild its economy, its infrastructure. The Committee
understands that rebuilding the economy of J&K is a great challenge for both the State
and the Central Governments and both the Governments should give sufficient attention
to the programme of rebuilding the economy of the State within a set time frame.

OBSERV ATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS
OF THE COMMITTEE- AT A GLANCE
Insufficient Preemptive Measures
The Committee is concerned to observe that the State Government of Jammu
and Kashmir received forewarning that State would receive heavier rainfall than the
normal rain but the kind of preemptive measures taken by State Government were
not sufficient to withstand the fury of the nature and the result was heavy casualties
in terms of human loss and properties including public infrastructure in the State.
The Committee notes that in the previous year when Phailin struck Odisha, the
State Government of Odisha had done a commendable job in terms of evacuation and
other facilities that were provided but comparatively, Jammu and Kashmir had more
death toll. (para 2.19)
Requirement of Better Disaster Manangment Appratus in the State
While the Committee would like to convey its gratitude to the many personnel
and the agencies of Central Government particularly, the Ministry of Defence who had
done a splendid work even at the risk of their own lives in this J&K flood. Over the
last fifteen years, the country has seen quantitative and qualititative development in
national capabilities in the matter of dealing with natural calamities viz ., handling
Phailin, wherein the death toll was limited. In the past, in a similar calamity in 1999
in Odisha, the country had lost almost 11,000 lives but in these last 15 years, in various
parts of the country, both at the national level and at the State level, the capabilities
have improved a lot which include early warning systems and efficient systems and
procedures of early mobilisation. The Committee is quite confident that the Disaster
Management apparatus could have done a much better job in the recent calamities in
J&K had there been an early warning followed by resilient set-up of systems and
procedures and smooth co-ordination and communication in place in the State of J&K
enabling the NDRF and the State Rapid Action Force to perform their entrusted task in
time. The Committee feels that it is not just about early warning systems, evacuation
system is also of paramount importance because, even if the state has an early warning,
evacuating people becomes very difficult in the absence of effective and efficient
evacuation system. In view of the heavy toll of human lives coupled with number of
missing persons, the Committee believes that there have been some lapses in this
regard on the part of the State Government. The Committee in this regard notes with
appreciation that except some hiccups initially, the delivery system after the devastation
was put in motion. The Committee here would like to caution that the duty of the
Government does not end here, as there is huge task of rehabilitation and
reconstruction before it. (para 2.21)
18

19
Central Assistance In Rehabilitation And Reconstruction Programme
The Committee would like the Government to ensure that the relief has reached
the needy on the ground level and the rehabilitation work has taken off. Since J&K is
a strategic and a sensitive State therefore, it needs to be rebuilt without any
procrastination. The Committee would like to be apprised of the planning and the
concrete steps to rebuild the State. The Committee is of the considered view that the
central Government should not shrug off its responsibility in re-building the state by
taking the plea that activities concerning the long term rehabilitation programme fall
within the jurisdiction of the State Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the Central Government should extend all support to the State Government at the
time of unprecedented crisis. In the effort for rebuilding that State, Central
Government should extend the requisite financial assistance to the State Government
and in fact both the Governments should work intandem in rebuilding the State. The
Committee therefore recommends that rehabilitation of affected people and
reconstruction of the infrastructure along with revival of economy in the State should
be taken up on utmost priority. (para 2.22)
Proper Assessment Of Loss Of Assets And Adequate Compensation
The Committee feels that the compensation amount given to victims is very low
because the guidelines regarding compensation amount, etc. were framed in 2001. The
Committee observes that the unprecedented flood situation in Jammu & Kashmir led to
collapse of the entire economy of J&K and immediate steps are required to help the
people who have lost their businesses. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
Government should undertake assessment of loss of assets and prepare comprehensive
rehabilitation and reconstruction plan. Concerted efforts must be taken to do early
rehabilitation and put the economy on the right path to get back the confidence of the
people of J&K. (para 2.24)
Census 2011 As Basis For Executing The Long Term Rehabilitation Plan
The Committee would like to point out discrepancies between the reported
feedback and the relief mechanism engaged in distribution of relief packages by the
Government agencies. The Committee has been given to understand that the food
packages were being distributed to the people of J&K on the basis of the 2001 census.
It is worthwhile to mention here that since 2001, the population has increased at a
considerable rate. The concern of the people and 2011 Census be made as the basis for
executing the long term rehabilitation plan. (para 2.25)
Compensation For Dilapidated Conditions Of Buildings
The Committee also desires to highlight the apprehension of affected people of
the Jammu & Kashmir regarding compensation against damages to buildings during the
flood. The Committee was given to understand that compensation was being given to
people whose buildings were completely damaged, whether it was concrete house or mud
house. It was brought to the notice of the Committee that there were a number of

20
buildings which were severely damaged and either started shattering or are on the verge
of collapse and the owners of such buildings apprehend that they would not get
compensation. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take
into account the concern of people whose buildings are in dilapidated conditions caused
due to floods. (para 2.26)
Compensation For Loss Of Cattles
The Committee observes that the presentation of the Ministry of Home Affairs
and State Government contained the assessment of land loss but none of the
Governments took into account the loss of cattles. The Committee understands that the
main source of the means of livelihood of the people of J&K is cattle, therefore, the
State Government should take into account loss of cattles during the flood. The
Committee recommends that the rehabilitation policy and plan must also take into
account compensation for loss of cattles so that the economy of affected people must
return to support their livelihood. (para 2.27)
Action Plan For Uncultivable Land
The Committee also takes into account the loss of land and the standing crops
which were totally washed away, which the Government would take into account but
siltation due to accumulation of mud, sand and stones on the land made the land
uncultivable. The Committee feels that such land may not be cultivable for a long time
unless the Government takes timely intervention for making such land cultivable. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should prepare Action Plan in
this regard too in order to enable the farmers to sow the crops without losing the
cropping cycle. (para 2.28)
Training Of District/State Personnel For Better Disaster Management
The Committee notes that even when the State of J&K had an early warning, the
State had not enough satellite phones available which resulted into break down of
communication system and there was no way to contact the officials at district level.
Secondly, even with an early warning, the personnel available with the State
Government were not trained, making them incapable to mobilize resources sufficiently
in advance. (para 2.29)
Comprehensive National Planning
The Committee is, therefore, of the view that in order to combat the natural
calamities/furies, the Central Government needs comprehensive national planning with
resilient system for better disaster management throughout the country, irrespective of
the frequency of disasters in a particular area/ region. For combating the possible
onslaught of natural fury, there is urgent need for better coordination between national
and State agencies. The Committee, therefore, feels that at the national level, the
country should have a much better pre-emptive action from the Central authorities,
particularly for the States which are not used to this kind of disaster frequently. The

21
Central Government should apprise the State Governments some kind of advanced
planning and mechanism that the State Governments must put in place invariably
without any failure. The Committee believes that the State Government must realize
the consequences of nature fury and should not be complacent at any time and must
have comprehensive planning for enhancing capabilities at the time of natural
calamities. (para 2.30)
Alert State Disaster Machinery
The Committee feels that States like J&K are not well prepared to combat
natural disasters and such States should not be caught on sleeping mode at the time of
disaster. The Committee, therefore, desires that training and updating of State
Government machinery should be on continuous basis and it should always be on alert
mode. (para 2.31)
Inadequate Reach Of Relief/Resource To The People
While appreciating the feelings of the Home Secretary, the Committee feels
that resource reach was not there in the interior valley, particularly in those villages
which are known to have extremism problem. It was pointed out to the Committee
that apart from all the issues of preventive planning, the reach of relief to the people
and other things was grossly inadequate despite the claim of both the Central
Government and the State Government that there was no dearth of resources. It was
also pointed out that there was increased feeling among the affected people that relief
was not reaching to them inspite of generous help from all quarters/ countries. The
Committee in this background is of the opinion that both the Central Government and
the State Government should understand the complexities involved in the matter as
the problem is not merely a question of providing relief to the people who are victims
of natural disaster but of winning hearts with relief service in their distress. The
Committee feels that if there is any truth in the allegation that relief is not reaching
the affected people in J&K, the Government should ensure that all the loopholes
should be plugged. (para 2.33)
Close Monitoring Of Utilisation Of Funds By Joint Team
The Committee takes into account the funds provided to the State Government
of J&K by the Central Government. The Committee feels that funds so released by the
Central Government must be utilized for the purpose and its utilization must be under
close supervision and monitoring. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should constitute Joint Team consisting of the representative of State
Government and the Central Government for better administration and implementation
of programmes with fair deal of justice and equitable distribution. (para 2.37)
Rampant Encroachment On River Banks And Natural Drains
The Committee was given to understand that there was rampant encroachment
on river banks and natural drains, for instances, in Poonch near Sher-e-Kashmir bridge

22
there was reportedly a colony of 250 buildings and in another area there was brick kiln
which were washed away by the floods. It has also been alleged that the real estate in
Jammu and Kashmir, especially, the Srinagar Valley, has been rampantly violating the
established norms and modalities. Needless to say it is well established fact that fiddling
with natural courses of rivers and drains by constructing buildings, etc, whether legal
or illegal, will, not only, have adverse impact on the ecology and environment but will
also invite natural disasters. Knowing fully well that these are the traditional pathways
for the outflow of water, the Committee wonders as to how the State Government and
the administration permitted constructions in such areas. The Committee observes that
on both the banks of Jhelum River where the disaster has taken place and in the major
areas of Srinagar city, there was water for three weeks. The Committee believes that
the accumulated water was not just allowed to flow through its normal and natural
route, as the same was blocked. The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure
as to why the local authorities allowed such encroachments on a large scale which led
to such disaster. The Committee is, therefore, of the considered view that the
Government should bring into force building bye laws keeping in view the topology of
the State so that encroachments on river banks are avoided. (para 2.38)

addressed this. The Committee, therefore, recommends that as a long-term measure,

PREFACE 
 I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliame ntary Standing Committee on Home 
Affairs having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, do hereby present 
this One Hundred Eighty Third Report on the Problem s being faced by Refugees and Displaced 
Persons in J & K. 
2. The erstwhile Department-related Parliamentary S tanding Committee on Home Affairs  on 
receiving request from representatives of Refugees and Displaced persons in J&K, heard the 
presentation of the Home Secretary and representati ves of the following organizations on the 
problems being faced by them:- (i) West Pakistan Re fugees; (ii) Pakistan Occupied Kashmir 
Refugees; and (iii) POJK (CHAMB) of 1947, 1965 and 1971 in its meeting held on 30 
th  July, 2013. 
3.  The  previous Committee had constituted a sub-Committee on Action Taken on 137 th  Report 
on Rehabilitation of J & K Migrants (List of Member s of sub-Committee-Annexure). The sub-
Committee visited Jammu and Kashmir from 5 th  to 7 th  November, 2013.    During the visit, the sub-
Committee had also occasion to meet representatives  of Refugees and Displaced persons in Jammu 
and Kashmir also whose historical background and pr oblems were found to be different from J& K 
Migrants.   The sub-Committee apprised the Committe e that it would be better if the Committee gave 
a separate report on the problems being faced by Refugees and Displaced Persons in J & K.   Keeping 
in mind the complexity of the issues involved and n ature of long pending grievances of the affected 
communities, the Committee decided to give a report  on the subject separately. However, the 
previous Committee could not consider the report due to general elections, 2014. 
 
4. The present Committee in its meeting held on 16 th  September, 2014 took up this subject for 
detailed examination and report. The Committee in i ts meeting held on 21 st  October, 2014, heard the 
presentation of the representatives of Ministry of Home Affairs on the subject.  In its subsequent 
meeting held on 11 th  November, 2014, the queries of Members raised duri ng its sitting on 21 st  
October, 2014 were duly replied by the Home Secretary and representatives of Government of J&K. 
 
5.       The Committee while finalizing its report, relied on the following papers/documents:- 
(i)    Background note and supplementary background  note furnished by the Ministry of 
Home Affairs; 
 (ii)   Oral evidence of non-official witnesses and  official witnesses; 
(iii) Comments of Ministry of Home Affairs on the m emoranda received from various 
organizations; and 
(iv)   Replies to the queries of Members raised dur ing its sittings.  
 
6.  The Committee in its sitting held on 18 
th  December 2014 considered and adopted the report.  
 
7. For facility of reference and convenience, obser vations and recommendations of the 
Committee have been printed in bold letters in the body of the Report.

CHAPTER I 
THE REFUGEES AND DISPLACED PERSONS IN  J&K 
1.1 INTRODUCTION  
1.1.1 The background note as furnished by the Minis try of Home Affairs states that at the time of 
partition which was followed by tribal invasion, mo re than 7000 families crossed to this side of the 
LoC and International Border from PoJK and the then  Western Pakistan.  Later on, during Indo-Pak 
wars of 1965 and 1971, nearly 10,000 families got d islocated from 47 villages of Chhamb area.  The 
families who had to migrate on various occasions since 1947, are categorised as under:- 
(i)  West Pakistani Refugees of 1947;    
(ii)  PoJK Refugees of 1947; 
(iii)  Chhamb Displaced Persons of 1965; 
(iv)  Chhamb Displaced Persons of 1971 (Camp); 
(v)  Chhamb Displaced Persons of 1971 (Non-Camp).  
   
1.2 WEST PAKISTANI REFUGEES           
1.2.1 The background note points out that as per th e report of the Wadhwa Committee of 2007 
constituted by the Government of J&K, around 5,764 families consisting of 47,215 persons migrated 
from West Pakistan and got settled mainly in differ ent areas of Jammu, Kathua and Rajouri Districts 
of Jammu Division.  No land was allotted to them by  the State Government.  However, these families 
had occupied 45,466 kanals of land (State land 10,4 78 kanals, Evacuee land including other types of 
land 25,976 kanals and other land (10,012 kanals) w hich was allowed to be retained by them without 
conferring upon them the title of land because of t heir non-permanent resident staus of the State.  
Lands upto 12 acres of Khushki (unirrigated) or 8 a cres of Aibi Land (irrigated),  subject to certain 
conditions were allowed to be retained by them.  As  a result, 46,466 kanals of State/EP land stands 
retained by these refugees under Cabinet Order No. 578-C of 1954.          
1.2.2 The Ministry of Home Affairs further informed  that the West Pakistani Refugees settled in 
Jammu and Kashmir  are very much the citizens of India. They have the right to vote in Parliamentary 
Elections but they do not enjoy voting rights to th e State Assembly and Local Bodies.  There is no 
provision of separate citizenship for the State.  However, they are not permanent residents of the State 
in terms of the J&K Constitution, therefore, these families could not be provided the benefits which 
had been provided  to PoJK refugees. The West Pakistani Refugees families can't avail the benefits of 
various social welfare schemes launched by the Stat e Government and the members of their families 
can seek neither Government employment in the State nor admissions in various professional colleges 
of the State.  No other benefits of any kind have been granted to these refugees.   
1.2.3 The Ministry of Home Affairs apprised the Com mittee about the problems/issues concerning 
West Pakistani Refugees which are enumerated  below:- 
(i)  Permanent Resident Right, right to contest in State  Elections, right to purchase property and 
recruitment to State Services, issuance of Domicile  Certificate/Caste Certificates :- The most 
important issue of Permanent Resident Right to West  Pakistani Refugees is under 
consideration of the Cabinet Sub Committee headed b y Finance Minister of the State.  The 

 11 
Committee has not yet formed a view.  Once the issu e is decided about the Permanent 
Resident’s Right, all other subsidiary benefits would follow automatically.   
(ii)   Right to Education in Technical/Professional Instit utes in the State :  The State Government 
was requested to consider the issue.  However, the State Government has not yet examined the 
possibility of issuing appropriate executive directions in this regard.  State Government should 
consider this issue as it is not linked to the Permanent Resident status  of these persons. 
(iii)  Extension of Credit facilities by banks with out collateral security : The State Government had 
informed that directives were issued to all the Dep uty Commissioners and as a result, no 
collateral security is required for loan upto Rs. 1 0 lakhs, and the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust 
for Micro and Small Enterprises extends loans of ab ove Rs. 10 lakh without collateral 
guarantee . 
(iv) Special financial package for rehabilitation :  It was informed by the State Government that 
they are in the process of submitting financial pro posal for rehabilitation to this Ministry.    
The total number of WPR families settled in the Sta te is 9,823 and retention of land was 
allowed by the State Government on per family basis .  State Government informed that it is 
not possible to say whether these refugees were all owed to retain land in proportion to the 
land left behind in the West Pakistan.    As per status in 1947, 4,745  families were 
given 45,466 canal of irrigated/unirrigated land.   No West Pakistani refugees settled in J&K 
received any assistance from the Ministry of Rehabi litation by way of allotment of 
construction of houses. 
1.3  DISPLACED PERSONS FROM POJK OF 1947.  
1.3.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs apprised the Com mittee that in the wake of Pakistani 
aggression in Jammu and Kashmir in 1947, mass exodu s of population from Pak occupied area of 
Kashmir (POK) took place.  The Ministry of Home Aff airs also stated that as per the available 
records, 31,619 families were registered with the R ehabilitation Organisation, out of which 26,319 
families opted to settle down within the State itse lf and 5,300 families settled outside the State of 
J&K (Delhi 1,901 families, Maharashtra 123 families , Rajasthan 495 families and other States 2,781 
families).  Out of 26,319 families, around 22,719 families opted to settle in rural areas, whereas 3,600 
families settled in urban areas.  However, no claim s for compensation in lieu of the properties left 
behind by these displaced persons were invited by t he Government of India as POJK was treated as 
an integral part of India. The Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 and the 
Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950 are not applicable to the State of Jammu and Kashmir. 
1.3.2 In order to mitigate the hardship of these fa milies, the Government of India decided to provide 
ex-gratia/rehabilitation assistance.  The details o f the rehabilitation assistance sanctioned   from t ime 
to time are given below:-  
(a) Assistance sanctioned in 1947-48: 
Rural Settlers 
  (i) 2-3 acres of irrigated land or 4-6 acres of uni rrigated land per family;  
(ii)  Rs.1,000/- per family as ex-gratia payment;   
(iii) For the State land allotted, ownership rights  were conferred on allottees in 1965;   

 12 
(iv) For evacuee land allotted, the State Govt. has  stated that occupancy tenancy rights 
were given under the Agrarian Reforms Act.  (These rights are more or less absolute in 
the sense that the allottees can transfer the right  of occupancy tenancy by sale, gift or 
exchange without permission of Government);   
(v) 46 Basties constructed by rural settlers on the ir own were regularized under the Slum 
Improvement Scheme of J&K.   
 
Urban Settlers  
(i)  Ex-gratia cash payment of Rs.3,500/- per family;   
(ii)  1600 residential quarters were constructed and allo tted by the Government of Jammu & 
Kashmir in Udhampur and Nowshera. Cost of the struc ture was deducted from the ex-
gratia grant of Rs.3,500/- per family.   
(iii)  In 123 cases, plots were allotted in Jammu by the State Housing Board free of cost.   
 
(b)  Rehabilitation packaged sanctioned in 2000 : The rehabilitation package sanctioned by 
Govt. of India in 2000 comprised of the following:  
(i)   Ex-gratia payment of Rs.25,000/- per family;  
(ii)   Cash compensation in lieu of land deficiency @ Rs. 5,000/- per kanal;  
(iii)            An amount of Rs.2 crore to be prov ided for the allotment of plots to  the displaced 
persons who have already been settled in urban area s of  J&K and who have not been 
allotted plots  in the past;  
(iv)              Rs.25 lakh for improvement of civic amenities in 46 regularized colonies.   
 
(c)   Rehabilitation package sanctioned in 2008: In 2008, Govt. of India sanctioned Rs.49 crore 
to the State Govt. of J&K for providing cash compen sation in lieu of land deficiency by increasing 
the amount from Rs.5,000/- per kanal to Rs.25,000/-  per kanal subject to a ceiling of Rs.1.5 lakh per 
family and Rs.2 lakh to be provided in lieu of plot s to the urban settlers, who have not been allotted  
plots in urban areas.   
 According to report of the State Govt. of J&K, in order to rehabilitate the Pakistan occupied 
Kashmir displaced persons of 1947.  For this, about  6,80,850 kanals of EP land and about 2,43,000 
kanals of State land were allotted to these familie s by the State Government.  Absolute ownership in 
respect of the State land allotted to Pakistan occu pied Kashmir Displaced Persons of 1947 was also 
granted by the State Government.  The State Govt. h as also granted occupancy right in respect of EP 
(Evacuee Property) land allotted to these displaced  persons.  As per the occupancy right given, the 
displaced persons will have 99% share and the perso ns who have migrated to PoJK will have 1% 
share.  The displaced persons who chose to settle i n urban areas, have been provided 1,628 quarters 
and 793 plots in 6 colonies.   
 
(d)    Disbursement made by the State Government  
Between March 2002 to March, 2004, an amount of Rs. 6.17 crores was released to the 
Government of J&K for providing relief assistance t o DPs from PoJK for implementation of the 

 13 
relief package announced in 2000.  In 2008, on the recommendation of the State Govt. of J&K, an 
amount of Rs.49 crore was released to the State Gov t.  It was also informed that out of Rs.55.17crore 
released so far, 2550 families have received the cash compensation to the tune of Rs. 31.07 crore.   
1.3.3  As per the scheme the following disbursement has be en made by the State Government till 
September, 2014: 
 
(i) Ex-gratia payment of Rs.25,000 per family :- Ou t of 1011 applications received  and 
verified, 1010 applications have been rejected and only one reimbursement has been made. As 
reported by the State Government the verifying comm ittee has rejected 1010 applications on  
the  ground that their monthly income  was more tha n Rs. 300 per month at the time of 
migration and in many cases only application forms were received without the supporting 
documents;   
(ii) Cash compensation in lieu of land deficiency @  Rs.5000 per kanal which is now revised to 
Rs.25,000 per kanal subject to a maximum of Rs.1.5 lakh per family:- The Committee was 
informed that out of 4988 claims received, 3948 cla ims have been verified.  Of these, 1028 
claims have been rejected, 2841 approved and cash c ompensation given in 2524 cases and 79 
cases are being re-verified;   
(iii) Allotment of plots to the DPs who have alread y been settled in urban areas of the State but not 
allotted any plot, payment of Rs.2 lakh per family instead of plot:-  As per the report  received 
from the State Govt., out of 198 applications recei ved by them, 48 applications were found 
complete. Out of these, 18 applications were placed  before the verification committee, of 
which 6 applications have been approved, 2 have bee n rejected and in 10 cases reverification 
is required. Remaining 30 applications will be placed before the verification committee; 
  (iv) Improvement of Civic Amenities in 46 recogni zed colonies:-  The State Government has 
constituted a Committee to prepare a survey report for improving the civic amenities in the 
recognized colonies.  However, the survey report has not yet been finalized by the State Govt.   
 
1.4 DISPLACED PERSONS OF 1965 (CHHAMB) 
1.4.1  The Committee was informed by the Ministry of Home Affairs that during 1965  Indo- Pak 
War, people from Chhamb Niabat migrated to Jammu an d some of them settled in some villages of 
Jammu District.  They did not go back to their nati ve place after the end of 1965 war and settled 
within the State. 
1.4.2 The Ministry also stated that according to th e State Govt. the displaced persons of 1965 war 
have already been rehabilitated.  Though the issues  of conferment of ownership right/occupancy right 
of allotted State/EP land are under consideration o f the State Govt., a proposal to pay cash assistanc e 
in lieu of land deficiency to some of the DPs of 19 65 is under consideration of State Government and 
a proposal in this regard would be submitted to MHA  for consideration. The Ministry also informed 
that the State Government’s proposal is awaited.  
 
1.5 CHHAMB DISPLACED PERSONS, 1971 (CAMP)  
1.5.1 The Ministry of Home Affairs apprised the Com mittee that as a result of delineation of the 
Line of Control along the Jammu and Kashmir border following the Shimla Agreement, the Chhamb 

 14 
Niabat area comprising about 39,000 acres of land i n Jammu and Kashmir fell on the Pakistan side of 
the Line of Control.   Over 18,000 persons comprisi ng about 4,600 families who had been uprooted 
from this area, were immediately provided relief as sistance in camps situated at Kishanpur, Manwal 
at a distance of about 70 kms. from Jammu. 
1.5.2 The Committee was intimated that  with a view  to ensuring effective and expeditious 
resettlement of these displaced persons, the then M inistry of Labour and Rehabilitation, Government 
of India set up a joint team headed by Chief Secret ary, Jammu and Kashmir to examine the problem 
of permanent resettlement of the Chhamb refugees and to propose measures.  On the recommendation 
of the joint team, a Central Authority, namely, Chh amb Displaced Persons Rehabilitation Authority 
(CDPRA) was constituted in 1974 under the chairmans hip of Chief Secretary, Jammu and Kashmir.   
Under different schemes implemented through the CDP RA, the families of displaced persons from 
Chhamb were accommodated in relief camps and subseq uently rehabilitated in Jammu and Kashmir 
in a phased manner.  The details of relief granted are as under :-  
(i) Eligible urban families were given grants to th e tune of Rs.14,800/- which included 
housing grant of Rs.7,500/- per family, ad-hoc main tenance grant of Rs.800/- per family, 
special resettlement grant of Rs.500/- per family, milch cattle grant of Rs.1,000/- per 
family, grant of Rs.3,000/- for construction of shop per family, grant of Rs.2,000/- for other 
structural requisites in shop per family, and loan per family of Rs.5,000/-.   
 (ii) The agricultural families were given 4 acres of irrigated or 6 acres of un-irrigated land per 
family.  Government of India had agreed to pay cost  of deficiency of land allotted @ 
Rs.5,000/- per kanal.  In addition, they were given  Rs.13,500/- rehabilitation grant which 
inter alia included housing grant of Rs.7,500/- per  family, ad-hoc maintenance grant of 
Rs.800/- per family, special resettlement grant of Rs.500/- per family, milch cattle grant of 
Rs.1000/- per family, grant of Rs.2,000/- for purch ase of bullock per family, seeds and 
fertilizers grant of Rs.1200/- per family, agricult ural implements grant of Rs.500/- per 
family, in addition to a, loan of Rs.1,875/- per family.   
(iii) Special assistance for widows and destitutes was given which inter alia included pension of 
Rs.60/- per month, ad-hoc maintenance grant of Rs.3 00/-, special resettlement grant of 
Rs.100/-, housing grant upto Rs.5000/- and small housing plots.   
1.5.3 The Ministry further stated that out of total  number of 4600 families in Chhamb 1971 (camp) 
category, 3900 families were allotted land.  Rest o f the families were excluded because some (300)

2.1.7 In the Committee's sitting held on 11 th  November, 2014, the representative of Government o f

2.1.8 Clarifying on the issue, the Home Secretary d eliberated in detail before the Committee which 
is as under:- 
"J&K has a particular law known as the Permanent Re sident Laws.  Earlier, it used to be 
known as the State Subject Law when the Maharaja wa s ruling.  Under the Permanent 
Residency Right, you can be deemed to be a permanen t resident only if you fulfil the 
norms prescribed under that law.  And the law says,  that you can be a permanent resident 
if you were the owner of land and property, sahib-e -jaidad, of J&K in the year 1944.  The 
law in 1944 in J&K specified that to be able to purchase land in the State of J&K, you had 
to be a resident in the State for a minimum of ten years.  So, in effect, what it means is that 
if you were living in the State since 1934, you cou ld own land in 1944.  If you were living 
in the State prior to that, you could obviously own  land earlier than that.  The 
fundamental requirement of being a permanent reside nt in J&K was that you should have 
ownership of land.  It could be as small as a few s quare feet or as large as the law 
permitted. A person, who was not a Permanent Reside nt or a State Subject, as it was 
called then, could not own land in the State of Jam mu and Kashmir, and if you did not

own land in the State of Jammu and Kashmir, you wer e not a State Subject.  So, you were 
automatically denied or deprived of certain facilit ies that were available to the State 
Subjects.  After 1947, when the nomenclature of ‘St ate Subject’ was converted to 
‘Permanent Resident’, it was called ‘Permanent Resi dent Certificate’.  Earlier, it used to 
be known as ‘State Subject Certificate’.  So, when the Permanent Resident Certificate law 
was brought into being, the fundamental requirement of the ownership still remained."
